drills.title: Pump Panel Evolution: Two Lines, Correct Pressures
drills.solo_note: An instructor calls mid-evolution changes and scores time to first water

solo_variant.substitutions: Instructor's mid-evolution changes become a shuffled deck of hose-lay cards you wrote in advance. Phone stopwatch on the running board replaces the timer. Voice recorder replaces the scorer — you call every pressure out loud and check the math later against a written key.
steps: Run this DRY. Wheels chocked, apparatus in the yard, no charged lines and no nozzle unattended. There is nobody to shut your water down if a line gets away from you.
Build the deck first, at the kitchen table: 25 cards, each a lay — length, diameter, nozzle type and pressure, elevation up or down. Write the correct pump discharge pressure on the back.

Full arrival sequence on the clock: transmission to pump, confirm the pump-engaged indicator, parking brake, tank-to-pump open, hand on the discharge. Stop the clock at the point where you would open the valve. Repeat until the sequence is identical every time without looking.
Flash rounds: start the recorder, draw a card face up, say the friction loss and the pump discharge pressure out loud inside 15 seconds, then flip the card and check.
Chain the cards: draw two, pump both lines in your head, then draw a third card that says 'line 1 shut down' or 'add 100 ft to line 2' and re-state both pressures.

Blind panel walk: stand at the panel and touch each control in the order you would use it, naming it out loud — governor, relief, tank fill, individual discharges, drains. Do it once with your eyes shut.
Review the recording. Any answer over 15 seconds or outside 5 psi goes back into the deck for the next block.
solo_variant.self_score: Stopwatch the dry arrival sequence — repeatable under 20 seconds with no missed step. Flash rounds: count cards correct within 5 psi and under 15 seconds; target 23 of 25. Blind panel walk: every control found first touch.
solo_variant.not_covered: This is the math and the muscle memory only. It does not cover water — no governor behavior under real flow, no relief valve set, no surge when the second line opens, no tank-to-hydrant transition, no feel for a line going soft. Time to first water cannot be trained solo. You still need a crew day for the wet evolution.

drills.objective: From arrival, engage the pump, supply an attack line at correct pressure within 60 seconds, then add a second line of different diameter without disturbing the first.
drills.setup: Engine staged as if arriving. Lines pre-connected. Operator alone at the panel.
steps: Arrival sequence: transmission to pump, parking brake, throttle discipline, tank-to-pump open.
Charge line 1 (1.75 in) to the calculated pressure for the load; verify at the gauge.
Announce and open line 2 (2.5 in) while managing the pressure change — line 1 must not surge or starve.
Transition from tank water to hydrant supply (if available) without interrupting flow.
Instructor calls changes: 'Line 1 shut down,' 'Add 100 ft to line 2' — operator recalculates and adjusts.
Score: time to first water, pressure accuracy within 5 psi, transition smoothness.
learning_points: The first line's pressure discipline sets the tone — an over-pumped line beats up the nozzle team.
Adding lines is where operators fail: the relief valve/governor and throttle interplay must be automatic.
The tank-to-hydrant transition done wrong causes the interior crew's water to stutter at the worst moment.
Friction loss math must run in the operator's head faster than conditions change.
common_mistakes: Driver changes pump pressure before confirming the nozzle team's actual flow problem, chasing a phantom.
Friction loss for the second line is not accounted for, so both lines end up under-pressured.
Driver opens and closes discharges too fast, causing pressure surges that hit the nozzle crews.
safety_notes: Chock wheels.
Never leave a charging line unattended at the discharge.
success_criteria: First water under 60 seconds
Pressures within 5 psi of calculated
No interruption on transitions

drills.title: Drafting Evolution
drills.solo_note: One operator plus one assistant; instructor induces the lost prime
drills.objective: Establish a draft from a static source, achieve prime, and sustain a target flow — then recover from a lost prime.
drills.setup: Engine positioned at the source within lift limits. One operator, one assistant.
steps: Position for minimum lift; connect hard suction with gasket checks at every coupling.
Submerge the strainer at correct depth (off the bottom, below whirlpool depth).
Close all discharges and drains — the air-tight check is the evolution's foundation.
Prime, watch for pressure indication, open a discharge slowly, and establish flow.
Instructor induces a lost prime (air leak or strainer breach); operator diagnoses and re-establishes.
Log time-to-prime and time-to-recover.
learning_points: Drafting failures are almost always air leaks — the diagnostic sequence is a checklist, not a guess.
Strainer depth is a live variable as tanks drain; whirlpools swallow prime.
Lift matters: every foot of elevation costs capacity, which drives apparatus positioning.
An operator who has recovered a lost prime under the clock does not panic at 2 a.m.
common_mistakes: Discharges are left open during the air-tight and priming check, so the pump never pulls a prime.
The strainer sits too shallow and pulls a whirlpool, losing prime as the level drops.
Driver over-throttles at draft and cavitates the pump instead of matching speed to available water.
safety_notes: Footing at water sources; use a rope on the strainer rather than reaching.
success_criteria: Prime under 2 minutes
Sustained target flow
Lost prime recovered under 3 minutes

drills.title: Apparatus Positioning & Aerial Spotting
drills.solo_note: Instructor sets scenarios; spotters required for all apparatus and aerial movement
drills.objective: Position engine and aerial apparatus at simulated incidents to optimize scrub area, water supply access, collapse-zone margins, and later-arriving unit access.
drills.setup: Instructor designates a fire building and conditions (fire floor, victims showing, overhead wires). Operators position on arrival.
steps: Brief positioning doctrine: trucks get the front of the building; engines position for supply and stretch; nobody parks in the collapse zone.
Run arrival sequences: operator positions, sets up (aerial: outriggers, target selection to a window/roof), and justifies the spot aloud.
Photograph each position; evaluate scrub area actually achieved vs. available.
Reposition rounds: instructor adds a second-arriving company — did the first spot leave them room?
Aerial-specific: spot to a rescue window in under 3 minutes from air brake, including outrigger deployment on the marked surface.
Debrief with the photos: inches of curb distance turn into degrees of aerial reach.
learning_points: Apparatus position is a decision you're stuck with for hours — made in the first 30 seconds.
Aerial scrub area is won by the driver before the stick ever moves.
Collapse zones are measured in building heights, and parked apparatus inside them is a documented LODD pattern.
First-due spotting that blocks the truck is a fireground-long tax on every operation.
common_mistakes: The engine takes the front of the building and blocks the truck's aerial access.
Apparatus is spotted inside the collapse zone instead of at a corner with two-side visibility.
The aerial is spotted without planning scrub area, so the ladder cannot reach the intended objective.
safety_notes: Spotters during all apparatus movement on drill grounds.
Overhead electrical check before any aerial movement.
success_criteria: Justified position on every round
Aerial to target under time
Second-due access preserved

drills.title: Tank-to-Hydrant Transition Without Losing the Line
drills.solo_note: A nozzle firefighter flows and reports pressure while the operator switches over
drills.objective: The pump operator completes the tank-to-hydrant switchover while a 1.75 in attack line stays continuously charged, with nozzle pressure never dropping enough for the nozzle firefighter to call 'losing water,' and correctly states the estimated remaining source capacity from the residual pressure drop within 30 seconds of the intake stabilizing.
equipment: One engine with booster/tank supply and functioning tank-to-pump valve
Preconnected 1.75 in attack line with combination or fixed-gallonage nozzle
Large-diameter supply hose (single section acceptable for lot evolution)
Hydrant or static source with adequate flow
Intake pressure gauge (apparatus master intake gauge)
In-line pressure gauge or clamp-on for verification (improvised: rely on nozzle firefighter feedback)
Cones to mark hydrant, apparatus spot, and nozzle position
Radios or face-to-face voice for pump/nozzle/officer communication
drills.setup: Spot the engine in a training lot with the pump panel accessible and the attack line flaked to a marked nozzle position; charge the attack line off tank water only. Stage the supply hose from the hydrant to the pump intake but leave the intake valve closed so the operator performs a live switchover. This is a dry-lot evolution with no live fire; flow discharged water to a drain or open lot area.
steps: Brief the crew: nozzle firefighter flows a steady pattern off tank water and reports any pressure change; the operator will transition to hydrant supply without interrupting that flow.
Direct the operator to note starting static/intake conditions and confirm tank-to-pump is the only supply feeding the discharge.

On the officer's order, have the operator charge the supply line, then slowly crack the intake valve open while watching the master intake gauge and discharge pressure — feeding hydrant water in as tank draw falls off.
Coach the operator to fully open the intake only after the intake gauge shows sustained positive pressure, then close or gate back the tank-to-pump valve and reset the tank fill line to refill.
Have the operator read residual intake pressure at flow, compare it to the static reading, and state out loud the estimated additional lines the source will support.
Run a safety pause: confirm no discharge pressure spike hit the nozzle team, verify tank refill is occurring, and reset for a repeat with a different crew member on the panel.
learning_points: A botched switchover starves the nozzle team mid-attack — if the operator opens the intake too fast or closes the tank valve too early, the line surges or goes soft while a crew is committed to a fire, which is exactly when they cannot afford to lose water.

The intake gauge is the operator's fuel gauge: reading the residual drop from static to flowing pressure tells the operator whether the hydrant will feed one more line or is already near its limit, before the officer commits additional crews.
Refilling the tank immediately after transition rebuilds the operator's reserve — if the hydrant fails later, that reserve is the only water the crew has to protect their egress.
The operator manages the transition by feel and gauge, not by clock — smoothness protects the interior crew, so the standard is 'the nozzle never noticed,' not 'fast.'
common_mistakes: Closing the tank-to-pump valve before the intake shows positive pressure, dropping the discharge and softening the attack line.
Snapping the intake valve fully open, causing a pressure spike the nozzle team feels as a jerk on the line.
Forgetting to reopen the tank fill line, so the reserve tank stays empty and there is no backup if the hydrant is lost.
Reading only the discharge gauge and never checking residual intake, so the operator cannot tell the officer how much water is left in the source.
No verbal cue to the nozzle team before the transition, so a pressure wobble reads as a problem instead of an expected event.
safety_notes: Charged hose under pressure whips if a coupling fails — keep non-essential personnel clear of the discharge and nozzle path.
Discharge flowing water safely to a drain or open area; wet pavement is a slip hazard around the pump panel and nozzle position.
Confirm the tank-to-pump and intake valves are the correct handles before the evolution; a wrong-valve operation can deadhead the pump.
success_criteria: Attack line remains charged throughout the transition with no 'losing water' call from the nozzle firefighter.
Operator opens the intake only after positive intake pressure is shown, verified by observer at the gauge.
Operator states an estimated remaining source capacity within 30 seconds of intake stabilizing.
Tank fill line is reopened and refill confirmed before the evolution is scored complete.

variations.name: Blind Transition by Feedback Only
variations.description: Cover or ignore the in-line verification gauge; the operator manages the switchover using only the master gauges and the nozzle firefighter's verbal pressure reports.
variations.adds: Trains the operator to trust crew feedback and gauge reading together when instrumentation is limited or unreliable.

variations.name: Weak Hydrant
variations.description: Gate the source or use a low-flow static supply so residual pressure drops sharply under flow.
variations.adds: Forces the operator to recognize a marginal source and report that only limited additional flow is available before the officer over-commits crews.

variations.name: Second Line During Transition
variations.description: Officer calls for a second attack line just as the operator is mid-switchover.
variations.adds: Trains task prioritization and communication under competing demands — when to say 'stand by' versus feeding the new line.

lodd_connection.lesson: Loss or interruption of water to a committed hose team has contributed to firefighter deaths and near-misses; a disciplined, gauge-verified supply transition and a maintained tank reserve keep water on the fire and protect the crew's egress.

drills.title: Relay Pumping the Long Lay: Two Engines, One Line
drills.solo_note: Two engines, two operators, a nozzle team, an officer, and a gauge observer
drills.objective: The source and attack engine operators establish and sustain a relay over a long supply lay so the attack line holds target nozzle pressure, with the relay-intake engine maintaining a positive residual intake pressure (never allowing intake to drop toward zero) throughout at least 5 minutes of continuous flow.
equipment: Two engines (source/relay engine and attack engine)
Large-diameter supply hose plus spare sections for a long lay (lay length limited by lot; simulate distance with all available sections)
Preconnected 1.75 in attack line with nozzle
Gated wye or manifold if locally carried
In-line and intake pressure gauges on both apparatus
Cones marking source engine, attack engine, and nozzle positions
Radios for engineer-to-engineer and officer communication
drills.setup: Position the source engine at the hydrant/static source and the attack engine near the marked fire position, connected by the longest supply lay the lot allows; the attack engine feeds the 1.75 in line to the nozzle. If distance is limited, simulate a long-driveway or rural lay by having the source engine pump against a set discharge pressure that mimics friction loss over distance. Dry-lot evolution, no live fire.
steps: Brief both operators and the officer on the relay plan: source engine supplies the attack engine's intake at a target residual pressure; attack engine boosts to nozzle pressure; nozzle firefighter reports stream quality.
Establish the initial supply: source engine charges the LDH lay while the attack engine flows the attack line off its tank, then transitions to relay water using the tank-to-intake sequence.

Have the source operator throttle up until the attack engine's intake gauge shows the agreed positive residual pressure, and hold it — coaching the source operator to feed the relay, not chase the discharge gauge.

Direct the attack operator to set nozzle pressure and confirm stream quality with the nozzle team, then increase or add flow while both operators watch that relay-intake pressure never falls toward zero.

Insert a demand change on the officer's order — open a second appliance off a gated wye or call for more flow — and require both operators to communicate and adjust before the intake pressure collapses.

Run a safety pause at 5 minutes of sustained flow: verify intake stayed positive, check couplings and hose for leaks, and confirm both operators can state what their next move is if the source begins to fail.
Shut down in sequence from the nozzle back, then debrief on decision quality and engineer-to-engineer communication rather than speed.
learning_points: A relay fails at the intake, not the discharge — if the source operator lets the attack engine's intake fall to zero, the attack pump cavitates and the nozzle team loses water at the worst possible moment on a long lay where there is no quick fix.
Positive residual intake pressure is the relay's margin of safety: holding it means the source engine can absorb a sudden demand increase without starving the next pump in line.

On a long driveway or rural lay, a single engine cannot overcome the friction loss and still deliver nozzle pressure — recognizing when a second pump is required prevents committing a crew to an interior attack the water supply cannot sustain.
Engineer-to-engineer communication is the control system for a relay; when both operators announce demand changes before making them, the relay stays stable instead of surging or collapsing.
Adding an appliance downstream changes the whole hydraulic picture — the operator who opens a wye without warning the source engine can drop the entire relay.
common_mistakes: Source operator watching only their own discharge gauge and letting the attack engine's intake drift toward zero.
Attack operator increasing flow faster than the source engine can supply, cavitating the attack pump.
Opening a gated wye or second line without notifying the upstream engine, collapsing intake pressure.
Treating the relay as a speed race and skipping the residual-pressure check that tells them how much reserve the relay has.
No pre-agreed target intake pressure, so the two operators are working to different numbers.
safety_notes: Long charged LDH lays store significant energy — inspect couplings before charging and keep personnel off and clear of the pressurized supply line.
Apparatus operating in a lot: use a spotter and cones, and keep the working area clear of personnel moving between two pumping engines.
Wet pavement and multiple discharge points create slip and trip hazards; route flowed water away from walking paths and gauges.
success_criteria: Attack line holds target nozzle pressure confirmed by nozzle-team feedback and gauge during the flow period.
Relay-intake pressure at the attack engine stays positive for at least 5 continuous minutes, verified by observer at the gauge.
Both operators announce a demand change before adjusting throttle or opening an appliance.
At the safety pause, each operator states their contingency if the source begins to fail.

variations.name: Source Begins to Fail
variations.description: Instructor gates back the source or signals a dropping static source mid-flow.
variations.adds: Trains recognition of a declining supply and the decision to reduce flow, protect the line, or call for additional water before the relay collapses.

variations.name: Radio-Only Relay
variations.description: Position the engines out of line-of-sight (or simulate it) so all coordination happens by radio.
variations.adds: Forces disciplined, unambiguous engineer-to-engineer radio traffic when operators cannot see each other's gauges or hand signals.

variations.name: Add a Third Demand
variations.description: Officer calls for a second attack line off the attack engine during sustained flow.
variations.adds: Trains the attack operator to judge whether the relay can support added flow and to communicate the limit to the officer before over-committing.

lodd_connection.lesson: Inadequate or interrupted supply on long lays and rural incidents has contributed to firefighter injuries and deaths; a properly established relay that maintains positive intake pressure keeps water to the attack crew and preserves their ability to withdraw.

drills.title: PDP Card Deck: Friction Loss Under Pressure
drills.objective: Answer 20 pump-discharge-pressure cards against a written key with 18 of 20 correct and an average of under 20 seconds per card, calculated in the head with no calculator.
equipment: Index cards or scrap paper to build a card deck (one hose/appliance scenario per card)
A written friction-loss and PDP key the operator builds first, using their own department's hose sizes, coefficients, and appliance losses
drills.setup: In quarters, the operator first builds a reference key: for each hose diameter and length their apparatus carries, the friction loss at the flows they actually pump, plus appliance and elevation adjustments. The hose sizes, coefficients, nozzle flows, and appliance losses on the key are examples only — build the deck from your own department's hydraulic policy and apparatus inventory, not from another department's numbers. Then write 20 scenario cards (line size, length, nozzle flow, elevation) with the worked answer on the back.
steps: Direct the operator to shuffle the 20-card deck face-up so only the scenario shows.
Start the timer and draw the first card; state line diameter, length, flow, and any elevation aloud.
Calculate friction loss, add appliance and elevation, add nozzle pressure, and speak the target pump discharge pressure before flipping the card.
Flip the card, compare against the worked key, and mark correct or incorrect.
Continue through all 20 cards without stopping the timer between cards.
Stop the timer, record total time and score, and re-work every missed card by hand until the error is found.
Log the run so the next session's deck weights the diameters and flows that were missed.
learning_points: A wet evolution gives you seconds, not minutes, to set a pressure — the math has to be reflex before the line is charged, or the nozzle team gets a soft stream while you do arithmetic at the panel.

Friction loss climbs with the square of flow, so a 25 percent bump in GPM is a 56 percent jump in friction loss — an operator who does not feel that in their hands will badly under-pump a high-flow line.
Elevation and appliance losses are the numbers most often forgotten under stress, and forgetting them on a standpipe or a hilltop stretch starves the nozzle exactly when reach matters most.
Working from a key you built yourself, with your own hose and coefficients, means the reflex you train matches the apparatus you will actually pump.
Self-scoring against a written answer removes opinion — you either hit the number or you did not, which is the same standard the fire will apply.
common_mistakes: Building the deck from generic textbook coefficients instead of the department's own hose and appliances, training a number that will be wrong at the panel.
Rounding friction loss down to make the mental math easier, which compounds across a long lay into a significant under-pressure.
Dropping the nozzle pressure term and reporting only friction loss as the PDP.
Slowing down to protect the accuracy score, which defeats the purpose — the standard is fast AND correct, because the fireground is timed.
success_criteria: 18 of 20 cards correct against the written key.
Total time under 400 seconds (20-second average) with the timer running continuously.
Every missed card is re-worked by hand and the specific arithmetic error is identified before the session ends.

variations.name: Standpipe and elevation set
variations.description: Rebuild the deck so every card includes a floor number or elevation change and a standpipe appliance loss.
variations.adds: Forces the elevation and appliance terms that flat ground-level cards let the operator skip, training the high-rise and hillside math.

variations.name: Two lines, one pump
variations.description: Each card specifies two simultaneous discharges of different diameter and flow from the same pump.
variations.adds: Trains reading and setting independent discharge gauges instead of a single governed pressure, the real multi-line problem.

variations.name: Speed ladder
variations.description: Run the deck three times back to back, cutting the target average by 3 seconds each round while holding the 18 of 20 accuracy floor.
variations.adds: Builds the automaticity that lets the operator talk on the radio and pump at the same time without the math collapsing.

references: IFSTA Pumping Apparatus Driver/Operator Handbook — hydraulics and friction loss chapters (general fire-service practice)
Operator-built department friction-loss and PDP key
drills.solo_note: Fully solo: the firefighter builds the key, times themselves against a continuous clock, and self-scores against the written answers — no second person needed.

drills.title: The Blind Panel Walk: Controls by Feel
drills.objective: With eyes closed, name and place a hand on every panel control in correct operating order — throttle, tank-to-pump, discharges, intakes, gauges, primer, drains — completing the sequence in under 60 seconds with zero controls missed or misnamed, self-verified on camera.
equipment: Engine in quarters, pump NOT engaged, no water moving
Phone camera on a tripod or ledge to film the panel and the operator's hands
Blindfold or the operator simply keeps eyes closed
A written operating-order list the operator builds for this specific apparatus
drills.setup: Position the engine in quarters with the pump not engaged and no water in the system — this is a dry, no-flow familiarization drill. The operator first writes the correct operating-order sequence for THIS apparatus (controls vary by manufacturer and by department spec), then sets the camera to capture both the panel and their hands.
steps: Direct the operator to film a slow eyes-open pass first, naming and touching each control in operating order to confirm the written sequence matches the apparatus.
Have the operator close and hold their eyes shut, standing at the normal operating position.
Start the timer and call for the sequence: the operator names each control aloud and places a hand physically on it, in operating order, without looking.
Require the operator to state the function of each control as they touch it (for example, 'tank-to-pump, opens water from the booster tank to the pump').
Stop the timer when the last control in the sequence is named and touched.
Review the film with eyes open: check each named control against where the hand actually landed and against the written order.
Re-run any segment where the hand missed the control or the naming was out of order until the full sequence is clean.
learning_points: At a real panel it is dark, raining, and loud, and you are watching the fire and the line, not the panel — the hand has to find the discharge without the eyes, or you take your attention off the crew to hunt for a control.
Naming controls in operating order, not just by location, trains the sequence that keeps you from opening a discharge before the pump is supplied or draining a line you meant to keep charged.
Stating each control's function out loud links the muscle memory to the hydraulic effect, so under stress you reach for the right control because you know what it does, not just where it sits.
Every apparatus is laid out differently — the reflex is only useful on the rig you build it for, which is why the sequence is written for this specific engine.
Filming turns a private guess into an objective record: the tape shows whether the hand actually landed on the intake or two inches off it.
common_mistakes: Peeking — cracking the eyes to confirm a control, which quietly defeats the entire drill and hides the gaps that show up at 0300 on the real fireground.
Touching controls by memorized location while naming them out of operating order, so the muscle memory and the correct sequence never actually connect.
Skipping the drains, primer, or a rarely used discharge because they are not 'the important ones' — those are exactly the controls the hand fumbles for during a real evolution.
Not filming, so a hand that lands close-but-wrong gets scored as a hit.
safety_notes: Keep the pump disengaged and the system dry throughout — this is a no-flow familiarization drill; never operate charged discharges or intakes blindfolded.
Perform the drill standing at the apparatus in quarters with clear footing; if the operator uses an actual blindfold, keep one hand available to steady themselves on the pump panel.
success_criteria: Every control in the written operating-order list is named and physically touched with eyes closed.
Sequence completed in under 60 seconds.
Film review confirms zero controls missed, mislocated, or named out of order.

variations.name: Cold start position
variations.description: The operator begins seated in the cab, dismounts, and starts the blind walk from the moment they reach the panel rather than pre-staged at the operating position.
variations.adds: Trains finding the operating position and first control by feel after a moving approach, closer to a real arrival.

variations.name: Named-target reach
variations.description: The operator has a partner or a recorded voice call a single control at random ('number two discharge,' 'left intake'), and the hand must go straight to it eyes-closed.
variations.adds: Trains direct random access to any control, not just the memorized sequence, for when an evolution jumps out of order.

variations.name: Glove degradation
variations.description: Repeat the blind walk wearing structural firefighting gloves.
variations.adds: Trains the reduced tactile feedback of gloved hands, which is how the operator will actually work the panel on the fireground.

drills.title: Arrival-to-Pump, Dry and Self-Timed
drills.objective: From a simulated stop, perform the dry arrival-to-pump sequence — set brake, transfer to pump, chock, exit, reach the panel and set the operating position — hitting every step in correct order and completing it within a self-set repeatable standard for three consecutive runs, verified on camera.
equipment: Engine in quarters, pump NOT engaged for the panel portion, no water moving
Chalk or tape to mark a simulated stopping spot
A written arrival-sequence checklist the operator builds for this apparatus and this department's procedure
drills.setup: Mark a stopping spot in quarters or on the apron with chalk or tape. The operator builds a written arrival-sequence checklist for THIS apparatus and department first — the exact steps and their order (brake, transmission-to-pump transfer, chocks, dismount, panel) vary by rig and by department procedure, so build it from your own manufacturer sequence and department SOP, not a generic list. Run the drill dry with no line pulled and no water moving; the pump-transfer step is performed per the apparatus procedure without flowing water.
steps: Direct the operator to write and verify the arrival-sequence checklist against the apparatus operating manual and department procedure before timing anything.
Have the operator start in the driver's seat at the marked stopping spot with the camera framing the cab, the wheels, and the panel.
On 'go,' start the timer: set the parking brake, complete the transmission-to-pump transfer per the apparatus procedure, and confirm the pump-engaged indication as the manufacturer sequence directs.
Direct the operator to dismount, chock the wheels on the correct side per department procedure, and move to the pump panel operating position.
Stop the timer when the operator is set at the panel in operating position with hands ready, and record the time.
Review the film against the written checklist: confirm every step happened, in order, with nothing skipped.
Repeat until three consecutive runs hit every step in order within the operator's self-set standard, then log the standard time to beat next session.
learning_points: The arrival sequence is the same every time precisely so it survives the chaos of a working fire — an operator who improvises the order under stress skips the brake or the chocks, and an apparatus that rolls is a catastrophe no water flow can offset.

Transferring to pump and confirming the engaged indication before leaving the cab is the difference between a panel that will make pressure and one that will not — discovering an incomplete transfer at the panel costs the interior crew their water.
Chocking is not optional and not last-if-there-is-time: on any grade a pumping apparatus can creep, and the muscle memory to chock every single time is built dry, in quarters, not on the fireground.
Self-timing to a repeatable standard, rather than chasing a fastest-ever, trains consistency — the fire needs the sequence right on the average run, not once on a perfect one.
Building the checklist from your own apparatus and SOP means the sequence you groove is the one your rig and your department actually require.
common_mistakes: Leaving the cab before confirming the pump-transfer indication, then finding at the panel that the pump never engaged.
Chocking on the wrong side or skipping chocks on a flat apron because 'it will not roll here,' training out the habit that matters on a grade.
Racing for a personal-best time and dropping a step, when the objective is every step in order on three consecutive runs.
Building a generic checklist instead of the manufacturer and department sequence for this specific rig, so the grooved order is subtly wrong.
safety_notes: Keep the drill dry with no water moving; the pump-transfer step is performed per apparatus procedure only to confirm the sequence, not to flow water.
Chock the wheels on every run as the drill requires, and ensure the apparatus is in a safe, level position in quarters or on a controlled apron before starting.
If the apron has any grade or traffic, run only the panel-and-chock portion and simulate the cab start from a fully secured apparatus.
success_criteria: Every step on the written checklist is performed in correct order on three consecutive runs.
The pump-engaged indication is confirmed on film before the operator leaves the cab on every run.
All three runs fall within the operator's self-set repeatable standard time.

variations.name: Night and gloves
variations.description: Run the sequence in low light wearing structural gloves and helmet.
variations.adds: Trains the arrival sequence under the reduced dexterity and visibility of an actual night response.

variations.name: Radio-loaded
variations.description: The operator gives a brief simulated on-scene size-up or acknowledgment aloud while completing the sequence.
variations.adds: Trains completing the physical sequence correctly while the mouth and ears are busy on the radio, the real multitask of arrival.

variations.name: Interrupted transfer
variations.description: The operator narrates a simulated failed or incomplete pump transfer on one run and must catch it and correct before proceeding.
variations.adds: Trains recognizing and recovering from an incomplete transfer instead of discovering it at the panel.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH and fire-service reports document uncontrolled apparatus movement and struck-by incidents on the fireground
lodd_connection.lesson: A skipped chock or rushed arrival step has killed and injured firefighters when apparatus moved unexpectedly; grooving the full sequence to reflex, chocks included, targets that pattern.

Apparatus manufacturer operating sequence and department arrival SOP (operator-provided)
drills.solo_note: Fully solo: one operator drives the simulated stop, runs the dry sequence, and scores every step against the checklist on camera playback alone.

drills.title: Gauge Read by Position: Hand Before Eyes
drills.objective: On 20 randomly called gauges and controls, place a hand on the correct one and state what it reads or governs within 3 seconds each, scoring 19 of 20 correct against the panel layout, verified on camera.
equipment: Engine in quarters, pump NOT engaged, no water moving
A written list of every gauge and control on the panel, built by the operator, used as the answer key
A shuffled prompt list or a recorded voice reading the 20 targets in random order
drills.setup: In quarters with the pump not engaged and no water moving, the operator builds a written inventory of every gauge and control on the panel — master intake, master discharge, individual discharge gauges, engine RPM/oil/temp, tank level, and each control — as the answer key. They then create a randomized prompt list of 20 targets (or record themselves reading them with pauses) so the calls come without a predictable pattern.
steps: Direct the operator to confirm their written panel inventory matches the actual apparatus, correcting any gauge or control that is mislabeled or missing.
Set the camera to frame the full panel and the operator's hands and position the operator at the normal operating stance.
Play or read the first randomized prompt (for example, 'master discharge pressure' or 'tank-to-pump valve').
Require the operator, within 3 seconds, to place a hand on the correct gauge or control and state what it reads or what it governs.
Continue through all 20 randomized prompts without coaching between calls.
Review the film against the written inventory: score each response for correct placement and correct function within the 3-second window.
Re-run any target that was slow or wrong until the hand goes to it directly, and log which gauges were weak for next session's prompt weighting.
learning_points: On the fireground you read the intake and discharge gauges in glances, between watching the line and the crew — if finding the right gauge takes a search, you are reading it too late to catch a dropping intake or a runaway discharge.

Naming what each gauge reads, not just where it is, means you understand a falling residual intake as a warning about your water supply rather than as a needle you have to interpret from scratch under stress.
Random-order prompting breaks the memorized left-to-right sweep and trains true direct access, which is what a real evolution demands when problems appear on gauges out of sequence.

The individual discharge gauges are the ones operators know least and need most when managing multiple lines — drilling them by position keeps a second line from stealing pressure from the first unnoticed.
Building and correcting your own panel inventory first guarantees you are training against the real layout of your rig, including the quirks a generic diagram would not show.
common_mistakes: Confusing master discharge with an individual discharge gauge, which on a multi-line fire means adjusting the wrong pressure.
Finding the gauge but not stating what it reads or governs, leaving the identification half-trained and useless under stress.
Falling back into a memorized sweep instead of direct access, so an out-of-order prompt causes a hunt.
Building the inventory from a generic panel diagram rather than the actual apparatus, missing rig-specific gauge placement.
safety_notes: Keep the pump disengaged and the system dry throughout; this is a no-flow identification drill with no charged discharges or intakes.
success_criteria: 19 of 20 targets: correct gauge or control touched and correct function stated.
Each response completed within 3 seconds of the prompt.
Film review confirms hand placement and stated function against the written inventory.

variations.name: Reading interpretation
variations.description: Instead of naming what a gauge governs, the operator states what a given reading would mean and one action they would take (for example, 'intake falling toward 20 psi means the hydrant is near max — I throttle back or add a supply line').
variations.adds: Trains interpreting the gauge, not just locating it, connecting the reading to a pump-operation decision.

variations.name: Gloves and low light
variations.description: Run the drill wearing structural gloves in reduced light.
variations.adds: Trains locating gauges under the degraded dexterity and visibility of the real fireground.

variations.name: Two-line focus
variations.description: Weight the prompt list heavily toward the individual discharge gauges and their controls.
variations.adds: Builds the least-practiced skill of managing independent discharge pressures on a multi-line fire.

references: IFSTA Pumping Apparatus Driver/Operator Handbook — pump panel gauges and controls (general practice)
Operator-built panel inventory for the specific apparatus
drills.solo_note: Fully solo: a recorded or shuffled prompt list supplies the random calls and the camera scores placement and timing on playback — no second person required.

drills.title: Preconnect Deployment to Target
drills.solo_note: Firefighter 1/2 split, pump operator required for charged line, stopwatch timing
drills.objective: Deploy a 200 ft preconnected 1.75 in line to a marked entry point with zero kinks, flaked for advance, in under 90 seconds.
drills.setup: Mark an entry door 150 ft from the apparatus. Place a cone at the flake-out point. Crew in full PPE, on air for the final evolution.
steps: Walk the evolution dry: identify the load, shoulder position, and drop point.
Firefighter 1 pulls the load and stretches toward the entry point; Firefighter 2 clears the bed and chases kinks.
Flake remaining hose at the door in a serpentine pattern with the nozzle on top.
Call for water, bleed the line, and check pattern before 'entering'.
Advance 50 ft flowing intermittently, then shut down and reload.
Repeat until the crew hits the drill's 90-second target on three consecutive evolutions.
learning_points: The stretch is won or lost at the door — hose flaked correctly before entry prevents the mid-hallway stall.

Kinks cut flow dramatically — enough that a kinked 1.75 in can lose a large share of its target GPM before anyone inside feels the line go soft. Flow-test your own line and pressure to see what it actually costs you.
The backup firefighter's job is hose management, not crowding the nozzle.
Bleeding air and checking the pattern outside is a discipline, not a delay.
common_mistakes: Crew pulls the load and stretches toward the door before confirming it reaches, then runs short with no hose left to flake.
Nozzle firefighter enters before the line is bled and pattern-checked, stalling mid-hallway on an air-filled line.
Backup firefighter crowds the nozzle instead of chasing kinks off the bed, so flow is lost before the crew feels it.
safety_notes: Hydrate and rotate crews in hot weather; this is a high-exertion drill in full PPE.
Charged-line evolutions require a pump operator dedicated to the drill.
success_criteria: Line at the door, flaked, charged, and bled in under 90 seconds
Zero kinks between apparatus and nozzle
Nozzle firefighter checks pattern before advance

variations.name: Narrow Hallway Stretch
variations.description: Use cones or salvage covers to create a 36 in wide corridor from door to fire room. Crew must manage hose through the pinch without shoulder-checking walls.
variations.adds: Hose discipline in tight residential hallways; teaches the push-pull advance rhythm.

variations.name: Obstacle Stretch
variations.description: Place parked-vehicle stand-ins, fencing, and landscaping obstacles between the engine and the door.
variations.adds: Estimating and routing the stretch; when to go over vs. around obstacles.

variations.name: Stairwell Stretch
variations.description: Deploy up an exterior or drill-tower stairwell to a second-floor landing.
variations.adds: Well-hole vs. wrap-the-rail methods; managing hose weight on stairs.

variations.name: Long Stretch / Courtyard
variations.description: Target is 250+ ft away; crew must extend the preconnect with a spare length or deploy a static bed.
variations.adds: Recognizing when the preconnect won't reach BEFORE pulling it — the most common stretch failure.

Department hose load SOPs

drills.title: Nozzle Mechanics & Door Control
drills.solo_note: Backup firefighter works the door; charged line needs a pump operator
drills.objective: Demonstrate correct nozzle operation: pattern selection, flow-and-move technique, and coordinated door control on entry.
equipment: Door prop or drill tower door
drills.setup: Charged line at a controllable door. One firefighter on the nozzle, one on backup/door.
steps: Review nozzle anatomy: bail control, pattern ring, and flow rating.
Practice smooth bail operation — full open, full close — without whipping the line.
Practice the O/Z/ceiling-sweep patterns while stationary, then while advancing.
Backup firefighter controls the door: crack for the line, close behind entry, and manage it as a flow-path control point.
Run entry sequences: door cracked, quick assessment, flow into the space, advance, backup feeds hose.
Swap positions and repeat.
learning_points: Water applied from the safest position first — hitting it from the door before advancing — resets the fire and buys survivability for occupants.
The door is a ventilation control device; leaving it wide open feeds the fire a flow path.
Nozzle reaction is managed with body position and the backup firefighter, not grip strength.
Pattern discipline: know what your fog vs. straight stream does to the thermal environment before you use it inside.
common_mistakes: Nozzle firefighter opens the bale fully in one motion instead of easing it, reacting to nozzle reaction instead of controlling it.
Crew works the door wide open, letting the flow path pull fire down the hallway toward the advancing line.
Firefighter cracks the door to check conditions but never controls it, so it is never used as a tactical barrier.
safety_notes: If using live fire, full NFPA 1403 compliance and instructor-in-charge required.
Manage nozzle reaction — sudden bail openings on a dry-run whip the line.
success_criteria: Smooth bail control with no line whip
Correct pattern for the assigned scenario
Door controlled at every stage of entry

variations.name: Flow and Move
variations.description: Advance while flowing continuously down a marked lane, keeping the stream on target.
variations.adds: Modern research-driven technique; coordination between nozzle and backup while water is moving.

variations.name: Reduced Visibility
variations.description: Run entry sequences with obscured facepieces.
variations.adds: Operating the nozzle and reading the line by feel.

lodd_connection.incident: Cherry Road, Washington DC (1999) — two firefighters killed when an uncoordinated opening created a flow path that drove fire over their position
lodd_connection.lesson: Door control and flow-path awareness are life-safety skills for the nozzle team, not just ventilation theory.

NIOSH F99-21

drills.title: Hydrant Hookup & Forward Lay
drills.solo_note: Officer calls the lay, driver lays in and connects, hydrant firefighter wraps
drills.objective: Complete a forward lay from hydrant to fire location with a charged supply line in under 3 minutes from air-brake set at the hydrant.
drills.setup: Identify a hydrant 300-500 ft from a simulated fire address. Assign hydrant firefighter, driver, and officer positions.
steps: Officer calls the lay; hydrant firefighter dismounts with the hydrant bag and enough LDH to wrap.
Wrap the hydrant, signal the driver, and dress the hydrant while the engine lays in.
Flush the hydrant, connect LDH with appropriate fittings, and stand by for the charge order.
Driver positions at the fire address, breaks the line, and connects to intake.
On order, hydrant firefighter charges the line slowly (count the turns).
Time the evolution from air brake at hydrant to water at the intake.
learning_points: The hydrant firefighter is alone — the drill builds independent competence with fittings, flushing, and charge discipline.
Charging too fast can rupture the LDH or knock down anyone standing over it.
Drivers must leave room for the truck when spotting at the address.
Every second before established water supply is a second the attack operates on tank water.
common_mistakes: Driver pulls away from the hydrant before the hydrant firefighter has wrapped and secured it, parting the supply line.
Hydrant firefighter forgets to bleed air and debris from the hydrant before charging, fouling the line.
The lay is started without confirming the hydrant location, forcing a re-lay that wastes the initial water window.
safety_notes: Nobody stands over LDH while it charges.
Watch traffic during street evolutions; use cones and a spotter.
success_criteria: Water at intake under 3 minutes
No missed fittings or leaks at hydrant
Controlled charge

variations.description: Attack crew drops at the fire, engine lays back to the hydrant.
variations.adds: When the attack pumper must be at the water source; different crew split.

variations.name: Split Lay
variations.description: Two engines complete the supply from a drop point at an intersection.
variations.adds: Radio coordination between companies; common in long-setback districts.

drills.title: High-Rise / Standpipe Pack Deployment
drills.solo_note: Pack load divided across the crew; nozzle team advances; instructor rigs the PRV
drills.objective: Carry, connect, and deploy a standpipe pack from the floor below the fire, flake for the attack, and charge with correct pressure.
equipment: High-rise packs (2.5 in or 2 in per SOP)
drills.setup: Stage crew in the lobby. Fire floor designated two flights up. Standpipe outlet on the floor below the fire.
steps: Divide the pack load: hose, fittings/gauge bag, tools. Everyone carries something.
Ascend to the floor below the fire — never connect on the fire floor.
Inspect the outlet: remove debris, check threads, control the pressure-reducing valve if present.
Connect the gauge and gated wye, then flake hose up the stairs toward the fire floor door with the nozzle team positioned to advance.
Charge, set pressure at the outlet for the nozzle/hose combination, and bleed.
Advance through the fire-floor door with door control, flow, and back out in order.
learning_points: Stairwell flaking determines whether the attack works — hose feeds down to the connection, not piled at the door.
Outlet pressure must be verified with a gauge; building systems lie.
Load discipline: a crew that arrives at the fire floor exhausted has already lost.
The floor-below connection keeps the crew out of the flow path while they set up.
common_mistakes: Crew connects to the standpipe on the fire floor instead of the floor below, staging in the hostile environment.
The in-line pressure gauge and needed fittings are left on the rig, so the crew cannot set the correct nozzle pressure.
The pack is flaked in the stairwell blocking the door and other crews instead of on the landing below the fire.
safety_notes: Stair evolutions in full PPE — monitor for overexertion.
Confirm attack stairwell vs. evacuation stairwell in scenario briefing.
success_criteria: Connection on floor below
Correct pressure verified at gauge
Hose flaked to support a full-floor advance

variations.name: Well-Hole Stretch
variations.description: If the stairwell has an open well, stretch the line up the well instead of flaking on stairs.
variations.adds: Massive time savings when geometry allows; rope/strap hose management.

variations.name: PRV Problem
variations.description: Instructor rigs the outlet to deliver low pressure.
variations.adds: Troubleshooting pressure-reducing valves — a factor in the One Meridian Plaza fire.

lodd_connection.incident: One Meridian Plaza, Philadelphia (1991) — three firefighters killed; improperly set pressure-reducing valves crippled standpipe streams
lodd_connection.lesson: Verify outlet pressure with your own gauge. Never trust the building's system blindly.

references: NFPA 14
USFA-TR-049 (Highrise Office Building Fire, One Meridian Plaza, Philadelphia — USFA Technical Report Series)

drills.title: Charged Line Advance & Interior Movement
drills.solo_note: Nozzle and backup pair, corner pinning, rotate every position, pump operator
drills.objective: Advance a charged 1.75 in line through a multi-room layout, managing corners, doorways, and stairs as a coordinated nozzle team.
drills.setup: Lay out a path with at least two 90-degree corners, one doorway, and one stair section. Crew of 2-3 on the line.
steps: Nozzle firefighter sets the advance rhythm; backup stays one arm's length back feeding hose.
At corners, the backup firefighter pins the hose to the inside corner to prevent friction lock.
At doorways, pause, control the door, flow if needed, then move.
On stairs, advance on the call — nozzle moves, then backup, keeping slack ahead of the nozzle.
Halfway through, call a simulated hoseline emergency (burst length) and back the line out under control.
Rotate every position through nozzle and backup.
learning_points: Most stalled lines fail at a corner — one firefighter dedicated to the pinch point solves it.
Slack management: give the nozzle a working bight of loose hose ahead of every push — 6-10 ft is a solid rule of thumb on 1.75 in, and you'll want more on the big line or a tight corner.
Backing a line out is a skill; crews that only train forward panic in reverse.
Communication is by feel and short calls — long sentences don't survive SCBA and noise.
common_mistakes: Crew advances faster than the backup can feed hose, dragging a dead-weight line that binds at every turn.
Nozzle firefighter loses contact with the wall reference and drifts off the advance path.
Team advances past unchecked fire on a flank because they fixate on the main body ahead.
safety_notes: Maintain three points of contact on stairs with a charged line.
On-air time counts toward air management training — log it.
success_criteria: Continuous advance without a stall over 30 seconds
Successful controlled withdrawal
All members rotated through nozzle

variations.name: Zero Visibility
variations.description: Obscured facepieces for the entire advance.
variations.adds: Orientation by hose, wall, and crew contact.

variations.name: Furniture Load
variations.description: Add furniture obstacles simulating a lived-in occupancy.
variations.adds: Real residences aren't empty drill towers.

variations.name: 2.5 in Big Line
variations.description: Same course with a 2.5 in line and 3-person team.
variations.adds: Big-line technique: kneel-and-flow, team repositioning, when the big line is the right call.

references: NFPA 1410

drills.title: Stretch Estimation Walkaround
drills.solo_note: Walk the district alone, write your estimates, verify with a measuring wheel, and self-score against 10 targets.
drills.objective: Accurately estimate hose length needed for a stretch to any point in a building using visual cues, within one 50 ft length.
drills.setup: During building familiarization or on-duty walkarounds, pick target points: rear bedroom of a ranch, third-floor apartment, rear of a strip mall unit.
steps: From the likely apparatus spot, estimate the stretch: setback + exterior path + interior path + working length.
Write the estimate down before verifying.
Verify with a measuring wheel or pacing.
Compare and identify what was missed (stairs count double, setbacks deceive).
Repeat across building types until estimates are consistently within 50 ft.
learning_points: Rules of thumb: one length per floor of stair climb, one working length for the fire floor.
Setbacks and rear-yard stretches are systematically underestimated.
Knowing your district's building stock converts this from math to recognition.
The short stretch is the most common and most preventable engine company failure.
common_mistakes: Crew eyeballs the setback instead of pacing it, and comes up a section short at the door.
The estimate ignores the interior stretch and stair climb, so the line reaches the building but not the fire floor.
Nobody adds hose for the flake-out and working length, so there is nothing left to advance with.
safety_notes: Exterior walkarounds only unless the occupancy grants access.
success_criteria: Estimates within one length on 8 of 10 targets
Stretch estimate documented before verification

variations.name: Photo-Based
variations.description: Use street-view imagery of district buildings for station-based estimation rounds.
variations.adds: High-rep, no-cost version for daily training; app-friendly format.

references: Engine company operations texts

drills.title: Rural Water Supply: Drafting & Tanker Shuttle
drills.solo_note: Multi-company: fill-site and dump-site engines, tanker drivers, officer tracking
drills.objective: Establish and sustain a target flow (e.g., 250 GPM for 20 minutes) using a static source, portable tanks, and tanker shuttle.
equipment: Static water source or filled tanks
drills.setup: Designate a fill site at the static source and a dump site with drop tanks near the simulated fire.
steps: Dump-site engine deploys the drop tank and sets up to draft from it.
Fill-site engine establishes draft from the static source and sets up tanker fill lines.
Tankers cycle: fill, travel, dump, return — officer tracks turnaround times.
Achieve prime and sustain the target flow at the dump-site engine.
Calculate actual sustained GPM from tanker capacity and cycle times; compare against target.
Rotate operators through the draft positions.
learning_points: Continuous flow is a math problem: tanker gallons divided by full cycle time.
Losing prime mid-operation is the classic failure — strainer depth and air leaks matter.
Dump-site layout determines whether tankers can cycle without blocking each other.
This is the fire that outlasts your tank water — rural crews live or die by this evolution.
common_mistakes: Draft is lost when the strainer sucks air because it sits too shallow or the tank drains into a whirlpool.
The dump site is positioned where an arriving tanker blocks the departing one, stalling the shuttle.
Shuttle cycle time creeps up unmeasured until the attack line outruns the water supply.
safety_notes: Tanker rollovers are a leading apparatus LODD cause — enforce speed discipline in the shuttle.
Traffic control at fill and dump sites.
success_criteria: Prime achieved and held
Target GPM sustained for the full duration
No shuttle safety violations

variations.name: Nurse Operation
variations.description: Tanker feeds the attack engine directly instead of via drop tank.
variations.adds: Simpler option for smaller flows; when to choose it.

variations.name: Dual Drop Tanks
variations.description: Two tanks with jet siphon transfer.
variations.adds: Scaling up supply for defensive flows.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH reports document tanker/tender rollover fatalities during water shuttle operations
lodd_connection.lesson: The shuttle itself is a hazard. Seatbelts, speed discipline, and route planning are part of the water supply plan.

ISO rural water supply criteria

drills.title: 2.5 in Line Deployment & Operation
drills.solo_note: Explicitly a 2-3 person team; rotate all members; needs a pump operator
drills.objective: Deploy, charge, and operate a 2.5 in handline as a 2-3 person team, including flowing while stationary and repositioning under flow.
drills.setup: Open area with a target (cone or hydrant flow target) 150 ft out.
steps: Review when the big line is indicated: heavy fire, commercial occupancy, defensive positions, exposure protection.
Deploy and flake with the same discipline as the attack line.
Charge and practice stationary flow: nozzle firefighter kneels, line anchored under the knee, backup applies weight.
Practice shut-down, 20 ft reposition, re-flow cycles.
Practice hitting a target through a 'window' prop from 40 ft (exterior stream placement).
Rotate all members through the nozzle.
learning_points: A 2.5 in line flowed correctly by two people beats three people fighting it standing up.
The big-line decision belongs in your first size-up, not your second — teach the size-up cues.
Reach and penetration of a smooth bore stream is exposure protection and transitional attack capability.
Crews avoid the 2.5 in because they don't train on it; familiarity removes the hesitation.
common_mistakes: Firefighters try to fight the 2.5 in standing up instead of anchored low, and get pushed around by nozzle reaction.
The big line is called for too late, after a smaller line has already failed on a growing fire load.
Crew avoids the 2.5 in entirely because it was never drilled, defaulting to an inadequate handline.
safety_notes: Nozzle reaction on a 2.5 in can injure an unprepared operator — brief anchoring technique first.
success_criteria: Controlled sustained flow by a 2-person team
Reposition under 30 seconds
Accurate stream placement on target

variations.adds: Fast water on arrival for heavy fire showings.

variations.adds: Extending operations off one supply stretch.

drills.title: Two-Line Deployment & Water Supply Handoff
drills.solo_note: Officer, two firefighters, driver-engineer, safety officer, dedicated pump operator
drills.objective: Deploy an attack line and a backup line, then establish a charged hydrant supply, within 4 minutes of arrival with zero kinks.
drills.setup: Spot the engine 150 ft from a marked entry door with a hydrant 100 ft to the rear. Crew in full PPE and on air for the working evolution. Designate a safety officer to watch charged-line footing.
steps: Officer sizes up, calls the attack plan, and assigns the attack line, backup line, and supply tasks.
Firefighter stretches the attack line to the entry door and flakes it for advance with the nozzle on top.
Second firefighter deploys the backup line to protect the means of egress.
Driver/engineer completes the hydrant hookup and charges the supply line to the pump.
Officer confirms both handlines are charged, bled, and pattern-checked before any advance.
Reset the evolution and rotate positions so each member runs the supply task once.
learning_points: A backup line is not optional; it protects the attack crew's egress if the fire outpaces the initial line.
The supply handoff fails when the driver/engineer is not assigned early and explicitly by the officer.
Kinks between the pump and the nozzle silently rob flow long before the crew feels it inside.
Clear task assignment at arrival prevents two firefighters from grabbing the same line.
common_mistakes: Two firefighters grab the same line at arrival because tasks were never assigned explicitly.
The supply handoff stalls because the driver-engineer was not assigned to it early by the officer.
Kinks between the pump and nozzle rob flow long before the crew feels it inside.
safety_notes: Rotate and hydrate crews; charged-line evolutions in full PPE are high-exertion.
Keep a dedicated pump operator on the drill so line pressures are controlled at all times.
success_criteria: Attack and backup lines both charged, bled, and pattern-checked within 4 minutes
Continuous hydrant supply established with no interruption to the attack line
Zero kinks between the pump and either nozzle
