drills.title: Solo Shoulder Load Build and Dry Flake
drills.objective: Working alone, build a 150 ft 1.75 in shoulder load, walk it 100 ft, and drop it flaked so the nozzle is free and no coil crosses another, in under 2 minutes, three consecutive reps.
equipment: 150 ft of dry 1.75 in hose in three 50 ft lengths
Full PPE including gloves and helmet
Phone timer and camera (tripod or a cone to prop the phone against)
Chalk or tape to mark the start line and the 100 ft drop point
Measuring wheel or a known 100 ft reference (bay stripes, apparatus lengths)
drills.setup: Stretch three dry 1.75 in lengths flat on the apparatus floor or ramp. Chalk a start line and a drop point 100 ft away, and set the phone to film the whole path from the side. Hose diameter and load pattern here are an example: substitute your department's attack line size and its standard shoulder load before running this drill.
steps: Film every rep from the side so the flake pattern at the drop point is visible on playback.
Build the shoulder load from the flat hose: nozzle set first at the shoulder, folds stacked so the load pays off from the top, coupling positions marked with chalk on the floor before you lift.
Start the timer at the chalk line, walk the 100 ft to the drop point at working pace without adjusting the load with your free hand.
Drop the load at the mark by rolling the shoulder forward, not by dumping it backward, and stop the timer when the nozzle is in your hand and clear of the pile.
Walk the dropped hose end to end and chalk an X anywhere a coil lies across another coil or a coupling sits under a fold.
Reset by dragging the hose flat, then run two more reps; on the last rep, watch the film back before you score yourself.
learning_points: A shoulder load that pays off from the bottom instead of the top locks itself on the walk — the firefighter feels it as hose that will not come off the shoulder at the door, and the stretch stalls where it is most exposed.

Coupling position inside the load decides where the line binds later: a coupling buried mid-fold becomes a hard point that catches on stair nosings and door frames when someone else is pulling from the far end.
Dropping the load backward scatters the folds into a bird's nest that takes longer to clear than the whole carry took — the time lost is time the nozzle is not making water.
Building the load alone, slowly, with the couplings chalked, is how the pattern gets into the hands; under fire conditions nobody re-derives the pattern, they reproduce whatever they practiced.
common_mistakes: Stacking folds so the nozzle ends up buried in the middle of the load instead of riding free at the shoulder.
Steadying the load with the free hand the whole walk, which hides the fact that the load is unbalanced and will not survive a real stretch with a tool in that hand.
Making the folds so long they drag the ground and get stepped on during the walk.
Dumping the load off the back of the shoulder, which crosses the coils and buries the nozzle.
Scoring the rep by feel instead of walking the drop and actually marking the crossovers.
safety_notes: Lift the load with the legs and keep the folds off the ground on the walk — a dry 150 ft 1.75 in load is a real shoulder and lumbar load, and with nobody in quarters there is nobody to find you if you go down.
Keep the walking path clear of apparatus and open compartment doors; filming from the side is not a spotter and will not stop you from walking into a bumper.
success_criteria: Three consecutive reps completed under 2 minutes each from start line to nozzle in hand.
Zero chalked crossovers on the dropped hose on at least two of the three reps.
Nozzle is free and pointed toward the direction of advance at the drop, on every rep.
Free hand is off the load for the full 100 ft walk on the final rep, verified on film.

variations.name: Tool in the free hand
variations.description: Carry a hand tool or an axe in the free hand for the entire walk and drop.
variations.adds: Forces the load to be balanced by build rather than steadied by hand, which is the actual condition on a real stretch.

variations.name: Stair segment
variations.description: Route the 100 ft walk over a flight of stairs or a ramp instead of flat floor.
variations.adds: Trains fold length and coupling placement against the geometry that actually snags loads.

variations.name: Blind build
variations.description: Build the load with the helmet face shield taped over or eyes closed, then open to walk it.
variations.adds: Moves the pattern from visual checking to hand memory, which is what survives low visibility.

variations.name: Cold start
variations.description: Do 60 seconds of stair climbs or hose pulls immediately before the timed rep.
variations.adds: Shows whether the load pattern holds when grip and breathing are already degraded.

references: IFSTA Essentials of Fire Fighting — hose loads, carries, and advances chapter
Department attack-line load SOP (operator supplies the local pattern)
drills.solo_note: Fully solo as written: one firefighter, dry hose, phone timer and camera. No pump operator, no charged line, no second set of hands needed.

drills.title: Reload the Bed to Your Department's Pattern
drills.objective: Reload a 200 ft preconnect into the bed to the department's own pattern, alone, with every coupling in the correct tier and the nozzle finished in its ready position, in under 12 minutes with zero pattern faults on the final rep.
equipment: 200 ft of dry 1.75 in hose in 50 ft lengths
An engine in quarters, or a spare hose bed / bench mockup of the same width
The nozzle that lives on that preconnect
Full PPE (gloves at minimum; the pattern must be built in the gloves it will be pulled in)
Phone camera on a tripod or propped for an overhead-ish angle of the bed
Chalk or tape to mark the bed width on a bench if no apparatus is available
The department's hose load diagram or a photo of a correctly loaded bed
drills.setup: Stage the 200 ft flat on the ramp or floor with the nozzle at the far end, and set the phone to film the bed as it fills. Load pattern, hose size, and preconnect length here are examples: use your own department's diagram and its actual preconnect before running this drill. If no apparatus is available in quarters, tape the exact bed width on a bench or the floor and load into that footprint.
steps: Photograph a correctly loaded bed first, or open the diagram, and keep it visible for the first rep only.
Drag the 200 ft flat, straighten every twist out of each length, and mate the couplings hand-tight before loading anything.
Load the first rep slowly with the diagram in view, saying each fold and each coupling tier out loud on camera so the reasoning is on the recording.
Close the diagram, reset the hose flat, and run a timed rep from bare bed to nozzle in its ready position.

Score the finished bed against the photo: mark every coupling that landed in the wrong tier, every fold that stands proud of the bed rails, and whether the nozzle finished where the puller expects it.
Reset and run a final timed rep, then compare the film of rep one and the final rep side by side.
learning_points: A bed loaded wrong does not fail in the bay, it fails at 0300 when someone pulls and gets 80 ft and a wall of hose — the reload is the deployment, done in advance.
Couplings that land in the wrong tier are what turns a clean pull into a hang-up, because the coupling is the rigid part that catches on the bed rail and on itself.
Loading in gloves matters: a pattern that only works bare-handed is a pattern that changes shape at the fire, and the change always shows up as folds that are too loose.
Building the pattern to a diagram rather than to memory is how a whole company loads the same bed the same way — the person who pulls it is rarely the person who loaded it.
Twists left in the hose during the load become kinks under pressure that nobody can chase, because they are buried inside the flake.
common_mistakes: Loading over twists instead of straightening each length flat first, which guarantees kinks that survive the pull.
Letting folds stand proud of the bed rails so the load catches wind and hands on the way out.
Finishing the nozzle somewhere convenient instead of in the department's ready position, so the next person has to dig for it.
Working bare-handed because it is faster, then never testing whether the pattern holds in structural gloves.
Skipping the coupling check and only scoring the bed on how tidy it looks from the top.
safety_notes: Loading a bed alone means climbing on and off the tailboard repeatedly — set the parking brake, chock the wheels, and never load with the apparatus in a position where it could be moved.
Keep the running boards and tailboard dry; most reload injuries in quarters are slips, not lifts.
success_criteria: Final timed rep completed in under 12 minutes from bare bed to nozzle in ready position.
Zero couplings in the wrong tier on the final rep, scored against the department diagram or photo.
No fold standing proud of the bed rails on the final rep.
Nozzle finishes in the department's ready position on both timed reps.

variations.name: Second load pattern
variations.description: Reload the same hose into a different pattern the department uses on another apparatus or another preconnect.
variations.adds: Trains the firefighter to load to a diagram rather than to a single memorized shape, which matters on detail and on a reserve rig.

variations.name: 2.5 in bed
variations.description: Repeat the drill with 2.5 in hose into its bed.
variations.adds: Larger, stiffer hose exposes fold-length and coupling-tier errors that 1.75 in forgives.

variations.name: Pull test
variations.description: After a scored load, pull the whole preconnect off dry to the length it is meant to deploy, then score the pull for hang-ups before reloading.
variations.adds: Closes the loop between how the bed was loaded and how it actually pays off.

references: IFSTA Essentials of Fire Fighting — hose loads and finishes chapter
Department hose load diagram / apparatus inventory SOP (operator supplies)
drills.solo_note: One firefighter, dry hose, and the department's load diagram. The camera replaces the observer; the diagram replaces the instructor's judgement.

drills.title: Blind Appliance Identification and Assembly
drills.objective: With vision blocked, identify 8 of 8 engine appliances by feel within 10 seconds each, then assemble a called-out configuration hand-tight and correctly oriented in under 45 seconds.
equipment: Gated wye, siamese, reducers and increasers, double female and double male, hydrant wrench, spanner set
Two 50 ft lengths of dry 1.75 in and one 50 ft of 2.5 in hose
A blindfold, blacked-out SCBA facepiece, or taped face shield (worn in quarters only, not in any confined or elevated space)
A shallow box, tarp, or bench top to lay the appliances out on
drills.setup: Lay every appliance on a bench or tarp in the bay in random order, then have the firefighter learn the layout with vision, mix the order, and cover their eyes. Appliance inventory here is an example: use the appliances that actually ride on your engine, and drop any this drill lists that your department does not carry. Run entirely at floor level in quarters — no stairs, no elevation, no confined space while vision is blocked.
steps: With vision, handle every appliance once and name it out loud on camera along with what it is for and which end is the inlet.
Mix the layout, cover the eyes, and film a timed identification round: pick up each appliance, name it, and state inlet versus outlet, 10 second cap per item.
Set aside any item missed or over time, then re-handle those items with vision before repeating that subset blind.
Still blind, assemble a called configuration from a written list drawn at random — for example 2.5 in to gated wye with reducers to two 1.75 in lines — hand-tight and with inlets facing the supply.
Uncover, film a walk-around of the assembly, and score orientation: any coupling cross-threaded, backward, or hand-loose is a fault.
Repeat the assembly for two more configurations, resetting the appliances into a mixed pile each time.
learning_points: Appliances get grabbed in the dark, in smoke, and out of a compartment by touch far more often than they get selected off a clean bench — the hands have to know a double female from a double male without the eyes.
Getting the inlet backward on a gated wye or siamese does not fail loudly; it fails as a line that will not flow when the water is already moving, and the crew reads it as a pump problem.

Cross-threading under time is what happens when someone forces a coupling instead of backing it off a quarter turn first — and a cross-threaded appliance is out of service for the rest of the incident.
Naming the appliance and its purpose out loud is how the item becomes a decision rather than a shape; the firefighter who can only recognize it visually cannot call for it on the radio.
common_mistakes: Confusing double female and double male by feel because they are identified by size rather than by thread direction.
Assembling a gated wye with the inlet facing the attack lines, which only reveals itself when water is called for.
Forcing a coupling instead of backing off a quarter turn to find the thread, producing cross-threading under the clock.
Leaving couplings finger-loose because they seem tight enough while dry.
Learning the bench layout by position rather than the appliances by feel, so performance collapses when the pile is mixed.
safety_notes: Vision-blocked work stays at floor level in the bay with a clear path — no stairs, no tailboard, no elevated or confined space, and nothing on the floor that was not there when the layout was learned.
Working alone with vision blocked means uncovering the eyes at any point the firefighter is disoriented or has moved off the bench; there is nobody present to stop the drill for them.
Cast-iron appliances dropped on a foot are the realistic injury here — full PPE including boots for every round.
success_criteria: 8 of 8 appliances correctly named blind, each within 10 seconds.
Inlet versus outlet correctly stated on every appliance that has a direction.
Called configuration assembled blind, hand-tight and correctly oriented, in under 45 seconds.
Zero cross-threaded or backward couplings across all three assemblies.

variations.name: Gloved and mixed diameters
variations.description: Run the whole drill in structural gloves with 2.5 in, 1.75 in, and reducer combinations in the same pile.
variations.adds: Removes fingertip discrimination, which is the real condition, and forces size identification by hand span rather than touch detail.

variations.name: Compartment retrieval
variations.description: Instead of a bench, the appliances live in their actual apparatus compartment and are retrieved blind from there.
variations.adds: Trains the location of each appliance on the rig, which is the half of the skill a bench layout cannot teach.

variations.name: Radio call version
variations.description: The firefighter records a radio-style request for the appliance and configuration needed before assembling it.
variations.adds: Trains the vocabulary to ask for the right appliance over the air, where the wrong word gets the wrong item delivered.

variations.name: Fault injection
variations.description: Set one appliance in the pile with a damaged or capped fitting, or a wye with a closed gate.
variations.adds: Trains the firefighter to detect an unserviceable appliance by feel rather than assembling around it.

references: IFSTA Essentials of Fire Fighting — hose appliances and fittings chapter
Department apparatus inventory / compartment layout SOP (operator supplies)
drills.solo_note: One firefighter alone at floor level in the bay; the phone times and films, and the configuration slips replace the instructor's call. No safety role is removed.

drills.title: Dry Kink Hunt: Find It Before the Water Does
drills.objective: Chase a 200 ft dry lay routed through two corners and a doorway and clear every kink and coupling fault, finding 10 of 10 planted faults in under 3 minutes, verified on film.
equipment: 200 ft of dry 1.75 in hose in 50 ft lengths
A nozzle for the working end
Chalk or tape to mark the route, the corners, and the doorway
A hydrant that may be inspected but not charged, or any fixed object to serve as the supply anchor
Optional: a hose roller, salvage cover, or spare section to pad a corner
drills.setup: Chalk a route across the bay or ramp that includes two 90 degree corners and passes through a doorway, then lay 200 ft dry along it. Before the timed rep, the firefighter deliberately builds ten faults into the lay — hard bends at the corners, hose crossing itself, a coupling jammed against a door jamb, hose under a wheel or a pallet — and photographs each one so the score sheet exists before the clock starts. Hose size and length here are an example: substitute your department's attack line.
steps: Walk the chalked route once and photograph each of the ten planted faults, numbering them in the camera roll so the score is fixed before the rep.
Start at the nozzle end and film the whole chase from a phone carried or clipped at chest height so playback shows what was passed.
Work the line from nozzle back to the supply anchor, clearing each fault by pulling slack toward the bend rather than fighting the bend itself, and calling each fault out loud as it is cleared.
Round every corner properly: pull slack past the corner and set the hose to the outside of the turn, or pad the corner, rather than letting it lie in the angle.
Stop the timer at the supply anchor, then walk the route in reverse and count how many of the ten planted faults are actually gone.
Watch the film back and mark any fault the chase walked past, then re-run the route with the same ten faults rebuilt.
learning_points: A kink is a hidden pressure loss the nozzle firefighter cannot see and will misread as a bad pump or a fire that will not go out — the crew's response is usually to call for more pressure, which does not fix the kink.
Corners are where lines strangle: hose left lying in the angle of a 90 pinches under pressure, and the fix is slack pulled past the turn before the line is charged, not after.
A coupling jammed against a jamb or a stair nosing is a hard stop the nozzle team feels as a line that will not advance, and it is invisible from inside where they are.
Chasing a line dry is the only time the faults can be found for free; once the line is charged, clearing a kink means moving a hose full of water with no help from the pump.
Calling faults out loud builds the habit of reporting them, which is what gets the door held or the corner padded on the real stretch instead of quietly fixed and forgotten.
common_mistakes: Fighting the bend at the kink instead of feeding slack from the direction the hose came from.
Walking the line from the supply end toward the nozzle, which pushes slack the wrong way and creates new kinks behind the chase.
Clearing the visible kink at a corner but leaving the hose sitting in the inside angle, where it will pinch again the moment it is charged.
Missing the coupling faults entirely because the eyes are trained on hose bends and not on where the couplings landed.
Scoring the rep from memory instead of against the numbered photos taken before the clock started.
safety_notes: Run this on dry hose only — no charged line, no pump operator present, and the hydrant is inspected but never charged.
The route must not cross an apparatus bay door track or a path a rig could be moved along while the firefighter is working the line alone.
Hose pulled from under a wheel or a pallet is a pinch and strain hazard; move the object rather than dragging the hose out from under it.
success_criteria: 10 of 10 planted faults cleared, verified against the numbered pre-rep photos.
Timed chase from nozzle to supply anchor under 3 minutes.
Both corners finished with hose set on the outside of the turn or padded, checkable on film.
Zero new kinks introduced behind the chase, counted on the reverse walk.

variations.name: Low light
variations.description: Run the chase in a darkened bay with a hand light only.
variations.adds: Forces the firefighter to find faults by hand along the hose rather than by scanning it visually, which is the actual interior condition.

variations.name: Stair segment
variations.description: Route 50 ft of the lay up a flight of stairs with a landing turn.
variations.adds: Trains the stair-nosing coupling fault and the landing kink, which are the two that stop real high-rise and garden-apartment stretches.

variations.name: Blind score
variations.description: Have the faults planted from a written list the firefighter does not read until after the rep, or plant them a day earlier and score cold.
variations.adds: Removes the advantage of knowing where the faults are, which is what the drill is really testing.

variations.name: 2.5 in line
variations.description: Repeat the chase with 200 ft of 2.5 in.
variations.adds: Larger hose kinks differently and takes real body weight to reposition, exposing technique that 1.75 in lets you muscle through.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH firefighter fatality investigation reports document interior crews operating with inadequate or interrupted water on the attack line
lodd_connection.lesson: Pattern-level: when the line does not deliver, crews have stayed in deteriorating conditions expecting water that was never coming. Kinks and pinched lines are one of the mundane, entirely preventable causes of that gap between what the nozzle team expects and what the line actually delivers. The lesson is aimed at the system that leaves lines unchased, not at the judgement of any crew.

references: IFSTA Essentials of Fire Fighting — fire hose and advancing hoselines chapters
NIOSH Fire Fighter Fatality Investigation and Prevention Program (pattern-level, public reports)
UL FSRI fire attack research on flow and line management (public research)
drills.solo_note: Fully solo: the firefighter plants and photographs the faults, then chases and scores against the photos. Dry line only, so no pump operator or safety role is removed.

drills.title: Decontamination Corridor Setup (Wet & Dry)
drills.solo_note: A decon team processes a separate entry team; instructor applies UV simulant
drills.objective: Establish a technical decon corridor within 15 minutes, process an entry team through wet decon, and execute a dry/emergency decon sequence for a contaminated civilian or firefighter.
equipment: Water supply with wands or handline at reduced pressure
Dry decon materials (absorbent wipes/mitts, e.g., FiberTect-type)
drills.setup: Marked hot/warm/cold zones. Entry team in suits ready to process through. Cold-weather variant planned if seasonal.
steps: Lay out the corridor: entry point from hot zone, tool drop, gross wash, technical wash/rinse, doffing station, medical evaluation point.
Decon team dresses to one level below entry team protection, or to the level your SOP specifies — check it before the drill, don't assume the rule of thumb.
Process the entry team: gross decon, methodical wash with attention to hands/boots/closures, doffing without touching contaminated exterior surfaces.
Dry decon round: process a 'contaminated' subject using blot-and-wipe sequence — no water — with contaminated materials bagged and controlled.
Emergency decon round: ambulatory civilian, strip-and-flush priority sequence in under 2 minutes.
Debrief runoff control, doffing errors (the most common contamination transfer point), and time to operational corridor.
learning_points: Decon fails at doffing — the choreography of exiting a suit without self-contamination is the perishable core skill.
Dry decon is not a lesser option: for water-reactive products, cold weather, and speed, it's the correct one.
Emergency decon for a viable patient outruns technical decon setup every time — know the trigger to skip formality.
Runoff is a legal and environmental problem the team owns from the first drop of water.
common_mistakes: Suit removal is not choreographed, so contamination transfers to skin and clean areas during doffing.
Decon is set up downhill or downwind of the corridor, recontaminating the clean end.
The corridor is opened before water, containment, and staffing are ready, backing up entry crews.
safety_notes: Decon team is inside the warm zone — they wear protection accordingly.
Cold weather: hypothermia risk from wet decon drives the dry-first decision tree.
success_criteria: Corridor operational under 15 minutes
Zero doffing contamination transfers (instructor uses simulated contaminant/UV powder)
Correct dry decon sequence and waste control

variations.name: UV Powder Verification
variations.description: Apply UV-visible simulant to entry suits; blacklight inspection after decon reveals transfer points.
variations.adds: Objective, visual scoring of decon effectiveness — turns opinion into evidence.

variations.name: Mass Casualty Decon
variations.description: Process 10+ ambulatory 'civilians' through an expedient corridor.
variations.adds: Throughput problem: sequencing, privacy, and instructions to non-firefighters.

references: NFPA 470
OSHA HAZWOPER 1910.120
Department decon SOPs
drills.prerequisites: Two levels in one drill. Emergency decon is defensive and any trained member may perform it. Operating the technical decon corridor — processing a suited entry team in the warm zone — is mission-specific work: an Operations-level member may staff it only where your department has adopted technical decontamination as a mission-specific competency and this member is trained and authorized for it. Absent that, it is technician work. Confirm who is authorized to be in the warm zone and at what protection level before you run it; the answer is a local one and this drill does not supply it.

drills.title: Air Monitoring & Detection Sweep
drills.solo_note: Instructor pre-stages reading cards and the team states interpretations together

solo_variant.substitutions: Write your own reading cards — 12 index cards, one reading each (O2, LEL, CO, H2S), shuffled and taped around the station at varying heights. A phone voice recorder is your evaluator: state every interpretation out loud. A phone timer replaces the instructor's pacing. Bump gas and your own meter, no simulated gas needed.
steps: Write 12 reading cards before you start, then shuffle and tape them at high, chest and floor level around the station — mix realistic and nasty combinations so you cannot pattern-match.
Fresh-air zero and bump check the meter. Photograph the cal-gas date and sensor expiry; an out-of-date bump makes the whole hour theatre.
Start the voice recorder. Sweep the space with the real meter, moving deliberately slower than feels natural, taking each level high/middle/low.
At each card, say aloud: the product this suggests, the action level crossed, and what you do — mask up, back out, ventilate, call for technicians.
Run the instrument-limits round out loud: what the LEL sensor cannot see, what poisons it, why the O2 reading matters before the toxic number.
CO gradient run: have a card deck with ascending CO values placed toward one room; work the gradient to the source and state where you would stop.
Play the recording back and mark each call right or wrong against the meter manual and your action-level chart.
solo_variant.self_score: Bump and zero done before the first card without prompting. Playback: every card gets a stated action level and correct action — count the misses, target zero. Sweep heights correct for the product on the card. Full sweep of the space in under the time you set.
solo_variant.not_covered: No one argues with your interpretation, so a confidently wrong action level stays wrong until you check the chart. You also lose the pace-setting of a partner and the two-meter cross-check that catches a drifting sensor in the real world.

drills.objective: Operate multi-gas meters correctly: bump/zero discipline, sweep technique, action-level interpretation, and instrument-limitation awareness.
equipment: Simulated readings via instructor cards if live gas unavailable
drills.setup: Instructor pre-stages scenario cards at locations ('reading here: O2 20.9, LEL 0, CO 150'). Team sweeps and responds to what the cards/meter show.
steps: Fresh-air zero and bump check — the meter that isn't bumped is a guess in a case.
Teach sweep technique: high/middle/low at each location (vapor density drives where products live), slow movement matching sensor response time.
Sweep the scenario space; at each card/reading, the team states the interpretation and action level response.
Instrument limits round: what does the LEL sensor NOT see? What poisons it? Why does an O2 displacement reading matter before the toxic reading?
Scenario: CO call at a residence — locate the source by following the gradient.
Debrief the decision points: where would you have masked up, evacuated, or ventilated?
learning_points: Sensor response lag means walking speed is a data-quality variable — sweep slower than feels natural.
Vapor density determines search height; sweeping at chest level only finds chest-level products.
Action levels are pre-commitments: decide at 10% LEL what you'll do, not when you're standing in it.
Every instrument has blind spots; knowing what your meter can't tell you is the mark of a competent operator.
common_mistakes: The meter is used without a fresh-air zero and bump check, so readings cannot be trusted.
Crew sweeps only at chest level and misses products that stratify high or low by vapor density.
Members move faster than the sensor response time, walking into a hazard before it reads.
safety_notes: Live-gas exercises only with proper training gas and ventilation.
Expired sensors/cal gas invalidate the exercise — check dates (and log them).
success_criteria: Bump/zero performed unprompted
Correct height sweeps for stated products
Correct action-level responses at all cards

variations.name: CBRN Detector Round
variations.description: Integrate department CBRN detection equipment (e.g., LCD-series) with its own operating and limitation drill.
variations.adds: Low-frequency, high-consequence equipment stays usable only through reps; includes consumables/expiration checks.

variations.name: pH and Paper Round
variations.description: Add pH paper and other colorimetric tools on simulated liquids.
variations.adds: The cheap tools that answer the corrosive question meters don't.

references: NFPA 470
Manufacturer sensor documentation
drills.prerequisites: Air monitoring and sampling is a mission-specific competency. An Operations-level member may monitor only where your department has adopted it as a mission-specific category and authorized that member for it; absent that, hot-zone monitoring and the action-level call belong to the technician. The CBRN detection variation is technician or specialist work in most jurisdictions. Verify with your AHJ who is authorized to monitor, where they may do it, and who owns the action-level decision — this drill does not draw that line for you.

drills.title: Hazmat First-Due: Isolate, Deny, Identify
drills.solo_note: Others take denial-of-entry positions while someone scores the sequence

solo_variant.substitutions: A photo deck on your phone or printed — placards, container shapes, railcar markings, box-truck mixed loads — replaces the staged scenario stations. Voice recorder replaces the scorer. A wind app or a length of flagging tape on the yard fence gives you real wind. Current ERG, book or app.
steps: Build or download a deck of 10 container/placard photos. Shuffle so you do not know the order.
Stand in the station yard, note the actual wind direction from tape or a wind app, and pick a physical 'incident' point in the yard.
Turn over one photo. Before touching the ERG, say aloud: container shape, hazard class, and where you would stage — uphill and upwind of the point you picked, and pace out that distance for real.
Look up the UN number or guide in the ERG. State the initial isolation distance and the protective action distance out loud, then check yourself against the page.
Transmit a full hazmat report into the recorder: product or best ID, container, quantity estimate, conditions, resources requested.
State what you as an operations-level responder will and will not do here before technicians arrive.
Next card. At the end, play back the recording and score guide numbers and distances against the ERG.
solo_variant.self_score: Correct ERG guide number and both distances on every card — count them, aim for 10 of 10. Every scenario staged uphill and upwind of the actual wind, paced out not estimated. Every radio report contains all five elements on playback.
solo_variant.not_covered: You cannot practice denial of entry with nobody to deny, and you never feel the pull of a crew wanting to move in — the restraint this drill is really about is easy alone and hard with four people looking at you.

drills.objective: Execute correct operations-level first-due actions: recognize the hazmat problem, isolate at proper distances, deny entry, identify from safe references, and set up for the technician response.
drills.setup: Scenario stations: overturned MC-306 placard 1203, railcar with markings, box truck with mixed placards, unknown odor at a business.
steps: At each station, the officer works the sequence: approach from uphill/upwind, stop at a defensible distance, and read what's visible through binoculars.
Identify via placard/UN number/container shape; look it up in the ERG and state the guide's isolation distance.
Establish and announce zones; assign denial-of-entry positions.
Transmit the hazmat report: product (or best identification), container, quantity estimate, conditions, resources requested.
Discuss what operations-level personnel will and will not do at each scenario before technicians arrive.
Score the sequence order — identification from a distance BEFORE approach decisions.
learning_points: Container shape identifies the hazard class even when placards are missing or wrong.
The ERG's initial isolation distances exist to be used in the first five minutes, not read later.
The first-due company's restraint — staging, isolating, resisting the rush in — is the tactical skill.
Wind direction and topography are size-up elements at every hazmat scene.
common_mistakes: Crew approaches to read placards up close instead of identifying the product from a safe distance.
ERG isolation distances are applied late instead of in the first few minutes.
Wind and slope are ignored when setting the approach and isolation perimeter.
safety_notes: Reinforce that recognition of a hazmat problem changes the entire operational tempo — slower is correct.
success_criteria: Correct ERG guide and distances at every station
Uphill/upwind approach every time
Complete hazmat radio report

variations.name: Clandestine Lab Recognition
variations.description: Photo-based scenario of a residence with lab indicators discovered during an EMS or fire call.
variations.adds: Recognition-and-withdraw discipline for the hazmat scene nobody dispatched you to.

references: Current Emergency Response Guidebook
NFPA 470
drills.prerequisites: Operations level, and defensive by definition: isolate, deny entry, identify from a distance. No entry, no product contact, no offensive mitigation. Teaching that boundary is the point of the drill, not a caveat on it — an Operations-level member goes offensive only where the department has adopted a mission-specific competency and authorized that member for that specific action. Confirm with your AHJ which mission-specific categories, if any, your department has adopted; the list of what your members will NOT touch is a local one.

drills.title: Technician Leak Control: Chlorine Kit & Patching
drills.solo_note: Suited entry requires a backup team and an established decon line before entry
drills.objective: Apply Chlorine A/B kit components, dome clamp, and patching/plugging techniques on training props while managing suit time and dexterity limits.
equipment: 150 lb cylinder and ton-container props (or drums for patching)
Level A or B ensembles per scenario
drills.setup: Leaking-prop stations (water or air charged). Entry teams in appropriate protection with backup team and decon (HZM-001) established.
steps: Dry-run the kit on the prop without suits: every hood, gasket, and yoke component handled and named.
Suited evolution: entry team approaches, assesses the leak point (valve, fusible plug, side wall), and selects the control method.
Apply the kit per the leak location; torque and verify.
Drum station: select and apply plugs, wedges, and patches to pressure-appropriate leaks.
Track suit time and compare task time in suits vs. the dry run — quantify the dexterity tax.
Full decon and doffing to close the loop.
learning_points: Suit dexterity loss is 40-60% on fine tasks — every kit skill must be overlearned bare-handed first.
Leak location dictates the kit component; misdiagnosis wastes irreplaceable suit time.
The backup team is dressed and ready before entry, always — it's the RIT concept in a different uniform.
Air management in encapsulating suits includes the work, the walk, and the full decon corridor.
common_mistakes: Kit skills are attempted in suit without ever being overlearned bare-handed first.
The leak point is misdiagnosed, wasting irreplaceable suit and air time on the wrong fix.
The backup team is left undressed and unready when the entry team needs relief or rescue.
safety_notes: Water/air-charged props only.
Heat stress monitoring and medical surveillance per SOP for suited evolutions.
Suit integrity checks before entry.
success_criteria: Leak controlled on the prop
Suit time within air budget including decon
Correct kit component selection

variations.name: Scenario Integration
variations.description: Full sequence from HZM-003 first-due through HZM-001 decon with this entry in the middle.

drills.prerequisites: Hazmat Technician. This drill is offensive — entry, product contact, and leak control on a pressurized container — and going offensive is precisely what technician certification qualifies a member to do. Operations-level members remain defensive: they observe from the cold zone, they do not enter, and they do not stand up as backup, unless your department has adopted a mission-specific competency that authorizes this action and this member for it. Verify certification, entry authorization, medical clearance for encapsulated entry, and your kit generation against your AHJ and team SOP before anyone dons a suit. This is a prerequisite, not a preference.

drills.title: Product Behavior Tabletop: Chemistry That Kills
drills.solo_note: A facilitator presents products and facilitation rotates among members

solo_variant.substitutions: Index cards replace the facilitator: one product per card — HF, sodium hydroxide, MMA with failed inhibitor, anhydrous ammonia — written product-side only, with the situation on the back. Shuffle them. A voice recorder is the group you would normally talk to. Phone timer for a 5-minute commitment window per card.
steps: Write four scenario cards, product and situation only, no answers. Shuffle face down.
Turn one over, start a 5-minute timer, and keep every reference shut.
Talk your answer into the recorder: what makes this product dangerous, how it behaves on release, and your tactical answer including decon and treatment implications.
When the timer goes, open the ERG, WISER or CAMEO and verify. Write what you missed on the back of the card.
Repeat for all four. On the MMA card, say out loud the specific runaway indicators and why the correct tactic is distance, not entry.
Then teach it: record a two-minute explanation of each product as if briefing a probationer. If you cannot explain it cleanly, you do not own it.
Keep the cards. Re-run in a month cold and see whether the misses stayed fixed.
solo_variant.self_score: Score each card against the reference: hazard mechanism, behavior on release, tactical answer, decon or treatment note — four points, sixteen available. Under 12 means run it again next week. HF card must include delayed presentation and calcium binding or it is a fail regardless of the rest.
solo_variant.not_covered: The disagreement is the drill in the crew version — somebody else's wrong answer forces you to defend yours. Alone you never get argued out of a comfortable assumption, and you do not get the reps of facilitating for others.

drills.objective: Predict product behavior and correct tactics for high-consequence chemicals using scenario discussion: HF, sodium hydroxide, monomer polymerization runaways, anhydrous ammonia.
drills.setup: Station or classroom. Facilitator presents a product and situation; group works the problem before references are opened, then verifies.
steps: Scenario 1 — HF exposure at an industrial site: group states why HF is different (systemic toxicity, calcium binding, delayed presentation) and the treatment/decon implications.
Scenario 2 — sodium hydroxide release: corrosive behavior, reaction with water and metals, decon considerations.
Scenario 3 — MMA or similar monomer with failed inhibitor: recognize polymerization runaway indicators (container heating, bulging) and why cooling and distance beat entry.
Scenario 4 — anhydrous ammonia leak: vapor cloud behavior, water application debate (when a fog curtain helps vs. when water on the liquid makes it worse).
Each scenario ends with the group's tactical answer, then verification against references.
Rotate facilitation among members — teaching it is the deepest rep.
learning_points: A handful of chemicals cause a disproportionate share of responder injuries — deep familiarity with the worst actors pays off.
Polymerization runaway is a container-catastrophe timeline, not a leak problem; the correct tactic is often withdrawal.
HF looks like a minor burn and kills a day later — the recognition failure is the fatal step.
Reference tools (WISER/CAMEO) are only fast in hands that use them monthly.
common_mistakes: HF exposure is treated as a minor burn, missing delayed systemic toxicity.
A polymerization runaway is worked as a leak problem instead of a container-failure problem.
Crew fixates on the visible release and ignores the product's next predictable behavior.
success_criteria: Correct hazard characterization before opening references
Tactically sound answers on all scenarios

drills.title: Placard & Container ID: Beat the ERG Clock
drills.objective: From a photo held at arm's length or read through binoculars, correctly name the placard/container clue and open to the correct ERG orange-bordered guide page in under 60 seconds on at least 8 of 10 shuffled cards.
equipment: Self-built shuffled deck of 20-40 placard, label, and container photos (bulk shots, rail cars, cargo tanks, cylinders, marine placards, four-digit UN panels)
Printed or app placard/container reference (answer key you build while assembling the deck)
drills.setup: Working alone, build the deck from open photos: capture or print placards and container shapes, and on the back of each card write the correct UN/ID number, ERG guide number, and container type so the card scores itself. Set the deck face down, timer ready, ERG closed at your side, and prop one card at the far end of a hallway or driveway so at least a few reps force a binocular read at distance.
steps: Shuffle the deck face down and start the voice recorder to narrate each rep for later review.

Flip one card (or read the distant propped card through binoculars), start the timer, and say aloud what you see: placard color, symbol, hazard class number, any four-digit number, and container shape.

Drive the clue into the ERG by the fastest correct path — yellow-bordered pages for a UN number, blue for a name, or the placard table when only the placard is visible — and stop the timer when you reach the correct orange guide page.
Flip the card and check your guide number, container type, and UN number against the answer on the back; log the elapsed time and whether it was a clean hit.
Sort every miss or over-60-second card into a retry pile and run that pile again at the end of the round.
After 10 cards, replay the recorder and check that each verbal size-up named color, symbol, and number before you opened the book.
learning_points: The ERG has three doors in — UN number (yellow), name (blue), placard (the placard table) — and picking the wrong door first is what burns the clock; a first-due firefighter who fumbles the lookup is standing still while a vapor cloud is not.

A placard gives a hazard class and often a four-digit number, but container shape and markings frequently tell you more than a weathered or missing placard, so training the eye to read the vessel means you still get an answer when the diamond is gone.
Speaking the size-up out loud before touching the book builds the on-scene radio report — the same words become your transmission to dispatch and to the incoming technicians.

Sixty seconds sounds generous at the kitchen table and evaporates on the ramp; compressing the clue-to-guide-page time is the difference between a protective-action call made early and one made after the plume moves.
common_mistakes: Grabbing the placard table when a clear four-digit UN number is present, when the yellow-bordered numeric index is the faster and more specific route to the material.
Reading the guide number off the placard's hazard class instead of the assigned UN/ID number and landing on a generic guide when a specific one exists.
Calling a container by family ('a tanker') instead of by type (MC-306/DOT-406 non-pressure vs. MC-331 pressure), which changes the product expectation and the guide.
Stopping the clock at the ERG index instead of the orange guide page, hiding the several seconds it takes to actually flip to the guidance that matters.
safety_notes: Do the binocular and reading reps stationary — never run this deck while driving or walking in traffic to a vantage point.
This is a cold-zone table drill only; it rehearses recognition, never approach to or contact with a real container.
success_criteria: 8 of 10 cards reach the correct orange ERG guide page in under 60 seconds, verified against the card's answer key.
Every verbal size-up on the recording states placard color/symbol, hazard class or UN number, and container type before the ERG is opened.
Container type is named specifically (pressure vs. non-pressure cargo tank, rail tank car vs. hopper, cylinder vs. bulk) on at least 8 of 10 cards.

variations.name: Weathered & Partial Placards
variations.description: Salt half the deck with photos of faded, torn, snow-covered, or absent placards where only container shape, stenciling, or rail reporting marks are visible.
variations.adds: Forces identification from the vessel and markings when the diamond fails — the real-world condition of many placards.

variations.name: Distance-Only Round
variations.description: Run the entire deck propped at the far end of a lot or hallway, read exclusively through binoculars, no arm's-length cards.
variations.adds: Trains the actual first-due skill of reading a placard from a safe distance rather than up close.

variations.name: Name the Downwind Hazard
variations.description: After reaching the guide page, also state aloud whether the material is primarily a fire, health, or reactivity threat and which ERG section drives the initial action.
variations.adds: Links recognition to a first tactical read instead of stopping at the lookup.

references: DOT/PHMSA Emergency Response Guidebook — how-to-use section and placard table
IFSTA Hazardous Materials for First Responders — recognition and identification
NFPA 470 competency areas for awareness/operations recognition (general reference; no compliance claimed)
drills.solo_note: Built for one firefighter: you assemble and self-score the deck, time yourself, and replay your own recording — no instructor, timer, or partner is required.

drills.title: ERG Distance Cards: Isolate and Pace Your District
drills.objective: Look up the correct ERG initial isolation distance and daytime and nighttime protective-action distances for 5 assigned materials in under 90 seconds each, then walk or map one isolation distance in your own district and land within 10 percent of the ERG figure.
equipment: Current Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG) including the green-bordered Table 1
Self-built card set of 8-12 materials that are highlighted (green-bordered) in the ERG, with UN numbers
Map of the firefighter's own district (paper or app with a measuring tool)
Wind indicator or weather app (for the small/large spill and day/night reasoning)
A known pace count or a phone/GPS distance measure for the field leg
drills.setup: Pick real intersections, the rail siding, or a fixed facility in your district as the notional release points and note them on the map. Build a card for each material with only its name and UN number on the front and the correct Table 1 figures on the back so the set self-scores. Target figures used as examples here come straight from the ERG edition in hand — confirm you are using the current edition, since the tabulated distances change between editions.
steps: Draw a material card, start the timer, and decide small vs. large spill and day vs. night, stating your reasoning into the recorder.
Find the material in the green-bordered Table 1 by UN number, read the initial isolation distance and the matching protective-action distance, and stop the timer when you have both.
Flip the card and check both figures and your small/large and day/night choice against the answer; log the time and any error.
Choose one card and mark its release point on the district map, then draw the initial isolation zone as a circle of that radius and the protective-action zone as the downwind box.
Take that isolation radius to the street: from the release point, pace it or measure it with GPS along a safe sidewalk or lot, and note the real landmark that sits at the edge of the zone.
Record a 30-second debrief naming what falls inside the isolation circle at that real location — which homes, roads, or occupancies you would be moving or blocking.
learning_points: Table 1 distances split on small vs. large spill and day vs. night, and picking the wrong column undersizes the zone — a night release of a heavier-than-air gas travels farther than the daytime number a rushed responder might grab.

An isolation distance is an abstraction until you stand at its edge; pacing it in your own first-due turns '400 meters' into 'the far side of the school,' which is the judgment you need at 0300 with no time to measure.

The initial isolation is a full circle around the release while the protective-action distance is a downwind footprint — confusing the two either strands people who should move or evacuates a whole circle needlessly.
Knowing which occupancies, roads, and exposures sit inside the zone before the call lets the first-due firefighter give a specific, actionable isolation order instead of a vague 'keep people back.'
These figures are initial and conservative, meant to buy time until technicians and monitoring refine them — treating the ERG number as the final answer, high or low, misreads its purpose.
common_mistakes: Reading the initial isolation distance and calling it the evacuation distance, skipping the separate protective-action column entirely.
Defaulting to the small-spill or daytime figure without justifying the choice, producing a zone too small for the actual conditions.
Looking the material up in the orange guides and never opening Table 1, so a highlighted material's specific distances are missed.
Pacing the distance in a straight ideal line on the map when buildings, rivers, or a highway would actually shape where people can and cannot be moved.
safety_notes: Pace the field leg only on safe sidewalks, lots, or shoulders; obey traffic and never step into a roadway to make the distance come out even.
Stay on public ground or property you may lawfully be on — do not trespass to complete a measurement.
This is a planning and pacing exercise around notional release points; there is no real product, container, or entry involved.
success_criteria: Correct initial isolation and both day/night protective-action figures pulled from Table 1 within 90 seconds on at least 4 of 5 cards.
The small/large and day/night column choice is stated and correct on at least 4 of 5 cards.
The paced or GPS-measured field distance lands within 10 percent of the ERG isolation figure and a real landmark at the zone edge is named.

variations.name: Wind Shift Recalc
variations.description: Midway through the map work, change the wind direction on the weather app and redraw the protective-action footprint from the new bearing.
variations.adds: Trains re-orienting the downwind zone on the fly instead of treating the first footprint as fixed.

variations.name: Rail Volume Jump
variations.description: Swap a highway small-spill scenario for a rail tank car large-spill of the same material and rerun the lookup and the map.
variations.adds: Shows how container volume drives the small-to-large jump and how much the zone grows with it.

variations.name: Non-Highlighted Material
variations.description: Add a material NOT green-bordered in the ERG and require the correct fallback to the orange guide's protective-action guidance instead of Table 1.
variations.adds: Teaches when Table 1 does and does not apply and where the isolation guidance lives otherwise.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH and hazmat after-action reports document responders positioned or holding the public too close to a release before isolation distances were properly established.
lodd_connection.lesson: Setting and physically understanding isolation and protective-action distances early keeps both responders and the public out of the zone that initial conservative guidance is designed to clear.

references: DOT/PHMSA Emergency Response Guidebook — green-bordered Table 1 (Initial Isolation and Protective Action Distances) and how-to-use section
IFSTA Hazardous Materials for First Responders — isolation and protective actions
NIOSH/hazmat after-action pattern literature on responder and public positioning (general reference)
drills.solo_note: One firefighter runs the whole thing alone: self-scoring cards, own timer and recorder, and a solo walk of the isolation distance in the district on foot.

drills.title: Cold-Zone Vantage: Wind, Slope, and the Safe Approach
drills.objective: For 3 district sites, choose an initial staging vantage that is upwind and upgrade of a notional placarded release and at or beyond the ERG initial isolation distance, read wind direction to within about 45 degrees, and justify each choice on the recorder in under 2 minutes.
equipment: Wind indicator (flag, ribbon, or grass) or a weather app with wind direction
Map of the firefighter's own district
Placard/container reference for choosing the notional material
drills.setup: Select three real district locations with different geometry — a rail siding in a low cut, a highway on a grade, and a fixed facility beside housing — and pick a plausible placarded material for each. Stand only at legal public vantage points well outside any real hazard; nothing is actually released. Note that any distance and material used here is an example for the exercise, not a prediction about those sites.
steps: At the first site, read the current wind with the flag/ribbon or app and state the direction it is coming FROM into the recorder, then confirm it against a second cue (smoke, grass, dust).
Name the notional material and pull its ERG initial isolation distance so you know how far out 'far enough' is.
Using the map and the terrain in front of you, pick a staging vantage that is upwind AND upgrade of the release point and outside the isolation distance, and mark it on the map.
From that vantage, use binoculars to confirm you can actually read the placard and container from there; if you cannot, move farther or reposition and note the trade-off out loud.
Record a 90-second size-up as if transmitting: material or best clue, wind, your position relative to the release, the isolation call, and the technician resources you would request.
Repeat at the other two sites, then replay all three recordings and check that every vantage was upwind, upgrade, and outside the isolation distance.
learning_points: Positioning upwind and upgrade is the free protection a first-due firefighter controls before any product is identified — most vapors and many liquids move downhill and downwind, so the wrong initial park spot puts the responder in the plume they are trying to report.

Wind is stated by where it comes FROM, and getting that backward flips the whole size-up; the discipline of confirming direction with a second cue prevents a single misread flag from placing everyone downwind.
A vantage has to satisfy two competing needs — far enough to be safe, close enough to read the placard through binoculars — and consciously trading one against the other is the real cold-zone skill.
Choosing the spot on real district terrain, not a flat map, teaches that a cut, a ridge, or a building row changes where the safe ground actually is, which a generic isolation circle never shows.
The vantage decision and the resource request are one act: identifying from distance is only useful if it is paired with calling the right technicians early rather than waiting to get closer.
common_mistakes: Reporting wind by the direction it is blowing toward instead of the direction it comes from, inverting the safe side of the incident.
Picking a vantage for the best view and backing into the hazard, letting the desire to read the placard pull the position too close or downwind.
Treating the isolation distance as flat-ground radius and ignoring a downhill draw or valley that funnels vapor past a nominally 'far enough' spot.
Stopping at identification and never stating the technician/mutual-aid resource request, which is the point of holding the line from the cold zone.
safety_notes: Stand only at legal, safe public vantage points for the whole drill; this rehearses where you WOULD stage, using notional releases, and never involves an actual product or approach.
Mind live traffic and footing at real roadside and rail vantage points, and stay clear of active rail right-of-way.
Do not enter private property to reach a vantage; use public ground or locations you may lawfully occupy.
success_criteria: All 3 chosen vantages are upwind and upgrade of the notional release and at or beyond the ERG initial isolation distance, verifiable on the marked map.
Wind direction stated as 'from' is within about 45 degrees of the confirmed reading at each site.
Each recorded size-up names the identification clue, the position rationale, and a specific technician/mutual-aid resource request in under 2 minutes.

variations.name: Wind Against the Slope
variations.description: Choose a site or a time when the wind pushes uphill against the terrain's natural downhill drainage, forcing a conflict between upwind and upgrade.
variations.adds: Trains resolving the two positioning rules when they disagree, and stating the reasoning for the compromise.

variations.name: Night / Low-Light Read
variations.description: Run one site at dusk or dark and judge whether the placard is even readable through binoculars, deciding what you can and cannot confirm from distance.
variations.adds: Forces honest limits on identification when vision fails and how that changes the resource request.

variations.name: Access Road Denial
variations.description: Declare the obvious approach road inside the hot zone, requiring an alternate ingress and vantage that keeps apparatus and staging clean.
variations.adds: Links personal vantage choice to where you would route and stage arriving apparatus.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH and hazmat after-action reports document responders overtaken by vapor or fire after positioning downwind or downhill of a release.
lodd_connection.lesson: Deliberate upwind, upgrade, outside-the-isolation-distance positioning at arrival removes the exposure before the product is even identified.

references: DOT/PHMSA Emergency Response Guidebook — initial isolation and general safety approach guidance
IFSTA Hazardous Materials for First Responders — scene control, approach, and positioning
NIOSH/hazmat after-action pattern literature on responder positioning relative to wind and terrain (general reference)
drills.solo_note: Designed for a lone firefighter: you read the wind, pick and map the vantage, and self-check the three recordings yourself with no partner or observer needed.

drills.title: Case Study Drill: Keokuk / Flow Path & Coordinated Attack
drills.solo_note: Charged-line evolution needs a pump operator plus door-control assignments
drills.objective: Study a flow-path LODD incident, then physically run the corrected evolution: door control, coordinated water-first sequence, and withdrawal triggers.
equipment: NIOSH report excerpts and timeline handout
drills.setup: Part 1 classroom (30 min): walk the incident timeline. Part 2 practical (60 min): run the scenario as it happened (talk-through) and as it should run (full evolution).
steps: Present the incident timeline without the outcome first; at each decision point, ask 'what would you do here?' and record answers.
Reveal the actual sequence and outcome; compare against the group's choices without judgment of the original crews.
Physical evolution: replicate the building flow (door positions, attack path) with the smoke machine showing air movement.
Run the corrected sequence: water ready before openings, door control assignments, coordinated ventilation.
Debrief the difference the crew could FEEL between the two runs.
Close with the memorial context: names, date, and what the fire service changed afterward.
learning_points: LODD reports are the fire service's most expensive textbooks — this format converts reading into muscle memory.
Decision-point pauses before the reveal defeat hindsight bias; crews discover they'd have made similar calls.
The physical run is the retention mechanism — flow path felt at a door outlasts flow path read in a report.
Honoring the fallen through competence, not just ceremony.
common_mistakes: The evolution is talked through but never physically run, so the flow-path lesson never becomes muscle memory.
Ventilation is drilled separately from attack, repeating the exact uncoordinated error from the case.
The debrief blames the original crew instead of examining the system that set them up.
safety_notes: Facilitate with respect — no armchair criticism of deceased firefighters. The framing is 'the system that put them there,' not the individuals.
success_criteria: Crew articulates the causal chain
Corrected evolution executed cleanly
Each member states one behavior they'll change

variations.name: Template for Any NIOSH Report
variations.description: This same three-part structure (blind timeline, reveal, corrected evolution) applies to any report. The app can present a rotating report each month with the drill auto-structured.
variations.adds: A renewable content engine: NIOSH publishes the scenarios; this format makes them trainable.

lodd_connection.incident: Keokuk, Iowa (1999) — three firefighters and three children died during a search-and-rescue attempt at an apartment fire; NIOSH's recommendations center on staffing, size-up, risk-versus-gain evaluation, defensive search, accountability, and fireground communications
lodd_connection.lesson: Every opening is a tactical decision. Water and ventilation are one coordinated act, not two independent tasks.

references: NIOSH F2000-04
UL FSRI flow path research

drills.title: Charleston Sofa Super Store: Big Fire Discipline
drills.solo_note: Multi-company evolution with 2.5 in lines, LDH supply, accountability PARs, and a facilitator
drills.objective: Study the 2007 Charleston LODD, then run the counterfactual evolution: commercial fire with big-line attack, sustained water supply, accountability, and early defensive triggers.
equipment: Large footprint building or marked area
drills.setup: Classroom timeline session, then a commercial-scenario evolution built to exercise the specific systems that failed: water supply, line selection, accountability, and command triggers.
steps: Timeline with decision-point pauses: initial attack line choice, water supply status, crew tracking, and the window in which withdrawal was possible.
Identify the systemic findings: small lines for a big fuel load, supply limitations, accountability breakdown, and command structure gaps.
Evolution: companies arrive at a 'commercial fire' — first line must be a 2.5 in with sustained supply established before deep commitment.
Accountability run exactly per SOP with PARs at benchmarks; command declares strategy and the withdrawal trigger criteria out loud at the start.
Inject deteriorating conditions; command executes the defensive transition (integrates MCO-003).
Debrief against the findings: which of tonight's behaviors map to which finding. Nine firefighters died at Charleston — the debrief earns that by being specific about the system that failed them.
learning_points: Commercial fuel loads outmatch residential attack habits — line selection is a survival decision.
Water supply is a precondition for interior commitment in big boxes, not a parallel task.
Withdrawal triggers declared in advance get executed; triggers invented under stress get negotiated.
Nine firefighters died in one building; the systemic reforms afterward touched nearly every finding this drill exercises.
common_mistakes: Crews reach for small attack lines on a large commercial fuel load.
Interior commitment is made before a sustained water supply is actually established.
Withdrawal triggers are invented under stress instead of being declared before entry.
safety_notes: Same respectful facilitation standard as LODD-001.
success_criteria: 2.5 in first line deployed
Supply established before deep interior benchmark
PARs on time
Defensive transition executed on trigger

lodd_connection.incident: Charleston Sofa Super Store (2007) — nine firefighters killed in a furniture showroom fire
lodd_connection.lesson: Big fires punish small-fire habits. Line size, water supply, accountability, and pre-declared triggers are the countermeasures.

references: NIOSH F2007-18
Routley Charleston independent review

drills.title: Case Study Drill: Bronx, Black Sunday — Bailout & Egress
drills.solo_note: Bailout reps demand a qualified instructor plus an independent belay
drills.objective: Study the Bronx fire of FDNY's Black Sunday (January 23, 2005), then train the associated survival skills: window ledge discipline, personal escape system deployment (per department equipment), and the mayday-first sequence a lost egress demands.
equipment: Personal escape systems if issued (bailout kits)
Low-height window prop with belay for any bailout practice
drills.setup: Classroom timeline, then practical skills scaled to department equipment: full bailout training if systems are issued and instructors qualified; ledge/last-resort discussion and RIT integration if not.
steps: Timeline: the fire below, the illegal subdivision that erased the expected layout, the loss of the stairway, the fact that the department had stopped issuing escape rope five years before, and the window decisions on the fourth floor.
Discuss the housing-stock intelligence angle: illegally subdivided occupancies change every assumption about layout and egress.
If equipped: escape system deployment reps on the low prop with belay — anchor selection, controlled exit, descent.

If not equipped: window discipline round — ledge positioning, calling the mayday from the window, ladder rescue integration (TRK-004), and the honest departmental conversation about whether systems should be purchased.

Crew integrity round: scenario reps on recognizing and calling loss of contact. Train this as a survival habit in its own right. If you want the Black Sunday tie, it belongs to the Brooklyn fire the same day (NIOSH F2005-04), where a firefighter and his officer became separated on a basement stairwell — it is not what happened in the Bronx.
Close with memorial context and the reform this fire drove — FDNY moving to issue personal escape systems, and the nationwide bailout adoption that followed.
learning_points: The incident that drove nationwide bailout equipment adoption is the reason the skill exists — context creates buy-in for a high-risk-to-train skill.
Building intelligence (illegal subdivision patterns in the district) is a survival input, not an inspection issue.
Crew separation is the precursor condition in a large share of survival incidents.
A window is a defensible position with a sequence: mayday, ledge discipline, ladder or system — panic jumps are what the sequence prevents.
common_mistakes: Bailout is practiced without an independent belay and low-height progression, setting up training injuries.
Crew separation is not recognized as the precursor condition that leads to the emergency.
The window is treated as a panic jump instead of a sequenced mayday-ledge-ladder bailout.
safety_notes: Bailout training ONLY with manufacturer-approved systems, qualified instructors, and independent belay — this skill has caused training injuries.
Low-height progression mandatory.
success_criteria: Causal chain articulated
If equipped: controlled deployment on belay
Crew integrity decision points correctly identified in scenarios

lodd_connection.incident: Bronx, NY (January 23, 2005) — one of two fires on FDNY's "Black Sunday," on which three firefighters died citywide. Six firefighters searching above the fire were cut off in an illegally subdivided apartment and went out fourth-floor windows: two were killed, four were critically injured, and one of those four died of his injuries in 2011

drills.title: NIOSH Report Study Template (Renewable Monthly Drill)
drills.solo_note: A facilitator prepares the blind timeline and the crew commits to choices together

solo_variant.substitutions: You prepare your own blind timeline: read the report once, then write decision points on index cards face down and do not reread the outcome. A voice recorder captures your commitment at each point before the reveal — that is the evidence you cannot retro-fit an answer. Pick a hands-on skill you can do alone: mask-up sequence, tool throw, hydrant hookup, ladder carry at ground level.
steps: Pick a NIOSH LODD or near-miss report you have not read. Read only the summary and incident description — stop before findings.
Write each decision point on a card in sequence, face down. Then work them one at a time.
BLIND TIMELINE, 15 min: turn a card, state into the recorder what you would do and why, then read the report's next section. No revising your earlier answer.
FINDINGS, 10 min: read the NIOSH contributing factors and compare honestly against your recording. Write down every point where you would have made the same call.
SO WHAT, HERE, 15 min: name the specific SOP, the specific building in your district, and the specific habit on your shift that this report touches. Vague answers do not count.

HANDS ON, 20 min: perform the skill the report points to — solo-safe only. No live fire, no charged line, no ladder work unheeled, no on-air entanglement props. If the report's skill cannot be done safely alone, do the nearest solo-safe component and note the gap.
Log the report number, the skill, and the one action item. Keep the log — the value is the accumulation.
solo_variant.self_score: Recording shows a committed answer at every decision point before the reveal. At least one NIOSH finding matched to a specific SOP, building or habit by name, not a generality. The skill physically performed for the full 20 minutes, not discussed. Log entry written before you leave.
solo_variant.not_covered: The blind timeline is compromised the moment you have skimmed the report, so you will never get it as clean as a facilitator can give it. You also lose the honest moment when three people commit to different actions and one of them matches what the dead firefighter did — that is the part that changes behavior, and you cannot manufacture it alone.

drills.objective: Run any NIOSH LODD or near-miss report through a standard four-part study structure that ends in a concrete, practiced skill — making the report library a renewable monthly training source.
equipment: Timeline handout prepared from the report
Whatever equipment the derived skill requires
drills.setup: Facilitator (rotate this role monthly) prepares the blind timeline and identifies the one trainable skill the report points to.
steps: BLIND TIMELINE (15 min): present the incident up to each decision point; crew commits to choices before the reveal.
FINDINGS (10 min): NIOSH contributing factors, compared honestly against the crew's own choices.
SO WHAT, HERE (15 min): map every finding to this department — which SOP, which building in the district, which habit on this shift.
HANDS ON (20 min): perform the single skill the report points to — a stretch, a PAR, a door-control sequence, a mayday rep.
Log the report number and the skill trained; the app tracks which reports the crew has completed.
Near-miss variant: use firefighternearmiss.com reports with the same structure for non-fatal lessons.
learning_points: The reports are free, and there is no shortage of them — every one is somebody's worst day, written down so it doesn't have to be ours. A standing structure turns them into a curriculum instead of occasional reading.
The 'So What, Here' step is where transfer happens; findings without local mapping evaporate.
Ending hands-on, every time, is the difference between a safety meeting and a drill.
Rotating facilitation builds every member's ability to extract lessons — a promotional-development side effect.
common_mistakes: The study ends at discussion with no hands-on skill, becoming just a safety meeting.
Findings are not mapped to this department's SOPs and buildings, so nothing actually changes.
Crews see the outcome before committing to a blind-timeline decision, losing the anti-hindsight value.
safety_notes: Respectful framing standard applies to every report.
success_criteria: All four parts completed
Local mapping produced at least one specific action item
Skill physically performed by all members

variations.name: App-Powered Selection
variations.description: The app suggests a report matched to the crew's recent drill history (e.g., crews that just trained stretching get a stretch-related LODD).
variations.adds: Spaced reinforcement — the case study lands on freshly trained skill.
