drills.title: Reading Engineered Construction: The Silent Collapse
drills.solo_note: Crews score photo rounds together; the tabletop needs radio role-players

solo_variant.substitutions: A shuffled photo deck replaces the instructor's rounds - build 30-40 images of trusses, I-joists, gusset plates, glulam and matched dimensional lumber, and let a week pass before you use them. Phone stopwatch for the 30-second rounds. Voice recorder for the tabletop transmissions. A worksheet you print and fill by hand so the misses are on paper.
steps: Build the deck: 30-40 photos from street, attic and basement viewpoints, with the answer written on the back or in a separate answer key. Shuffle it and leave it a week so you are recognizing, not remembering.

PHOTO ROUNDS: 10 images, 30 seconds each on the stopwatch. Write on the worksheet: assembly type, the feature that identified it, above or below a likely fire, and the tactical implication. No going back to change an answer.
Score against the key. For every miss, write down the feature you should have seen - not just the right answer.
TEACHING BLOCK on yourself: for each miss, say out loud why that assembly fails at the connection or the web while dimensional lumber chars and telegraphs. Silent failure, no sag, then sudden loss.

TABLETOP: draw a floor plan, pull a scenario card you wrote earlier - basement or cockloft fire in an engineered building - and set a random hidden failure window on a countdown timer you cannot see. Start the recorder.

Feed yourself time-since-arrival and fire-location cues only, at intervals. Transmit the assembly-based limit out loud when you make the call - roof off the table, no crews on the floor above, defensive transition - and state the recognition trigger in words.
Check the transmission time against the hidden timer. Late is late, and write down the earliest cue you had that should have triggered it.

NON-ENTRY WALK: pick a building you may lawfully walk around. Street level only, alone - no roof, no floor openings, no mechanical spaces, no fire-damaged or posted-unsafe structure, and nothing that needs a safety officer watching your feet. Call each visible assembly aloud into the recorder and name one place you would refuse to operate and why.
Log the day's photo score and the tabletop decision times. Track them week to week - the score is the drill.
solo_variant.self_score: 8 of 10 or better on the photo rounds, each correct call carrying a written identifying feature - a right answer with no feature is not a point. Tabletop transmission recorded before the hidden timer expires, with the trigger stated in words. Every late call has its earliest available cue written on the worksheet.
solo_variant.not_covered: You do not get another set of eyes calling a feature you missed, which is most of the value of scoring photo rounds as a crew. No radio net, no officers pushing back, no driver-engineer read from the panel. And the walk-through is street level only - the attic access and exposed floor assembly need a second person controlling movement, so you lose them.

drills.objective: Each crew correctly identifies the construction assembly (truss roof, I-joist floor, or dimensional) in at least 8 of 10 photo rounds and, in the tabletop scenario, calls the correct 'off the roof / off the floor above' decision before the instructor-defined failure window based on fire location — not on a clock.
equipment: 10-15 photographs or drawings of engineered assemblies (open-web parallel-chord trusses, wooden I-joists, gusset/gang-nail plates, glue-laminated beams) shown from street, attic, and basement viewpoints
Matched set of dimensional-lumber photos for contrast
Portable radios (one per crew for the tabletop command net)
Access to a training tower or bay, or any real building the crew may lawfully walk around/into for a non-entry assembly-spotting round
drills.setup: Run in a classroom or bay with a projector or printed photo rounds staged in numbered stations. Pre-select a real building for the non-entry walk-through where crews can view a roofline, an attic access, and an exposed floor/ceiling assembly (parking garage, unfinished bay, mechanical room) WITHOUT entering any weakened or fire-damaged space and WITHOUT loading any real floor or roof. Any fire behavior timing, target GPM, apparatus placement, or roof-operation policy referenced in the tabletop is an example only — substitute your department's tactical SOGs and construction-era building stock before running.
steps: Brief the pattern, not one incident: multiple NIOSH line-of-duty reports document firefighters killed or injured when engineered and lightweight assemblies failed early and with little or no warning. Frame the day's goal as recognition and decision timing, not speed.

PHOTO ROUND: Advance through 10 numbered images. For each, crews have 30 seconds to write on the worksheet: (a) assembly type, (b) how they identified it, (c) whether it is above or below a likely fire, and (d) the tactical implication. Score after all ten.

TEACHING BLOCK: Using scored rounds, contrast why a gusset-plate truss or I-joist web fails at the connection/web — often in minutes once fire reaches it — while dimensional lumber chars and telegraphs. Emphasize the failure is silent: no sag, no sponginess, then sudden loss.

TABLETOP SCENARIO: Present a projected floor plan with a basement or attic/cockloft fire in an engineered building. Assign company officers, firefighters, and the driver-engineer real roles on the radio net. Feed time-since-arrival and fire-location cues, NOT collapse warnings.

Require the IC/company officer to make and transmit the assembly-based decision — roof off the table, no crews on the floor above, defensive/exterior transition — and state the trigger in words ('fire in the truss loft' / 'fire below the engineered floor'), before the instructor's hidden failure window.

NON-ENTRY WALK-THROUGH: Move to the pre-selected building. Crews identify each visible assembly from the street, then from a lawful non-entry vantage of the attic and the floor/ceiling assembly, calling out where they would and would not operate and why.

AFTER-ACTION DEBRIEF: Review recognition misses and decision timing. For every late 'pull' call in the tabletop, reconstruct the earliest cue that should have triggered it. Close on the command discipline of removing crews from above/below a compromised assembly before it announces itself.
learning_points: Engineered assemblies fail at the connection or web, not the member — a single burned-through gusset plate or I-joist web can drop a floor or roof with no sag warning, so the traditional 'feel for the spongy floor' cue arrives too late or never.

Time-since-arrival must be read against the assembly and fire location, not a generic collapse clock: fire in a truss loft or below an engineered floor changes the timeline to minutes, and the crew above or below is the exposure.

A basement or first-floor fire in an I-joist building turns the floor above into the collapse zone — recognizing this from the exterior (walkout basement, floor framing type, era of construction) shapes where the attack can and cannot go before entry.

Roof operations over lightweight trusses offer almost no margin: once fire is in the cockloft or attic, the roof is a work platform over a truss that may already be failing, which is why 'roof off the table' is a size-up decision, not a mayday reaction.

The command failure the pattern reveals is not ignorance of collapse but late decision timing — the discipline is pulling crews on the recognition cue, before the building gives a physical warning it may never give.
common_mistakes: Crews identify the assembly correctly on photos but still commit to the floor above or the roof in the tabletop because they anchor to a collapse-time rule of thumb instead of fire location.
Officers wait for a reported warning sign (sag, smoke from the eaves, spongy floor) that engineered assemblies frequently never provide, delaying the pull decision past the failure window.
The driver-engineer and firefighters treat this as an officer-only exercise; the recognition cue often comes from the nozzle or outside team and must be transmitted, not held.
Confusing exterior finish with structure — a masonry or brick-veneer face hides lightweight wood floor and roof framing, and crews call it 'ordinary/heavy' from the street.
Debrief drifts into second-guessing a real deceased firefighter's judgment instead of examining the tactical and command system that put crews on a compromised assembly.
safety_notes: Non-entry walk-through only: do not enter any fire-damaged, weakened, or posted-unsafe space, and do not load any real floor or roof to 'test' it — the drill trains recognition, not proof-testing.
Conduct the exterior/interior walk with a designated safety officer controlling movement near roof edges, floor openings, and mechanical spaces.
If using an occupied or active building, coordinate access in advance and keep crews clear of vehicle traffic and operating equipment.
success_criteria: Each crew scores at least 8 of 10 correct assembly identifications on the photo round, with a written identifying feature for each correct call.
In the tabletop, the IC transmits the correct assembly-based operational limit (roof/floor-above/defensive) before the instructor's hidden failure window, and states the recognition trigger in words.

On the walk-through, each crew correctly names every visible assembly type and identifies at least one location where they would refuse to operate, with the reason tied to fire-versus-assembly, not habit.
The debrief reconstructs the earliest available cue for every late tabletop decision, documented on the worksheet.

variations.name: Mixed-Era Building
variations.description: Add photos and a tabletop of a building with original dimensional framing and an engineered addition or renovated floor system.
variations.adds: Trains crews to detect the transition line between old and new construction, where the collapse hazard is not uniform across the footprint.

variations.name: Driver-Engineer Exterior Read
variations.description: Run a round where only the driver-engineer, from the pump panel position, must call the roof/floor construction and relay it to the interior crews over the radio.
variations.adds: Trains the apparatus operator's role as a fixed exterior observer who can flag lightweight construction and eave/roofline changes the interior crew cannot see.

variations.name: Zero-Cue Compression
variations.description: In the tabletop, remove all traditional warning signs entirely and shorten the fire-location-to-failure window, forcing the decision purely on recognition.
variations.adds: Trains committing to a pull decision on assembly type and fire location alone, mirroring the silent, no-warning failures the pattern documents.

lodd_connection.lesson: Firefighters have been killed when engineered assemblies failed sooner and more suddenly than dimensional lumber; the recurring system lesson is recognizing the assembly and pulling crews from above or below it based on fire location and time-since-arrival, before any physical warning.

drills.title: Blind-Timeline Study: Decide Before You Read the Ending
drills.objective: Working alone from a NIOSH or near-miss report you source yourself, log a written decision at 4 or more marked pauses BEFORE reading each outcome, then score how many of your calls matched what actually happened and name every point where you had less information than you assumed.
equipment: A published NIOSH firefighter fatality investigation report or a near-miss report the firefighter pulls themselves
Notebook or phone to record decisions
Printed or written blind-timeline template (three columns: what I know now / my decision / what actually happened)
Opaque paper, sticky notes, or a folded sheet to physically cover the un-read portion of a printed report (or scroll-lock discipline on a phone)
drills.setup: Choose one report and skim only its incident summary and building description so you know the setting, not the ending. Cover everything below the first decision point so you cannot see the outcome. If reading on a phone, agree with yourself to stop scrolling at each pause and not thumb ahead.
steps: Read only the size-up and building description, then set the timer for the session and write the department, building type, and staffing you actually know from the text so far.

Advance to the first decision point and STOP before the outcome sentence; write, in your own words, the decision you would make and the single piece of information you most wish you had. A written decision is specific and actionable, not a feeling — for example, at a point where a report notes a crew working above the fire: "Decision: pull the crew off the floor above and reposition them to a protected stairwell; hold interior operations. Wished-for: whether fire had already extended into the void spaces beneath them." A vague "be careful here" is not a decision and scores nothing.
Uncover the outcome for that point, write what actually happened, and mark your call as match / partial / miss without arguing with the report.
Repeat the cover-decide-reveal cycle for at least three more decision points across the timeline, keeping each written decision to one or two sentences.
After the final reveal, count your match / partial / miss tally and circle every pause where you wrote a decision based on information the crew on scene did not actually have yet.
Close by writing one sentence naming the recurring gap between what you assumed you knew and what was knowable at that moment.
learning_points: Reading a report outcome-first quietly rewrites your memory of the decision — you credit yourself with a call you only made because you already knew the ending, so the study teaches hindsight instead of judgment under uncertainty.
Committing a decision in writing before the reveal is the only way to measure your own size-up against reality; an uncommitted 'I would have known better' is worth nothing on a real fireground.
Naming the information you wished you had at each pause trains the habit of identifying decision-critical unknowns early, which is exactly the gap that turns a routine job into a fatality.
The distance between what you assumed you knew and what was actually knowable is where line-of-duty deaths live; measuring that distance on paper is cheaper than measuring it in a basement.
common_mistakes: Thumbing ahead to the outcome 'just to check' before committing the written decision, which destroys the entire value of the method — the cover discipline is the drill.
Writing decisions so vague they cannot be scored ('be careful', 'consider a second line') instead of a committed call a crew could act on.
Arguing with the report at the reveal to protect the ego instead of honestly marking a miss.
Scoring only match/miss and skipping the assumed-vs-knowable review, which is where the transferable lesson actually is.
success_criteria: At least four written decisions are logged with each one dated before its corresponding outcome was uncovered (visible in the template order).
Each logged decision is specific enough that a second firefighter could act on it without asking a clarifying question.
A match / partial / miss tally is completed for every decision point.
The session ends with at least one written sentence naming a specific assumed-vs-knowable information gap.

variations.name: Timeline reconstruction first
variations.description: Before the blind read, build your own blank minute-by-minute timeline from only the dispatch and size-up information, predicting when key events should occur, then check it against the report's actual timeline.
variations.adds: Trains a sense of fireground tempo and how fast conditions can outrun a plan, not just discrete decisions.

variations.name: Two-report pattern pass
variations.description: Run the blind method on a second report of a different incident type and compare which of your information gaps repeat across both.
variations.adds: Surfaces your personal recurring blind spots as a pattern rather than a one-off, so the fix targets a habit.

references: NIOSH Fire Fighter Fatality Investigation and Prevention Program report structure (firefighter sources the specific report)
Near-miss reporting program narratives as an alternative source
General fire-service after-action review practice
drills.solo_note: Built for one firefighter alone with a report, template, and timer; the cover-decide-reveal discipline replaces any need for an instructor to withhold the outcome.

drills.title: Contributing-Factor Map: Findings to Your Own District
drills.objective: From a report you source yourself, extract at least 5 distinct contributing factors and tie each one to a specific habit, SOP, or actual building or block in your own first-due district, ending with every factor marked as already-covered, partially-covered, or exposed for your own crew.
equipment: A published NIOSH fatality investigation report or near-miss report the firefighter pulls themselves
Printed or written contributing-factor mapping template (factor / mechanism / where it lives in MY district / our current status)
Optional: a map or list of target buildings in your first-due area
drills.setup: Pull one report and read it once all the way through so you have the full picture — this framework is not blind. Have your first-due district in mind: specific streets, occupancy types, and known problem buildings you can name.
steps: Read the report fully, then list the contributing factors it identifies in the recommendations or contributing-factors section, in the report's own terms, aiming for at least five distinct factors.
For each factor, write one sentence describing the mechanism — how that factor actually contributed to the outcome, not just its label.
For each factor, name a specific place it could recur in your own world: a habit you or your crew have, a current SOP or gap in one, or a real building, block, or occupancy in your first-due area.
Mark each factor already-covered (your crew reliably manages it), partially-covered (managed sometimes or by some members), or exposed (no current defense).
Pick the single most exposed factor and write one sentence on what would have to change — a habit, a pre-plan, a size-up cue — for it to move toward covered.
Re-read your 'where it lives in my district' column and cross out any entry that is generic ('older buildings') and rewrite it as a named place or a named habit.
learning_points: A contributing factor stated in the abstract ('inadequate size-up') teaches nothing until it is anchored to a real building or a real habit you own; the anchoring is what converts someone else's fatality into your prevention.

Naming the mechanism, not just the label, forces you to understand HOW a factor kills — the same factor label can operate very differently in a garden apartment versus a strip mall, and the defense differs with it.

Honestly marking exposed factors is uncomfortable precisely because it names a gap in your own crew; a study that produces only already-covered marks is almost certainly dishonest or too generic to act on.
Tying findings to specific first-due buildings turns abstract report-reading into de facto pre-planning — you leave the session knowing one more thing about a structure you will actually respond to.
common_mistakes: Copying the report's factor labels without writing the mechanism, so the factors stay abstract and never connect to home.
Filling the district column with generic categories ('commercial buildings') instead of a named street, block, or occupancy you actually run on.
Marking everything already-covered to avoid naming a real gap, which makes the whole map worthless.
Extracting only one or two factors from a report that lists many, cherry-picking the comfortable ones.
success_criteria: At least five distinct contributing factors are extracted and each has a written one-sentence mechanism.
Every factor has a district anchor that names a specific habit, SOP, or real place — no generic categories survive the final pass.
Every factor carries an already-covered / partially-covered / exposed status mark.
One most-exposed factor is identified with a written one-sentence change that would move it toward covered.

variations.name: Route-walk anchoring
variations.description: Do the mapping with your actual first-due running card or a district map open, and physically point to or note the closest real building for each factor.
variations.adds: Sharpens the anchoring from 'a building like that' to 'that building on that street', which is what pre-planning value requires.

variations.name: Crew-status honesty pass
variations.description: For each partially-covered mark, write which members or shifts reliably manage the factor and which do not, keeping it about systems and training, not blame.
variations.adds: Surfaces training-consistency gaps across a crew rather than treating the company as uniformly competent.

references: NIOSH Fire Fighter Fatality Investigation and Prevention Program report recommendations (firefighter-sourced)
Near-miss report contributing-factor narratives
General fire-service pre-planning and district familiarization practice
drills.solo_note: One firefighter works alone with a report and their own district knowledge; no observer needed, and the honesty of the status marks is self-checked against named places.

drills.title: One-Change Discipline: End Every Study in a Practiced Fix
drills.objective: From a report you source yourself, convert your reading into exactly ONE concrete personal action item, physically rehearse or draft it before the session ends, and log it with a self-verifiable done-signal — reaching one rehearsed change in a single 40-minute session.
equipment: A published NIOSH fatality investigation report or near-miss report the firefighter pulls themselves
Notebook or phone to log the action item
Printed or written one-change template (what I read / the one change / how I rehearsed it today / how I will know it stuck)
Whatever a small personal skill needs: your own PPE/SCBA for a manipulation drill, a hood, gloves, or nothing at all for a knowledge or size-up change
drills.setup: Pull and read one report, or reuse a report you have already studied with another framework. The point of this session is not broad understanding but conversion: turning reading into one small change you actually rehearse today, alone, with no crew and no live evolution.
steps: Read (or review) the report and write, in one or two sentences, the single most useful thing it revealed for YOU — resist listing several.

Translate that insight into exactly one action item small enough to rehearse alone today: a glove or SCBA manipulation, a size-up phrase you commit to memory, a tool check you add to your routine, or a specific fact to look up and record.

Rehearse it now — physically run the manipulation several times, recite the phrase until it is automatic, or complete the lookup and write the fact in your own words; set the timer to keep the rehearsal honest, not token.
Write the done-signal: a self-verifiable way you will know the change stuck — a rep count you can hit, a phrase you can recite cold next shift, a checklist line you added — never 'ask my officer'.
Log the single action item with today's date and schedule one self-check on your own calendar for a future shift.
Delete or strike any second and third 'also I should' item, keeping the session to one change so it is actually done rather than merely intended.
learning_points: A study session that ends in intentions changes nothing; the discipline of exactly one rehearsed change is what converts reading into a skill your hands or memory actually own.
Small and rehearsed-today beats big and someday — one glove manipulation you drilled ten times will be there under stress, while a page of ambitious notes will not.
A self-verifiable done-signal makes the change auditable without anyone else, which is what lets a lone firefighter train honestly instead of just feeling productive.
Capping the session at one item fights the real failure of report study: generating a wish-list so long that nothing on it is ever practiced.
common_mistakes: Ending with a list of five changes and rehearsing none, which feels productive but trains nothing.
Choosing an action item too big to rehearse alone today, so it becomes an intention instead of a rep.
Writing a done-signal that depends on someone else ('have my officer check me') instead of one the firefighter can verify solo.
Treating the rehearsal as a checkbox — one token rep — instead of enough reps to make the change stick.
safety_notes: If the chosen change is a physical PPE or SCBA manipulation, rehearse it in a safe, non-IDLH setting at ground level; never restrict air, remove the facepiece in any simulated-IDLH way, or defeat PPE for realism — this is a routine manipulation practiced clean.
success_criteria: Exactly one action item is logged — not zero, not several — with today's date.
The action item was physically rehearsed or fully drafted during the session, evidenced by a rep count, a recitable phrase, or a completed written fact.
A self-verifiable done-signal is written that requires no other person to confirm.
One future self-check is scheduled.

variations.name: Streak log
variations.description: Keep a running one-change log across multiple report sessions and review the last several before starting a new one, confirming each prior change actually stuck.
variations.adds: Builds accountability over time and exposes changes that were logged but never truly retained.

variations.name: Manipulation-only focus
variations.description: Constrain the action item to a hands-on PPE, SCBA, or tool manipulation you can rep alone, excluding knowledge-only items for this session.
variations.adds: Forces conversion of a report lesson into muscle memory rather than a note, for reports whose lesson is a physical skill.

General fire-service practice on deliberate practice and single-behavior change
After-action review to action-item discipline

drills.title: First-Alarm Coordinated Evolution
drills.solo_note: Full first alarm: 2-3 engines, truck, command, RIT, safety officer, instructor cadre
drills.objective: Execute a full first-alarm residential fire assignment: water supply, stretch and attack, search, laddering, ventilation timed to attack, command, and RIT staging — as an integrated timeline.
drills.setup: Companies respond in staggered arrival order. Instructor cadre injects conditions. Every function from the individual drills in this library is now performed simultaneously.
steps: Dispatch and staggered arrivals per realistic response times.
First engine: report, stretch, water supply decision. Second engine: supply completion, backup line.
Truck: front-of-building position, search team in, ladders thrown, ventilation crew standing by for coordination call.
Command establishes, assigns, tracks accountability, and calls PARs at benchmarks.
Injects: victim found (removal sequence), extension discovered (second line deployment), and optionally a mayday (full RIT sequence).
Hotwash immediately after, then a structured debrief against the timeline: time to first water, time to primary complete, vent-attack coordination gap.
learning_points: Individual competence doesn't automatically compose into fireground competence — sequencing and communication are their own skill.
The vent-attack timing gap is measurable: how many seconds between water on the fire and the coordinated opening?
Benchmarks (water established, primary complete, under control) give command and crews a shared language for progress.
The debrief timeline is the deliverable — it converts the evolution into department-specific improvement targets.
common_mistakes: Companies execute their own tasks well but never sequence them together, so timing collapses.
Ventilation openings are made before water reaches the fire, worsening conditions on the attack crew.
Benchmark times are not recorded, so the crew cannot find where the minutes are being lost.
safety_notes: Dedicated safety officer and instructor cadre.
NFPA 1403 governs any live-fire version.
Rehab established for full evolutions.
success_criteria: All benchmark times recorded
Ventilation coordinated (no uncoordinated openings)
Accountability maintained through all injects

variations.adds: Task prioritization when there aren't enough hands — the real-world version.

drills.title: Two-In/Two-Out & Initial RIT Discipline
drills.solo_note: Scenario rounds assign an entry pair and an IRIC pair; the crew debriefs as a group

solo_variant.substitutions: Crew and scenario rounds become a shuffled scenario deck you write in advance, run on paper at the table. Voice recorder replaces the crew debrief — you argue both sides out loud. Your department's SOP and the two-in/two-out rule in writing, open in front of you, replace the instructor.
steps: Run this on paper only. No live rounds, no entry, no prop, no SCBA. Solo you cannot staff a standby pair, and there is no version of this drill where you enter anything alone.

Write the rule out longhand from memory first: what two-in/two-out requires, what the standby pair must actually be capable of, and what the rescue exception permits. Then open the SOP and mark every place you got it wrong.
Build 12 scenario cards: vary staffing (3, 4, 5 on the rig), conditions, occupancy, time of day, and whether there is a credible report of someone inside.
Draw a card, start the recorder, and talk it through as if you are on the radio: who enters, who stands by, what tools the standby pair has in their hands, and where they are standing.
On any card with a credible trapped occupant, state the exception decision out loud as a decision — name it, give your reasoning, and say what you are accepting.
Argue the other side of the same card out loud before you move on. If you cannot make the opposing case, you do not understand the card.
Play the recording back with the SOP open and mark any answer where the standby pair had other work, no tools, or no eyes on the door.
solo_variant.self_score: Score each card against the written SOP: correct or not, with the standby pair's tools and position stated explicitly. Target 12 of 12 with no vague answers. Any exception decision that was not named out loud with reasoning counts as a fail regardless of the outcome.
solo_variant.not_covered: This is the decision only. It does not cover actually holding the discipline when your crew is keen and the door is open — that is the failure this drill exists to prevent and it only happens with real people. No IRIC posture demonstrated, no tools staged, no reading whether your standby pair is genuinely ready. No honest group argument about the gray areas.

drills.objective: Correctly implement two-in/two-out on arrival: entry team, initial rapid intervention crew composition, and the known-rescue exception decision.
drills.setup: Crew arrives at scenarios varying occupancy, conditions, and staffing.
steps: Review the rule: interior IDLH entry requires two in, two out — and what the standby pair must actually be capable of (immediate rescue).
Scenario rounds: crew of 3 with fire showing and no report of victims — walk through the legal and tactical options.
Scenario: credible report of a trapped occupant — apply the rescue exception, document the decision aloud.
Scenario: 4-person crew — assign entry pair and IRIC pair explicitly, with the IRIC verbalizing their readiness posture.
Debrief the gray areas honestly: what the exception permits, what it doesn't, and what the department's SOP says.
learning_points: Two-in/two-out is decided in the first minute of every working fire — crews without a rehearsed answer improvise one.
The IRIC is a real assignment with tools staged and attention on the entry team, not two people standing near the pump.
The rescue exception is real and legitimate — and it must be a conscious, announced decision, not a habit.
Understaffed arrivals are exactly when the discipline matters and exactly when it erodes.
common_mistakes: The standby pair works near the pump or staging instead of staying ready for immediate rescue.
The rescue exception to two-in/two-out becomes a habit rather than a conscious, announced decision.
Understaffed crews improvise two-out on scene because it was never drilled ahead of time.
safety_notes: If any scenario round is run live rather than on paper, the standby / IRIC pair must be fully equipped and immediately available for rescue — never assigned other work. Treating two-out as a paperwork formality is the exact failure this drill exists to prevent.
success_criteria: Correct application in all scenario rounds
Exception decisions verbalized with reasoning
IRIC posture demonstrated
references: NFPA 1500

drills.title: Defensive Operations & Collapse Zone Discipline
drills.solo_note: Multi-company withdrawal, PAR, master streams, plus a freelancer inject
drills.objective: Transition from offensive to defensive operations: emergency traffic, personnel withdrawal and PAR, collapse zone establishment, and master stream placement.
drills.setup: Offensive operations in progress (simulated interior crews). Instructor triggers deteriorating conditions.
steps: Command recognizes the trigger (structural compromise report, fire progression) and transmits emergency traffic: all crews withdraw.
Crews exit with their equipment discipline per SOP, and PAR is conducted immediately.

Collapse zones established at your department's multiple of building height — 1.5x is the common teaching default and what this drill runs unless your SOP says otherwise — physically marked, corners identified as the safe approach positions.
Master streams positioned outside the zones with effective reach; apparatus repositioned if inside the zone.
Instructor tests the zone: sends a 'freelancer' toward the building — who catches it and how fast?
Debrief withdrawal time, PAR time, and any zone violations.
learning_points: The offensive-to-defensive transition is a command decision with a mechanical sequence — hesitation on the trigger is the killer.
PAR after withdrawal is the whole point of the withdrawal; incomplete PAR means someone may still be inside.
Collapse zones fail by erosion: five minutes after establishment, people drift in. Enforcement is a standing assignment.
Corner positions offer the geometry with the least collapse exposure.
common_mistakes: Command delays the offensive-to-defensive transition past the point the building can be held.
Withdrawal is ordered without completing PAR, so no one confirms everyone actually got out.
The collapse zone erodes as members drift back in, and no one enforces the perimeter.
safety_notes: Zone discipline is enforced during the drill exactly as it would be enforced on scene.
success_criteria: Withdrawal complete and PAR under target time
Zones marked and held
No streams operated from inside a zone

variations.name: Reversal
variations.description: After knockdown, command evaluates re-entry for recovery under strict criteria.
variations.adds: The disciplined re-entry decision — often made sloppily in reality.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple LODDs document firefighters killed by collapse while operating in unestablished or violated collapse zones during defensive operations
lodd_connection.lesson: Defensive means nobody dies for a building already lost. The zone only works if it's marked, announced, and policed.

references: NIOSH collapse-related reports
Brannigan/Corbett building construction principles

drills.title: Standpipe Assignment: Lobby-to-Attack Company Handoffs
drills.solo_note: Two engines and a truck, instructor dispatch and freezes, radio handoffs between companies
drills.objective: Two engines and one truck execute a mid/high-rise standpipe operation in which lobby control, FDC supply, stairwell support, and above-fire attack are established with a working line charged at the standpipe outlet below the fire floor within 12 minutes of the first company's arrival, with zero freelance moves and all inter-company handoffs confirmed by radio.
equipment: Two engines and one truck or quint (or closest local equivalent)
Two standpipe/high-rise packs (150 ft of 2.5 in with smooth-bore or low-pressure nozzle, gated wye, spanners, door chocks, in-line pressure gauge)
Ground ladders (for FDC/window marking or as improvised prop)
Portable radios on two channels (Command and Tactical)
Multi-story training tower or parking structure with a standpipe system or simulated standpipe outlets
Full PPE and SCBA (no live fire)
Traffic cones or tape to mark lobby control point and staging floor
drills.setup: Requires a multi-story training tower or parking structure with functioning or simulated standpipe outlets on at least three floors; designate one floor as the fire floor. Stage both engines and the truck at a realistic setback from the building with a marked FDC location. Pre-assign one engine as attack, one engine as supply/support, and the truck as lobby control and stairwell support; brief officers on the reported fire floor but not on which stairwell is tenable. Target pressures and hose sizes here are examples only: standpipe pressure policy and high-rise pack composition vary widely between departments, so before running this drill the officer must substitute their own department's standpipe pressure policy and high-rise pack.
steps: Instructor gives a dispatch brief: reported fire on a specific upper floor, occupants reported, standpipe-equipped building. First-arriving officer must transmit an on-scene report and assume Command.

Truck company establishes lobby control: identifies both stairwells, locks out or accounts for elevators (elevator discipline — no crews ride cars above two floors below the fire), and reports which stairwell is designated attack and which is evacuation.

Supply engine driver-engineer connects to and charges the FDC to the target discharge pressure while the officer confirms the supply assignment on the Command channel; attack engine officer leads the attack company to the standpipe outlet on the floor below the fire with the high-rise pack.

Attack company connects to the outlet below the fire floor, flakes the line in the stairwell, sets the in-line gauge, and calls for water on the Tactical channel; support firefighter controls the stairwell door and manages hose feed at the landing.

Instructor calls a safety pause when the line is charged: crews confirm PAR, staging location below fire floor, and that no crew has advanced onto the fire floor before water is confirmed at the nozzle.

Attack officer announces readiness to advance to Command; Command confirms ventilation status and holds crews until the truck reports stairwell and door control, then authorizes advance to the fire floor door.

Instructor freezes the evolution at the fire floor threshold and runs the debrief on coordination quality: every handoff, every radio transmission, and every decision point where a company waited for or committed without another.
learning_points: Connecting to the standpipe outlet on the fire floor instead of the floor below puts the attack team's water source and reserve hose inside the hazard — a burst or kink on the fire floor then leaves the crew with no protected connection to fall back to.

Elevator discipline exists because crews who ride a car past the fire floor on a smoke-detector-recalled or heat-affected system have died trapped in the shaft; lobby control owns that decision so an eager company cannot make it alone.

The FDC supply and standpipe pressure management is invisible to the attack crew — they only feel it at the nozzle as inadequate reach, so the supply engineer and attack officer must confirm target pressure by radio before anyone commits.

Two radio channels only help if traffic is disciplined: Command channel for strategic assignments and PAR, Tactical for the attack/support interface — mixing them buries the one transmission that matters under routine chatter.

The most dangerous minute is between 'line charged' and 'crews advance'; without a confirmed handoff between attack, support, and truck, one company commits to the fire floor while another is still staging equipment, splitting the operation.
common_mistakes: Attack company connects to the fire-floor outlet to save stair-climbing, eliminating the protected floor-below staging point.
Supply engineer charges the FDC but never confirms the achieved pressure to the attack officer, who then advances on a soft line.
Lobby control is skipped or nominal — nobody actually controls the stairwell doors, so the attack stairwell fills with smoke from an unmanaged door.
Both companies talk on the Command channel, so Command cannot hear the attack team's water and PAR reports.
Truck company begins ventilation before the attack line is charged and staged, drawing fire toward crews still in the stairwell.
safety_notes: Inspect standpipe outlets and any weight-bearing stairwell/landing props before loading crews and equipment; do not exceed rated occupancy on training-tower landings.
Elevators used in the evolution must be under confirmed lobby control at all times; no crew rides a car above two floors below the designated fire floor.
Stair-climbing in full PPE with SCBA induces real cardiac and heat stress — rotate crews, provide rehab, and monitor members after the climb.
success_criteria: Working line is charged at the outlet below the fire floor within 12 minutes of first-company arrival, verified by stopwatch.
Attack company connects below the fire floor (not on it) and sets the in-line gauge — verified by observation.
Every inter-company handoff (lobby control established, FDC charged and pressure confirmed, line charged, ready-to-advance) is transmitted and acknowledged on radio with zero freelance advances.
Command and Tactical channel traffic stays separated: no member is observed transmitting tactical hose/water traffic on the Command channel.

variations.name: Wrong Stairwell
variations.description: Instructor declares the initially designated attack stairwell untenable (smoke-charged) after the pack is staged, forcing lobby control and the attack company to relocate to the second stairwell.
variations.adds: Trains the stairwell-reselection decision and the discipline to move an entire operation without losing accountability.

variations.name: FDC Supply Problem
variations.description: Supply engine loses a pump or the FDC connection is fouled; the second engine must be repositioned to supply while the attack crew holds below the fire floor.
variations.adds: Trains recognition that inadequate standpipe pressure is a stop condition and forces a coordinated water-supply recovery without committing crews.

variations.name: Reduced Staffing
variations.description: Run the evolution with three-person companies, forcing the officer to choose which tasks are sequenced rather than run in parallel.
variations.adds: Trains task prioritization and honest sequencing when there are not enough hands to do lobby control, supply, and attack simultaneously.

lodd_connection.incident: One Meridian Plaza fire
lodd_connection.lesson: Standpipe pressure and supply failures and communication breakdowns in a high-rise contributed to the loss of three firefighters; the interface between the supply engine, standpipe pressure, and the crews operating above must be confirmed, not assumed.

references: IFSTA Essentials of Fire Fighting — standpipe operations and high-rise firefighting chapters
FSRI/UL high-rise and vertical ventilation research
NIOSH firefighter fatality investigation reports on high-rise standpipe operations
Department high-rise/standpipe operations SOP (operator-provided)

drills.title: Transitional Attack Handoff: Reset, Confirm, Commit
drills.solo_note: The drill is the handoff between two companies confirmed to Command
drills.objective: Two engines and one truck execute a transitional attack in which an exterior stream is applied into the fire compartment to reset conditions and is then verifiably shut down and confirmed to Command before the interior company commits, with ventilation coordinated to the interior advance and every transition decision voiced on the radio — all handoffs completed with zero interior commitment while water is flowing exterior.
equipment: Two engines and one truck or quint
1.75 in preconnect (attack) and a second 1.75 in or 2.5 in line
Smooth-bore or combination nozzle capable of a straight stream for exterior application
Portable radios on two channels (Command and Tactical)
Training lot or fire prop with a defined 'fire compartment' opening (marked window/door); no acquired structure required
Cones/tape to mark the compartment, the exterior stream position, and the interior entry point
Full PPE and SCBA (no live fire)
drills.setup: Requires a training lot or ground-level prop with a clearly defined fire compartment — a marked window or door opening into a simulated room; no acquired structure or live fire needed. Designate one engine as the initial exterior/attack company, one engine as the interior company, and the truck for ventilation and laddering. Mark the exterior stream position outside the compartment opening and the interior entry point, and brief officers that the scenario begins with fire showing from the marked compartment.
steps: Instructor sets the scene: fire showing from the marked compartment with a reported but unconfirmed occupant. First engine officer completes size-up, calls the transitional attack, and directs the exterior stream into the compartment from outside — straight stream off the ceiling, not fanned across the opening.

Exterior nozzle team applies water for a defined reset interval (instructor-called, simulating darkening) while the officer narrates conditions on the Tactical channel; truck company ladders and prepares ventilation but does NOT open up yet.

First engine officer calls the transition: orders the exterior stream shut down, and the nozzle firefighter confirms 'water off' back to the officer, who then confirms 'exterior water off, compartment reset' to Command on the Command channel.

Instructor calls a mandatory safety pause: no interior crew moves until Command has heard and acknowledged 'exterior water off.' Confirm PAR and that the exterior line is repositioned clear of the entry point.

Interior company officer requests permission to commit; Command confirms exterior water is off and directs the truck to coordinate ventilation with the interior advance — vent opened only on the interior officer's readiness, not before.

Interior company advances through the marked entry to the compartment with the thermal imager, completing the primary search of the reset room while the exterior line stands by as backup; truck ventilation supports the advance direction.

Instructor freezes at compartment entry and runs the debrief centered on the transition: who called it, whether 'water off' was confirmed before commitment, and whether ventilation was timed to the advance or defeated it.
learning_points: Transitional attack works because the exterior straight stream resets the compartment's energy before crews enter; fanning or bouncing the stream around the opening can push fire and steam toward interior openings instead of cooling the room.

The single most dangerous failure in a transitional attack is an interior crew committing while the exterior line is still flowing — steam and products get driven onto the advancing team, so 'water off' must be spoken, confirmed, and acknowledged before anyone enters.
The transition call belongs to one identified officer and is confirmed to Command; if two companies each believe they own the timing, the exterior line shuts down late or the interior commits early.

Ventilation opened before the interior team is ready gives the reset fire fresh air and can undo the reset — the truck opens up on the interior officer's readiness, coordinated through Command, not on its own initiative.

The officers must exchange specific information before crews advance: exterior water off, compartment reset, interior ready, ventilation coordinated — a missing element in that exchange is a missing safety check, not a formality.
common_mistakes: Nozzle team fans the stream across the opening instead of a straight stream off the ceiling, pushing steam and fire rather than resetting the room.
Interior company creeps to the entry point and commits while the exterior line is still flowing because 'it looked knocked down.'
The 'water off' confirmation is assumed by hand signal or sight instead of voiced and acknowledged on the radio.
Truck opens the roof or window on its own timeline, re-energizing the compartment before the interior team advances.
Nobody clearly owns the transition call, so the shutdown and the commitment happen out of sequence.
safety_notes: Because this is a no-live-fire rehearsal, discipline the 'water off' confirmation even harder — the whole point is the verbal handoff, so do not let crews shortcut it with hand signals.
Keep the exterior stream and the interior entry point physically separated and marked so the two teams do not converge at the opening during the transition.
Inspect any prop opening and ladder placement before loading; ground-ladder work in full PPE around the compartment opening is the physical hazard in this drill.
success_criteria: Exterior stream is verifiably shut down and 'exterior water off' is transmitted and acknowledged on the radio before any interior crew crosses the entry point.
Zero interior commitment occurs while water is flowing exterior — observed and scored pass/fail.
Truck ventilation is opened only after the interior officer signals readiness and Command coordinates it — verified by sequence, not just occurrence.
The transition is called by one identified officer and confirmed to Command, with the four-part exchange (water off, reset, interior ready, vent coordinated) completed.

variations.name: Confirmed Rescue in the Compartment
variations.description: Instructor confirms a viable victim in the fire compartment before the exterior stream is applied, compressing the reset interval and forcing a faster but still-confirmed transition.
variations.adds: Trains the risk/benefit decision to shorten the exterior reset when a savable life is known, without abandoning the water-off confirmation.

variations.name: Radio Failure at the Transition
variations.description: The first engine officer's portable fails just as the transition is called; the crew must use a designated face-to-face relay or backup channel to confirm water off.
variations.adds: Trains a communications-failure contingency so the confirmation still happens when the primary channel drops.

variations.name: Wind-Driven Condition
variations.description: Instructor introduces a strong wind from the fire side toward the interior entry point, making the compartment opening a flow path.
variations.adds: Trains recognition that ventilation and entry-point choice must account for wind, and that opening up downwind can turn the compartment into a blowtorch toward crews.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH firefighter fatality reports document interior crews caught by rapid fire progression when ventilation and stream operations were not coordinated
lodd_connection.lesson: Uncoordinated water application and ventilation timing repeatedly place interior crews in the path of driven fire and steam; the transition from exterior to interior must be a confirmed, single-owner decision, not an assumption.

references: FSRI/UL Study of Coordinated Fire Attack Utilizing Acquired Structures
IFSTA Essentials of Fire Fighting — fire attack and ventilation coordination chapters
NIOSH firefighter fatality investigation reports on rapid fire progression
Department fire attack / transitional attack SOG (operator-provided)

drills.title: Photo-Based Size-Up & Initial Radio Report
drills.solo_note: Images are flashed by someone else; the size-up is transmitted to a partner as dispatch

solo_variant.substitutions: Instructor flashing images becomes a phone slideshow set to a 10-second auto-advance, or a folder you scroll blind. Phone voice recorder replaces the partner acting as dispatch. Your SOP format card, printed, replaces the scorer.
steps: Build a deck of 15 images the night before, so you see them cold: street-view grabs of buildings in your first-due, plus fireground photos from anywhere. Do not look at them while you collect them beyond what you need to save the file.
Set the slideshow to 10 seconds per image and start the voice recorder running for the whole session.

Image up: look for 10 seconds, then the screen goes dark and you transmit — building (size, height, occupancy, construction), conditions (smoke location, volume, velocity, density, color), actions (mode declaration, first assignment), needs (alarms, utilities, water supply).
Do not stop and restart. A fumbled report is a rep; finish it and move on.
Run all 15, then go back through the recording with the image open beside you and the format card in front of you. Mark missing elements and wasted air time.
Follow-up round: pick 5 images, re-open them, and give a CAN update as if two minutes have passed and your first line is in.
Every fourth session, rebuild a third of the deck so you are never reciting from memory.
solo_variant.self_score: On playback: stopwatch each report — under 30 seconds. Tick every format element against the card; a report missing construction or strategy is a fail. Count how many of 15 declared offensive or defensive out loud. Track the fail count session to session.
solo_variant.not_covered: A photo is a flat, silent, single-angle building — no walking the arrival, no sound, no smell, no 360. It does not cover transmitting to a real dispatcher who talks over you, or arriving companies acting on what you said and getting it wrong because you were sloppy. No feedback from an officer who knows the building.

drills.objective: Deliver a complete, structured initial radio report from a photo or street-view image in under 30 seconds, including conditions, actions, and needs.
equipment: Fire scene photos/videos or street-view images of district buildings
drills.setup: Officer sees the image cold for 10 seconds, then must transmit. High-rep format — 10-15 images per session. Extremely app-friendly.
steps: Flash the image; officer builds the report: building (size, height, occupancy, construction), conditions (smoke/fire location and behavior), actions (mode declaration, first assignment), needs (additional alarms, utilities).
Transmit to a recorder or partner acting as dispatch.
Play it back; score against the format: what was missing, what was wasted air time.
Escalate: images with victims showing, exposures, solar arrays, basement indicators.
Follow-up round: same image two minutes 'later' — officer gives a CAN (Conditions, Actions, Needs) update.
learning_points: The initial report is the incident's operating system — every arriving company acts on it.
Smoke reading is a trained skill: volume, velocity, density, color tell you stage and location of the fire.
Declaring the strategy (offensive/defensive) out loud commits and aligns the fireground.
CAN reports keep command decisions supplied with ground truth; officers who go silent starve the IC.
common_mistakes: Officer gives a report but never declares a strategy (offensive or defensive), leaving crews without a mode.
Smoke conditions (stage, location, volume) are not read, so the report misses the fire's real story.
Officer goes silent after the on-scene report instead of feeding command continuous updates.
success_criteria: All format elements present
Under 30 seconds
Strategy declared
Accurate smoke read

variations.name: Video With Evolving Conditions
variations.description: Use fireground videos; pause at 0:10 for the initial and 2:00 for an updated report.
variations.adds: Recognizing change over time — the skill photos can't teach.

variations.name: Your District Deck
variations.description: Build the image deck exclusively from district buildings.
variations.adds: Pre-incident familiarity compounds with reporting skill.

lodd_connection.incident: Numerous NIOSH reports cite incomplete size-up — especially missed basement fires and misread building construction — as contributing factors
lodd_connection.lesson: The 360 and the report aren't formalities. Fires attacked from the wrong side of wrong assumptions kill firefighters above them.

references: Reading Smoke curriculum (Dodson)
Department radio report SOP

drills.title: Tactical Decision Games (Sand Table / Whiteboard)
drills.solo_note: A facilitator runs the clock and plays other units; peers observe and rotate in

solo_variant.substitutions: Facilitator becomes a phone timer set to a 3-minute repeating alarm plus a shuffled inject deck drawn face down. Film yourself rather than only recording audio — peers watching you command read your bearing, and audio playback cannot show it. Other units become you, out loud, in a different voice. Sand table stays as-is: a whiteboard, or masking tape and coins for units.
steps: Write two decks in advance: 8 scenario cards (dispatch plus arrival picture) and 25 inject cards. Injects should include fire through the roof, PAR due, civilian reporting a person trapped side C, attack crew low on air, second-due delayed 8 minutes, hydrant dry, and a mayday.
Lay out the building on the board. Draw a scenario card, start filming with the board in frame, start the repeating 3-minute timer.
Give the initial report and the first assignments in real radio language, out loud, full sentences. No summarising, no 'and then I would basically'.
Every time the timer sounds, draw an inject blind and respond inside 60 seconds. Move the unit markers on the board as you go so positions are always current.
Play the other units badly on purpose: give yourself a delayed answer, a report with no location in it, a company on the wrong channel. Say those out loud too.
Run 20 minutes, then close it out — terminate or transfer command.
Debrief yourself on the video the next day, not the same hour. Write down what you knew at each decision and what you did with it — and watch once with the sound off, for how you carried it.
solo_variant.self_score: Count injects answered inside 60 seconds — target every one. At the end, the board must show every unit's current assignment and location with nothing lost. On playback, count transmissions that were summary rather than real radio language; that number should drop each session.
solo_variant.not_covered: You are writing your own injects, so nothing genuinely surprises you and nothing punishes a bad decision. It does not cover reading a real crew's radio traffic, hearing stress in a voice, or holding your ground when a peer or a chief pushes back. No observers to show you the option you never considered.

drills.objective: Make and defend rapid tactical decisions in evolving low-fidelity scenarios, building pattern recognition for strategy, assignments, and resource requests.
equipment: Whiteboard or sand table with building mockups
drills.setup: Facilitator runs the clock and injects. Officer commands; peers observe and then rotate in.
steps: Present the dispatch and arrival picture; officer gives the initial report and assignments.
Inject every 2-3 minutes: 'fire through the roof,' 'PAR request due,' 'civilian reports a person trapped side C,' 'attack crew reports low air.'
Officer must verbalize every decision and radio transmission in real language, not summary.
Facilitator plays all other units, imperfectly — delayed responses, wrong channels, incomplete reports.
Freeze at a decision point; ask observers what they would do; resume.
Debrief on decisions, not outcomes: what was known at the time, what the officer did with it.
learning_points: Command competence is recognition-primed decision making — reps build the pattern library cheaply here.
Verbalizing real radio language exposes the gap between knowing and articulating.
Injects teach that the fireground never waits for your last decision to settle before demanding the next.
Debriefing on information-at-the-time builds honest decision review culture instead of outcome bias.
common_mistakes: The scenario moves faster than the officer's radio calls, exposing a gap between deciding and communicating.
Judges apply hindsight bias, grading on the outcome instead of the information available at the time.
Officer knows the right action but cannot articulate the assignment clearly enough for a crew to execute.
success_criteria: Decisions made within the inject tempo
Assignments trackable on the board
Officer can reconstruct their reasoning in debrief

variations.name: Mayday Inject
variations.description: Mid-scenario mayday forces the dual-incident command problem.
variations.adds: Pairs with RIT-005 as the command-side rehearsal.

variations.name: AI-Facilitated Solo Version
variations.description: Officer runs scenarios against an app or LLM playing dispatch and companies.
variations.adds: Self-paced command reps without needing a facilitator — a natural feature for the app itself.

references: Blue Card / command training methodologies
Klein, recognition-primed decision research

drills.title: Accountability & PAR Management
drills.solo_note: Multiple crews, a command element, and an instructor pulling a member as an inject
drills.objective: Maintain crew accountability continuously and conduct Personnel Accountability Reports quickly and accurately under normal and emergency conditions.
equipment: Accountability system per department (tags, boards, electronic)
drills.setup: Companies distributed through a building on simulated assignments. Command element with the accountability board.
steps: Establish accountability at 'arrival': tags/entries per SOP as companies deploy.
Command calls a routine PAR; each officer physically verifies their members before answering.
Time the full PAR; identify the slow links.
Emergency round: instructor removes one member from a crew without the officer's knowledge; call the PAR.
The unaccounted member drives the missing-firefighter sequence: last known location, mayday procedures initiated.
Debrief: how long did it take to detect a missing firefighter, and what does that number mean?
learning_points: A PAR answered without physically verifying members is a false report — and false PARs appear in LODD timelines.
The officer's continuous awareness of their crew is the real accountability system; the board is the backup.
Time-to-detection of a missing member is the metric that matters — measure it honestly.
PAR discipline degrades exactly when it matters most: during chaos. Drill it into the routine.
common_mistakes: Officer reports PAR without visually or physically confirming every member.
The accountability board is treated as accountability itself instead of continuous crew awareness.
Nobody measures how long it takes to detect a missing firefighter, so the gap is never trained down.
safety_notes: Brief all members that a 'removal' inject may occur to avoid real alarm.
success_criteria: Full PAR under department time standard
Missing member detected on the emergency round
Correct escalation sequence initiated

variations.name: Channel Chaos
variations.description: Run the emergency PAR with heavy simulated radio traffic.
variations.adds: Realistic conditions for the moment accountability matters.

lodd_connection.incident: Charleston Sofa Super Store (2007) — nine firefighters killed; accountability breakdown was among the systemic findings
lodd_connection.lesson: Accountability isn't paperwork. It's how command knows to start the rescue clock before it's too late.

references: NIOSH F2007-18
Department accountability SOP

drills.title: Reading Smoke Video Sessions
drills.solo_note: Written as a taught session: instructor teaches, members write predictions, group compares

solo_variant.substitutions: Instructor teaching the attributes becomes your own written one-page reference. The group's written predictions become a notebook you must fill in before you press play. Nobody grades you — the video does.
steps: Write the four attributes on one page from memory: volume, velocity, density, color, and what each one tells you. Check it against your reference and fix the gaps before you watch anything.
Queue 6 fireground videos. Watch to 0:15, pause, and put the phone face down.
In the notebook, write three things before you touch play: where the fire is, what stage it is in, and what happens in the next two minutes. Date the entry. No hedging — commit to one answer.
Play through and compare. Write what actually happened underneath, in a different color if it helps.
Do the same run for signature patterns: turbulent smoke pushing under pressure from openings, yellowish-grey seeping from cracks and gaps, brown smoke from structural spaces.
Every fifth session, re-run three videos from your earliest notebook entries. If you now call them right, the skill moved. If you remember the answer rather than reading the smoke, replace them.
Add helmet-cam interior clips: pause and write the exact timestamp you would have called for withdrawal, then watch what happened.
solo_variant.self_score: Count correct calls out of the three written items per clip and keep a running percentage per session. Track it across months — the number goes up or the sessions are not working. On the withdrawal clips, compare your timestamp to the moment conditions actually turned.
solo_variant.not_covered: No group argument, and that argument is where most of the learning is — hearing someone read the same smoke differently forces you to justify your call. Video is flat, framed, and edited; it does not carry the sound, the heat coming off a doorway, or the 360 you would have walked. It does not cover making the read while people are waiting on your decision.

drills.objective: Interpret smoke volume, velocity, density, and color from real fireground video to predict fire location, stage, and impending events (flashover, backdraft indicators).
drills.setup: Video paused at early moments; members commit predictions in writing before watching the outcome.
steps: Teach the four attributes: volume (fire size), velocity (pressure/heat), density (fuel content and survivability), color (stage and material).
Pause a video at 0:15; each member writes: fire location, stage, and what happens in the next 2 minutes.
Play the outcome; compare predictions to reality.

Highlight signature patterns: turbulent smoke pushing from openings (flashover proximity), yellowish-gray from cracks (backdraft caution), brown smoke (structural wood burning — collapse conversation).
Run 5-8 videos per session; track prediction accuracy over time.
learning_points: Smoke is the fire talking; velocity and turbulence are the urgency indicators most crews undervalue.
Brown smoke from structural spaces means the building itself is burning — the collapse clock is running.
Committing predictions in writing before the reveal defeats hindsight bias and builds real skill.
This skill transfers directly to the initial report (OFF-001) and to interior go/no-go judgment.
common_mistakes: Members predict conditions only after seeing the outcome, so no real reading skill develops.
Brown smoke from structural members is misread as ordinary smoke, missing the collapse warning.
Velocity and turbulence indicators of impending flashover are undervalued in the read.
success_criteria: Prediction accuracy improving across sessions
Correct identification of flashover warning signs in test clips

variations.name: First-Person Interior Clips
variations.description: Helmet-cam footage; call the moment conditions dictate withdrawal.
variations.adds: Interior condition-reading and the discipline to say 'back out' aloud.

references: Dodson, The Art of Reading Smoke
UL FSRI fire behavior materials

drills.title: Transfer of Command: First-In IC to Arriving Chief
drills.solo_note: An arriving-chief role-player, radio role-players, and an evaluator scoring the checklist

solo_variant.substitutions: Film yourself rather than only recording audio — a chief taking command reads your bearing and eye contact, and playback of audio alone cannot show those. Prop the phone at eye level. It stands in for the chief and the evaluator; you score the playback against a printed five-element checklist. Index cards written a week earlier supply the incident script. Phone stopwatch for the 90 seconds.
steps: Write 10 incident cards in one sitting: occupancy, fire location, three or four companies assigned, one unresolved task, one accountability problem. Shuffle them and do not read them again that day.
Draw a floor plan on the whiteboard. Pull one card blind, fill the command board to match it, and give yourself 60 seconds to absorb it.
Start filming at eye level and start the stopwatch. Deliver your initial radio report and assign your first two companies out loud in real radio discipline.

Announce your own 'Chief 1 on scene' and immediately deliver the transfer of command. Cover all five: situation, resources and their assignments, accountability status, tactical priorities, and what has NOT been done. Stop the clock when you finish.

Then play the chief yourself on the recording: ask the three probing questions a chief would ask about that card - who is on the roof, what is your accountability, what have you not got done - and answer them from the board.
Close the loop out loud: 'Chief 1 has command, command confirmed,' then transmit your own reversion - your company, your new assignment.
Watch the whole thing back with the checklist and a pen. Mark each of the five elements present or absent — then watch once with the sound off, for bearing and eye contact.
Run the radio-only version on the next card: no board in front of you during the transfer, worksheet face down.
solo_variant.self_score: Transfer complete in under 90 seconds on the stopwatch. All five elements audible on the playback and tickable on the checklist - a 4 of 5 is a failed rep, not a good one. What has NOT been done is stated explicitly, not implied. Explicit two-way command confirmation on the recording. Your own reassignment announced before you stop the tape.
solo_variant.not_covered: A live chief who interrupts, talks over you, or asks the one question you had no answer for. Real channel congestion. The pressure of a peer watching you fumble the accountability status. And you cannot rehearse the failure this drill exists to prevent - two officers both believing they hold command - because there is only one of you.

drills.objective: Acting as first-arriving IC, verbally transfer command to an arriving chief covering all five required elements (situation, resources and their assignments, accountability status, tactical priorities, and what has NOT been done) with a confirmed hand-off in under 90 seconds and zero duplicate-command overlap.
equipment: Portable radios on at least two channels (or radio simulator)
Pre-written incident script for the evaluator (index cards)
drills.setup: Run at a bay tabletop or classroom. Post a floor plan of a 2-story commercial or multi-family occupancy on the whiteboard and pre-stage a partially filled command board reflecting a fire in progress. The officer under test plays first-in IC; a second person plays the arriving chief; remaining members role-play assigned companies on the radio. Radio channels, hose/pressure figures, and staffing on the script are examples — substitute your department's assignment terminology, channel plan, and command SOG before running.
steps: Brief the IC candidate with a 20-second dispatch and initial size-up scenario, then start the timer and have them establish command and assign the first two arriving companies.
Feed two radio events over 3-4 minutes (a benchmark report, a request for a line) so the command board reflects real assignments and accountability before transfer.

Announce the chief arriving on scene and prompt the candidate to conduct transfer of command — evaluator decides in advance whether it is face-to-face or radio-only and does not tell the candidate which until it starts.
Score the transfer against the five-element checklist while the chief actively probes for missing items (asks 'who is on the roof?' or 'what's the accountability status?').
On the chief's acknowledgment, require an explicit 'command confirmed' exchange and a radio announcement that the chief is now IC, then verify no one is still directing companies as the old IC.
Direct the candidate to revert to a company role: acknowledge their reassignment, rejoin/pick up their crew, and confirm their new assignment on the radio.
Reset and rotate a new candidate into the IC seat with an altered script (different occupancy, different unresolved task).
learning_points: A transfer that omits 'what has NOT been done' hands the new IC a false picture — the incoming chief assumes the roof is opened or the search is done and commits resources that leave a gap on the fireground.

Face-to-face transfer lets the chief read the incident action plan on the board and see the building; radio transfer strips that away, so the verbal report must carry more detail and be slower and more deliberate, not faster.
Two officers each believing they hold command produces conflicting orders on the same channel — the confirmed 'you have command / command confirmed' exchange is the only thing that closes the loop.
Accountability status must transfer as a hard fact (who is where, who is unaccounted for), not a vague 'everybody's good,' because the new IC now owns every firefighter's location.
The reverting officer is a firefighter again the moment they hand off — continuing to direct other companies after transfer is a classic source of freelancing and duplicated tasks.
common_mistakes: Candidate gives a narrative 'story of the fire' instead of a structured resource-and-tasks report, and never states what remains undone.
Transfer happens but no explicit confirmation is exchanged, so both officers keep talking to companies on the tac channel.
Accountability is reported as a feeling ('crews are fine') rather than a location-by-location status.
After transfer the candidate keeps giving orders out of habit, effectively running a second command.
Radio transfer is delivered at the same speed as a face-to-face and the chief misses half of it.
safety_notes: This is a tabletop cognitive drill; the primary risk is training scars — enforce that role-players use real radio discipline so bad habits are not rehearsed.
Do not let the drill teach an abbreviated transfer as acceptable 'because it's just practice'; score omissions as failures.
success_criteria: All five transfer elements verbally delivered and captured by an observer's checklist.
Explicit two-way command-confirmation exchange occurs on the radio or face-to-face.
No company receives an order from the original IC after the confirmation is stated.
Reverting officer announces their new company assignment before the drill stops.

variations.name: Radio-Only Transfer
variations.description: Force the transfer entirely over the radio with the chief still responding, no face-to-face, no shared view of the board.
variations.adds: Trains the officer to build a complete verbal picture when the chief cannot see the command board or the building.

variations.name: Degraded Board
variations.description: Erase or omit one category on the command board (e.g., roof assignment blank) partway through before the chief arrives.
variations.adds: Forces the officer to recognize and flag their own accountability gap during transfer instead of passing a false 'all assigned' picture.

variations.name: Chief Assigns You a Priority
variations.description: Immediately after transfer, the chief assigns the reverting officer's company to an urgent task (e.g., relocate the attack line).
variations.adds: Trains the mental switch from strategic to task-level thinking and prompt acknowledgment of a new assignment.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH firefighter fatality reports cite incomplete command transfer and unclear command structure as contributing factors
lodd_connection.lesson: When command changes hands without a complete, confirmed transfer, accountability and undone tasks fall through the gap — the new IC commits resources against an incomplete picture.

references: IFSTA Company Officer / Fire Officer principles of command transfer
Blue Card / incident command transfer-of-command practice
NIOSH Fire Fighter Fatality Investigation Program reports (command structure findings)
Local incident command and passport/accountability SOG (operator-provided)

drills.title: Command Under a Mayday: The First 60 Seconds
drills.solo_note: Role-players staff a down member, RIT, and two crews; an evaluator times the 60 seconds

solo_variant.substitutions: Voice memos hold the pre-recorded mayday and the LUNAR reply so the transmission arrives when you are not expecting it. A second phone or a laptop plays routine traffic over the top of it to make the channel genuinely congested. Stopwatch for the 60 seconds. Whiteboard command board. Printed six-action checklist for the playback.
steps: A day or two ahead, record five mayday transmissions on your phone, each with a different location, cause, and air status. Record two of them garbled or missing an element. Record separate routine-traffic clips - a benchmark report, a request for a line. Do not listen back.
Set the board: floor plan, three or four companies assigned and operating, fire located. Give yourself one routine radio cycle out loud to get the rhythm.
Set a random countdown timer between 60 and 180 seconds, start recording yourself, and start the mayday clip on shuffle with a routine clip playing across it. You do not know which mayday you get.

The instant you hear it: start the stopwatch and work the six actions out loud - acknowledge the mayday, isolate it (emergency traffic, move the working crews), get LUNAR back and write it on the board, assign RIT and name a rescue group supervisor, order fire attack to hold or advance, initiate a PAR.
Stop the clock at 60 seconds and freeze. Write down, from memory, the order you actually said things in.

Play your recording back against the checklist. Score presence AND order: acknowledge and isolate first, LUNAR second, resources third, PAR last. Compare the LUNAR on your board to the LUNAR on the clip, word for word.
Reset with a new card and a new random delay. Run four to six reps. Use the garbled clips deliberately - score whether you asked for the missing element instead of guessing it.
solo_variant.self_score: All six actions on the recording inside 60 seconds, in priority order - out of order is a miss even if all six are there. Mayday acknowledged before you answer any routine traffic on the clip. LUNAR written on the board matches the recording with no invented details. Named rescue group supervisor, not just RIT go get him. Fire attack given an explicit order.
solo_variant.not_covered: A second mayday landing mid-rescue. A RIT officer whose radio dies on you. Role-players keying over each other unpredictably. Most of all, it does not cover the thing that actually degrades an IC - the voice on the radio being someone you know, and the knowledge that being slow costs them. You will run this calm every time.
