drills.objective: Acting as IC, manage the first 60 seconds after a mayday by acknowledging and isolating it, obtaining LUNAR, assigning RIT/rescue group, controlling the channel, initiating a PAR, and preserving fire attack — completing all six actions in correct priority order with no dropped mayday transmission.
equipment: Portable radios on at least two channels (or radio simulator)
Scripted mayday transmission and LUNAR details on cards for role-players
drills.setup: Bay tabletop or classroom. Post a working-fire floor plan and pre-stage a command board with three to four companies already assigned and operating. The candidate is seated as IC; role-players staff a down member, a RIT company, and two working crews on the radio. Channel designations, RIT staffing, and emergency-traffic procedure on the script are examples — replace them with your department's mayday and channel SOG before running.
steps: Brief the IC candidate with the current incident status (companies assigned, fire location) and let them run one routine radio cycle to establish rhythm.
Have the down-member role-player transmit a scripted mayday over the working channel while a second crew simultaneously attempts a routine transmission to create channel congestion.
Start the timer; score whether the IC acknowledges the mayday first, isolates it (declares emergency traffic / moves working crews to another channel), and captures LUNAR back from the member.
Require the IC to assign RIT and establish a rescue group with a clear supervisor, while verbally directing the fire attack company to continue holding or advancing the line.
Prompt a PAR and score whether the IC obtains it without stepping on the rescue channel or losing the mayday member's updates.
Stop the timer at 60 seconds, freeze the scene, and capture the order and completeness of what command SAID on the whiteboard for debrief.

Run the after-action debrief on decision quality and radio discipline — reconstruct the sequence, identify any point command lost control, then rotate a new candidate with an altered mayday location and LUNAR.
learning_points: If command does not isolate the mayday to its own priority — emergency traffic or a dedicated channel — the down member's LUNAR gets buried under routine traffic and the rescue starts blind.
Assigning RIT is not enough; naming a rescue group supervisor gives the IC a single point of contact so the IC is not personally coordinating every rescuer and losing the rest of the fireground.
Abandoning the fire attack to focus only on the rescue lets the fire grow toward the trapped member — holding or advancing the line is often what makes the rescue survivable.
A PAR taken too early crowds the channel; taken too late, the IC does not know whether a second member is also missing — timing and channel management are the skill, not just the words.
The order command speaks in matters: acknowledge and isolate first, LUNAR second, resources third, PAR to confirm scope — reversing this loses either the member's information or the channel.
common_mistakes: IC talks over the mayday member trying to give orders instead of getting quiet and capturing LUNAR.
Working crews are never moved off the channel, so the rescue and the fire attack fight for the same airtime.
RIT is deployed but no rescue group supervisor is named, and the IC ends up trying to run the rescue personally.
IC pulls all crews to focus on the rescue, the fire attack stalls, and conditions deteriorate on the trapped member.
No PAR is initiated, so command never confirms whether only one member is down.
safety_notes: Tabletop cognitive drill; the main hazard is rehearsing bad radio habits — require role-players to key up realistically so channel congestion is genuine, not simulated politely.
Do not let the drill reward speed over completeness; a fast sequence that drops the LUNAR is a failure, and the debrief must say so.
success_criteria: Mayday acknowledged before any routine transmission is answered.
Emergency traffic / channel isolation declared and complete LUNAR captured on the board.
RIT assigned AND a named rescue group supervisor established.
Fire attack company receives an explicit order to continue, and a PAR is initiated within the 60-second window.

variations.name: Garbled LUNAR
variations.description: The down member transmits an incomplete or broken LUNAR (location unclear or air status missing).
variations.adds: Trains the IC to recognize the gap and direct a specific follow-up question rather than accepting an unusable report.

variations.name: Second Mayday
variations.description: A second member declares mayday 30 seconds into the first rescue.
variations.adds: Forces the IC to prioritize between two rescues and decide whether to split the rescue group or request additional alarms.

variations.name: Radio Failure
variations.description: The RIT company's radio fails during assignment (role-player goes silent).
variations.adds: Trains the IC to detect a missing acknowledgment and re-assign or send a runner instead of assuming the order was received.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH firefighter fatality reports document maydays degraded by radio congestion, no PAR, and freelancing during the rescue
lodd_connection.lesson: The first minute of a mayday is won or lost on channel control and priority order — when routine traffic buries the down member and no PAR confirms who else is missing, the rescue starts behind and stays behind.

references: IFSTA Company Officer / mayday management principles
NFA / Blue Card mayday and RIT command practice
FSRI/UL fireground research on tenability and coordinated attack during rescue
NIOSH Fire Fighter Fatality Investigation Program reports (mayday/communications findings)
Local mayday, RIT, and emergency-traffic SOG (operator-provided)

drills.title: Lieutenant Oral Board: Accountability After a Miss
drills.objective: Within 45 minutes, answer one accountability-themed oral board prompt plus 3 follow-up probes aloud, then score the recorded response against strong-answer indicators covering ownership, corrective action, and crew impact.
drills.setup: Sit across a table from a facilitator who reads the prompt cold and holds the follow-up probes back until you finish. No prep time on the primary prompt — the board will not give you any.
steps: Facilitator reads the primary prompt: 'You are the lieutenant on Engine 12. During overhaul at a residential fire, a firefighter on your crew removed their SCBA facepiece without your knowledge or an air-quality reading. Nobody was hurt. The battalion chief did not see it. Walk us through what you do.' Candidate answers aloud, uninterrupted, in 3-5 minutes.
Probe one: 'The firefighter is your most senior member and tells you he has done it that way for twenty years. What changes about your approach?'
Probe two: 'Your captain tells you to let it go because there was no injury and no complaint. How do you respond?'
Probe three: 'Two weeks later the same firefighter does it again. Take us through that conversation and what you document.'

Candidate self-scores the recording against the answer-quality checklist: did the answer separate the immediate correction from the follow-up conversation, name a specific documentation step, and address crew culture rather than one individual?
Rerun the primary prompt once more on the recorder, correcting only the two weakest checklist items — do not rewrite the whole answer.
learning_points: A strong answer sequences accountability: stop the unsafe act immediately, address it privately, then decide the documentation level — candidates who collapse these into one step sound like they either ignore problems or overreact to them.
Boards probe seniority and pressure from above specifically to see whether your standard bends. The strong answer holds the standard while changing the tone and setting, not the expectation.
Escalation on repeat behavior is a scoring gate. Candidates who describe an identical second conversation lose points; the second time must show a documented, progressive step.
Answers that mention the rest of the crew watching score higher than answers that treat this as a two-person problem, because supervision is judged by what the crew learns from how you handle it.
common_mistakes: Weak answer: leading with discipline language and paperwork before describing the immediate on-scene correction.
Weak answer: agreeing with the captain to let it go, which reads to a board as a candidate who will not hold a standard without cover.
Weak answer: claiming to quote a specific department policy number or general order — boards can tell when a candidate is bluffing, and it costs credibility on every later answer.
Reasoning trap: describing the conversation entirely in the abstract ('I'd have a coaching conversation') without a single line of what you would actually say.
safety_notes: Verbal exercise only — no live evolution or PPE use.
Where your own department has policies, SOGs, or contractual processes, those govern over anything in this drill; localize terminology and procedures before using this for group training.
success_criteria: Primary prompt answered in one structured pass without restarting or trailing off
All three probes answered with a specific action and a specific spoken line, not a general principle
Self-score identifies at least two named checklist gaps and the second recording closes them

variations.name: Hostile Probe
variations.description: Facilitator interrupts the primary answer twice with 'that isn't what I asked' and moves on before the candidate finishes.
variations.adds: Trains recovery and composure when a board member is deliberately unhelpful.

variations.name: Cold Open
variations.description: Candidate draws the prompt blind from a face-down deck with no idea of the topic area.
variations.adds: Removes the mental warm-up the candidate would not get on exam day.

drills.solo_note: A board needs someone to read prompts and probe. Alone, use a face-down prompt deck, a voice recorder, and playback self-scoring against the checklist.

solo_variant.substitutions: Replace the facilitator with a face-down deck of index cards: the primary prompt on one, each probe on its own card. Film yourself rather than only recording audio — a board reads your posture, eye contact and hands, and you cannot hear those on playback. Prop the phone at eye level. The printed answer-quality checklist replaces board feedback; a kitchen timer replaces their clock.
steps: Write the primary prompt and the three probes on four index cards, shuffle the probes, and place all four face down.
Start filming at eye level, flip the primary card, read it aloud once, then answer immediately with no prep pause.
Flip one probe card at a time and answer each on the recorder before flipping the next.
Stop recording and wait at least ten minutes before playback so you hear the answer as a stranger would.
Watch the video with the checklist in hand and mark each indicator hit or missed, noting timestamps — and watch yourself with the sound off once, for posture, eye contact and fidgeting.
Rerecord only the primary prompt, targeting the two weakest indicators, and compare the two takes.
solo_variant.self_score: Score five indicators: sequenced correction, specific documentation step, at least one verbatim spoken line, concrete escalation on repeat behavior, and crew-level impact addressed. Three or fewer hits means rerun the drill the same week. Mark any answer over five minutes, or with more than three filler restarts, as a fail on delivery regardless of content.
solo_variant.not_covered: Solo practice cannot reproduce a live board's interruptions, skeptical body language, or unscripted follow-ups that chase a weak spot you did not anticipate. It also gives no outside read on tone — whether you came across as firm or as harsh. Book at least one session with a real officer before the exam to cover both gaps.

drills.title: Lieutenant Oral Board: Crew Conflict Under Pressure
drills.objective: Within 40 minutes, deliver a spoken oral board answer to a crew conflict prompt plus 3 probes, then score the recording for whether the response separates the surface complaint from the actual problem and commits to a concrete supervisory action.
drills.setup: Table-top interview posture. Candidate sits, hands empty, no notes. Facilitator reads once and does not repeat the prompt — boards rarely do.
steps: Facilitator reads the primary prompt: 'You have been the lieutenant on Truck 7 for four months. Two firefighters on your crew have stopped speaking to each other. Station work still gets done, but radio traffic between them on the last two calls was short and cold. Neither has come to you. Tell the board what you do.' Candidate answers aloud in 3-5 minutes.
Probe one: 'You talk to each of them separately and get two completely different stories about what started it. Now what?'
Probe two: 'One of them tells you the real issue is that they believe the other made a comment about their family. What changes, and who else do you involve?'
Probe three: 'Your crew is running calls tonight. What do you do before the next tone drops, as opposed to what you do over the next month?'

Self-score the recording: did the answer distinguish a personality friction from a conduct issue, name the point at which it goes above the lieutenant, and give a same-shift action separate from the long-term fix?
Write out in one sentence the single supervisory principle the answer was built on, then rerecord the primary prompt leading with that sentence.
learning_points: Boards score conflict prompts on whether you gather information before acting — candidates who resolve the conflict in the first thirty seconds of their answer are marking themselves as officers who act on one side of a story.

The strongest answers name the threshold explicitly: friction the lieutenant owns, versus conduct that goes up the chain the same day. Candidates who never draw that line score as either overreaching or as passing every problem upward.

Operational impact is the officer's real justification for intervening. Cold radio traffic between two crew members is a safety issue, and saying so out loud converts a personality problem into a supervisory one the board recognizes.
Separating the immediate action from the long-term fix is a scoring pattern across most conflict prompts, because it shows you can supervise tonight while still solving the underlying issue.
A candidate who anchors the whole answer to one stated principle sounds like an officer with a philosophy; a candidate who lists tactics sounds like someone who studied a list.
common_mistakes: Weak answer: putting both firefighters in a room together as the first move, before understanding what the conflict actually is.
Weak answer: treating a possible harassment issue as something the lieutenant quietly handles at station level.
Weak answer: describing only long-term culture building with nothing that happens before the next call.
Reasoning trap: answering as a peer or friend rather than as the supervisor of record.
safety_notes: Verbal study exercise only.
Use fictional names; do not rehearse using real crew members as examples.
success_criteria: Candidate gathers information separately before proposing a resolution
Answer explicitly names the threshold where the issue leaves the lieutenant's level
Answer contains a distinct same-shift action and a distinct long-term action
Recording is under five minutes with no restart of the opening

variations.name: Compressed Clock
variations.description: Candidate has two minutes total for the primary prompt instead of five.
variations.adds: Forces the candidate to lead with structure rather than warming up into it.

variations.name: Chief's Chair
variations.description: Rerun the same prompt as a battalion chief being briefed by the lieutenant.
variations.adds: Sharpens the distinction between what you handle and what you escalate.

drills.solo_note: The prompt and probes need a reader. Alone, draw cards blind from a prompt deck, record every answer, and self-score on delayed playback against the checklist.

solo_variant.substitutions: A face-down index card deck replaces the facilitator: primary prompt on one card, the three probes shuffled beneath it. A voice recorder replaces the board panel, and the printed answer-quality checklist replaces their scoring sheet. Set a timer where the board's clock would be and keep it in view.
steps: Build the deck: primary prompt on one card, each probe on its own card, all face down and shuffled below the primary.
Start the recorder and the timer, flip the primary card, read it aloud once, and begin answering with no pause to think.
Answer each probe card in turn on the recorder, flipping the next only after you have finished the previous.
Set the recording aside for at least ten minutes so playback is not colored by what you meant to say.
Play it back with the checklist and mark each of the five indicators hit or missed, noting timestamps.
Write your one-sentence supervisory principle, then rerecord the primary prompt leading with it and compare takes.
solo_variant.self_score: Five indicators: separate information gathering, escalation threshold named aloud, operational justification, distinct same-shift and long-term actions, and one stated principle. Four or five hits is exam-ready on this prompt. Three or fewer means rerun it within the week. Score delivery separately — over five minutes, or a restarted opening, is a fail.
solo_variant.not_covered: Alone you cannot practice reading a skeptical board member's reaction, recovering from an interruption, or handling a probe that goes somewhere your deck did not anticipate. You also cannot judge your own tone reliably. Before the exam, run this prompt at least once with an officer who will push back mid-answer.

drills.title: Build Your Own Lieutenant Exam Question Deck
drills.objective: Within 60 minutes, working alone, build and run a 12-question multiple-choice deck on fire-service supervision and crew accountability, then self-score against written rationales and log every miss with the reason it was missed.
equipment: Your own department's SOG binder if you have one (optional)
drills.setup: Kitchen table, alone. You are both the test writer and the candidate. Write the deck first, walk away from it for at least ten minutes, then sit back down and answer it cold. These are practice questions you wrote — they are not predictions of any real exam and they do not quote any department's policy.
steps: Write 12 scenario stems on index cards, one per card — short supervision situations at a fictional department: a crew member skipping a hoseline check, a probationary firefighter freezing at a doorway, a station argument over a rig assignment, a driver who took an unapproved route. Two to three sentences each, no more.

On the back of each card, write four answer options labeled A through D. Make one option clearly strongest, one plausible-but-passive (defer it, document it, wait for the chief), one plausible-but-overreaching (discipline immediately, take the crew out of service), and one that solves the wrong problem.

Under the options, write two lines of rationale for the strongest answer — why it is best AND what specifically makes the runner-up weaker. If you cannot write the second line, the question is not good enough; rewrite the options.
Break for at least ten minutes. Do something else entirely so the answers go cold.
Return, shuffle the deck, and answer all 12 with a 90-second-per-question timer, writing your letter choice on a separate sheet. Do not flip cards while answering.

Self-score against your own rationales. For every miss, write one sentence naming why you missed it: misread the stem, chased the distractor, guessed, or genuinely did not know the supervision principle.
Sort the misses into two piles — reading errors and knowledge gaps. Rewrite the three knowledge-gap questions harder and put them at the front of tomorrow's deck.
learning_points: Writing the distractors teaches you more than answering them — you cannot build a convincing wrong answer until you understand why it is wrong.
Most written-exam misses at lieutenant level are reading errors, not knowledge gaps. Separating the two tells you whether to study harder or slow down.

Supervision questions usually reward the answer that addresses the behavior directly, at the lowest appropriate level, and documents it — not the one that escalates fastest or avoids the conversation entirely.
A rationale you can write in two lines is a principle you actually hold. One you cannot write is one you are guessing at.
common_mistakes: Writing four options where three are obviously silly — real exam distractors are all defensible on a fast read, so build them that way.
Answering the deck immediately after writing it, which tests recall of what you just wrote rather than reasoning.
Scoring only the number right and never writing down why a question was missed.
Building every stem around fireground tactics and none around personnel, policy judgement, or station-level conflict.
safety_notes: Paper-and-pen study only; no apparatus, equipment, or physical evolution involved.
success_criteria: 12 stems written, each with four defensible options and a two-line rationale
Deck answered cold under time with choices recorded before any card was flipped
Every miss labeled as a reading error or a knowledge gap, with three questions rewritten for the next session

variations.name: Blind Trade
variations.description: Swap decks with another candidate and answer theirs cold instead of your own.
variations.adds: Removes all residual recall and exposes you to stems framed the way someone else thinks.

variations.name: Rationale First
variations.description: Write the two-line rationale before writing any options, then build four options around it.
variations.adds: Forces the supervision principle to drive the question instead of the question drifting to fit a clever distractor.

drills.solo_note: Fully solo: you write the deck, cool off for ten minutes, answer it cold under time, then self-score against your own written rationales.

drills.title: Solo Timed Set: Supervision and Policy Judgment
drills.objective: Within 45 minutes, working alone, run a timed 20-question set weighted toward policy judgment and crew accountability, then self-score and rebuild the three weakest questions into a carry-forward list you retest in 48 hours.
equipment: Question set on paper or in a notes app
drills.setup: Alone, one sitting, no interruptions. Use a deck you built in a previous session or write 20 fresh stems the night before so they are cold. Twenty questions in 25 minutes, then 20 minutes of scoring and diagnosis. Nothing here quotes or certifies any department policy — the scenarios and any procedures in them are fictional.
steps: Set the timer for 25 minutes and answer all 20 questions without stopping. If a question stalls you, mark it, pick your best guess, and move on — do not let one stem eat four minutes.
Stop when the timer stops, even mid-question. Record how many you left marked as uncertain.
Score the set. Write the raw number, then separate it into three counts: right and confident, right but guessed, wrong.
Read the rationale for every wrong answer and every lucky guess. Lucky guesses matter as much as misses — they are knowledge gaps that happened to break your way.
For each wrong answer, write one line naming the trap: over-escalation, under-action, solving the wrong problem, or missing a qualifier in the stem such as 'first', 'best', or 'most appropriate'.
Pick the three questions that exposed real gaps, rewrite them with different scenarios but the same underlying principle, and add them to the carry-forward list.
Diary the session: date, raw score, dominant trap. Retest the carry-forward list in 48 hours before starting a new set.
learning_points: Timed conditions change your reasoning — answers that felt obvious untimed become coin flips at 75 seconds each, and that gap is what you are training to close.
Qualifiers carry the question. 'First action', 'best action', and 'most appropriate action' can point to three different options from the same stem.
A right-but-guessed answer is not a point earned, it is a gap you have not found yet. Tracking it separately keeps your score honest.
Tracking your dominant trap across sessions is more useful than tracking your score — the trap tells you what to fix, the score only tells you how you felt that day.
Retesting the same principle in a fresh scenario 48 hours later is what makes it stick; re-reading the same card does not.
common_mistakes: Letting one hard question consume the clock instead of guessing and moving on.
Counting a lucky guess as a point and never revisiting it.
Skimming past qualifiers like 'first' or 'most appropriate' and answering the question you expected rather than the one written.
Chasing a rising raw score while the same trap shows up in every session.
safety_notes: Written study only; no equipment or physical activity.
success_criteria: 20 questions attempted within 25 minutes with uncertain items marked
Score split into right-confident, right-guessed, and wrong
Each wrong answer labeled with a named trap, and three questions rewritten onto the carry-forward list

variations.name: Tight Clock
variations.description: Cut the time to 18 minutes for the same 20 questions.
variations.adds: Trains fast triage and shows which principles you hold well enough to apply without deliberation.

variations.name: Explain Out Loud
variations.description: After scoring, say the rationale for five questions aloud as if answering an oral board.
variations.adds: Bridges written recognition into spoken reasoning, which is where most candidates lose ground later in the process.

drills.solo_note: Built for one person: timed set answered alone, self-scored against written rationales, with a carry-forward list you retest in 48 hours.

drills.title: Blind-Draw Size-Up Reps: First-Due Scenario Cards
drills.objective: In 45 minutes, draw six fictional incident cards blind and deliver a timed initial size-up, priorities, resource request and crew assignments aloud for each — then score your own recordings against a fixed indicator list.
equipment: Index cards or printed scenario cards (10-15 written in advance)
Blank paper for a tactical worksheet
drills.setup: Kitchen table. Write your scenario cards on a different day than you run them so the details are cold. Each card carries only: time of day, occupancy type, what is showing, reported occupants, and what is on the first alarm. Shuffle face down. Timer and recorder within reach.
steps: Write 10-15 fictional incident cards in a separate sitting — mixed occupancies, mixed times of day, some with nothing showing. Keep each card to five lines so information stays deliberately incomplete.
Shuffle, draw one card face down, flip it and start a 60-second timer. Read the card once only, then put it face down again — you answer from memory, the way you would from the seat.
Record aloud: initial radio report, incident priorities in order, your strategic mode, and the assignment for your own crew. Stop at the timer.
Restart the timer for 90 seconds and record a second transmission: what you are requesting and why — water supply, additional companies, and the specific job each is coming for.
Write one line on the worksheet naming the risk you accepted and what you got for it. If you cannot name the benefit, you have not made a decision — you have made a habit.
Repeat for six cards without playback, so fatigue and pattern-breaking are part of the rep.
Play back all recordings and self-score against the performance indicators, marking every transmission where you named a tactic without naming who was doing it.
learning_points: A size-up is a decision, not a description — the observations only earn their place if an assignment follows from them.
Resource requests are judged on justification, not volume; asking for two more companies with no stated job reads as panic, asking with a job reads as command.
Working from a card you have already put face down forces the same partial-recall pressure you get on the fireground and in the assessment room.
Risk/benefit reasoning only counts when both halves are spoken aloud; candidates routinely name the risk and leave the benefit implied.
common_mistakes: Reading the card three times and building a perfect answer — that is a comprehension exercise, not a size-up rep.
Recording assignments as tactics only ('we'll get a line in') without naming the crew, the entry point, or the objective.
Requesting resources by alarm level with no stated task, so the debrief cannot tell whether the request was reasoned.
Skipping playback because it is uncomfortable to listen to yourself — playback is where the whole drill pays off.
Reusing the same three favourite occupancies, so the deck never surprises you.
safety_notes: Study exercise only — no apparatus movement, no live evolution, no PPE required.
success_criteria: Six cards run with recorded transmissions inside the timer for each
Every crew assignment names a crew, a task and a location
Every resource request states the job the resource is coming to do
Self-score sheet identifies at least three specific transmissions to redo

variations.name: Nothing Showing Deck
variations.description: Build a deck where every card reports nothing visible on arrival and the information arrives only through the card's dispatch lines.
variations.adds: Trains investigation-mode discipline and stops you defaulting to an offensive announcement before you have anything to base it on.

variations.name: Short Alarm
variations.description: Halve the companies listed on every card before you draw.
variations.adds: Forces explicit prioritisation and makes the risk/benefit sentence do real work.

variations.name: Written Instead of Spoken
variations.description: Handwrite the transmissions rather than recording them, one card per page, still inside the timer.
variations.adds: Useful in a quiet house or shared space, and produces a marked-up artefact you can revisit weeks later.

drills.solo_note: Built for one person alone: write the card deck on an earlier day, draw blind, record transmissions against a timer, then self-score on playback.

drills.title: Escalating Incident Board: Decision Checkpoints
drills.objective: Run a 60-minute tabletop on a fictional escalating incident with four timed decision checkpoints, defending resource requests and crew assignments against live probes, and close with a structured debrief against named strong-answer indicators.
equipment: Hand-drawn incident sketch on flip paper or whiteboard
Four escalation cards prepared in advance
Counters or coins to represent companies
drills.setup: Kitchen table or watch room. One person facilitates and holds the four escalation cards; one or two others act as arriving officers and dispatch, answering only what is written on the cards. The candidate faces the sketch with counters for companies and a worksheet. Fictional occupancy — a two-story mixed retail and residential block on a fictional street.
steps: Candidate is given the dispatch line and 90 seconds to deliver an initial size-up, priorities and first assignments, moving counters onto the sketch as they commit companies.
Checkpoint one at eight minutes: facilitator plays escalation card one (a condition change), candidate has 60 seconds to restate priorities and say what, if anything, changes.
Checkpoint two at sixteen minutes: card two introduces a resource constraint — something requested is delayed. Candidate must re-sequence rather than repeat the request.
Checkpoint three at twenty-four minutes: card three introduces an exposure or occupant development that tests the risk/benefit position taken earlier.
Checkpoint four at thirty-two minutes: card four extends the operational period; candidate addresses accountability, relief and the plan for the next thirty minutes.
Role-players probe with 'why that crew', 'what tells you it is working', and 'what would make you change strategy' — no coaching, no hints, just the question.

Structured debrief from the recording: walk the counters back through each checkpoint and name where the plan changed, where it should have changed and did not, and two strong-answer patterns the candidate hit.
learning_points: Checkpoints test adaptability, not memory — assessors want to see a plan revised for a reason, and they equally want to see a plan held for a reason.
Re-sequencing under a resource delay is a stronger answer than repeating the original request louder.
Moving physical counters exposes companies you committed and then forgot, which is the most common silent failure in tactical stations.
A defended decision beats a fashionable one; probes are looking for your reasoning, not your agreement.
Extending the operational period surfaces relief, accountability and rehab thinking that short scenarios never reach.
common_mistakes: Changing strategy at every checkpoint to look responsive, with no trigger named for the change.
Leaving counters on the board with no current task — companies committed and mentally abandoned.
Answering the probe with a policy phrase instead of the reasoning behind it.
Facilitator softening cards or hinting when the candidate stalls, which removes the entire training value.
Debriefing from impression rather than from the recording and the board state.
safety_notes: Tabletop study exercise only — no apparatus, no evolution, no PPE.
Fictional incident and fictional address; not modelled on any real assessment center scenario.
success_criteria: Initial assignments made inside 90 seconds with crew, task and location named
Each checkpoint answered inside the timer with a stated trigger for changing or holding the plan
Every counter on the board accounted for with a current task at the final checkpoint
Resource requests justified by task at every stage

variations.name: Silent Facilitator
variations.description: Facilitator hands over each escalation card face up and says nothing at all for the whole run.
variations.adds: Removes conversational scaffolding and shows whether the candidate can drive the scenario without being drawn along.

variations.name: Hostile Probe
variations.description: Role-players push back on one correct decision as if it were wrong, and hold the pushback for a full minute.
variations.adds: Trains defending sound reasoning without collapsing, which is a recurring failure point under assessment pressure.

variations.name: Two-Candidate Rotation
variations.description: Two candidates alternate checkpoints on the same incident, each inheriting the other's board state.
variations.adds: Forces reading someone else's plan quickly and adopting or changing it deliberately.

drills.solo_note: As written it needs a facilitator and role-players to probe. Alone, run the solo variant: blind-drawn cards, phone timer, recorder and playback scoring.

solo_variant.substitutions: The facilitator becomes a sealed deck of escalation cards written on an earlier day and drawn face down. The role-players become a fixed written list of six probe questions you answer aloud at every checkpoint. The clock becomes a phone timer set for four checkpoints. The debrief partner becomes your voice recorder plus the counters left on the board.
steps: On an earlier day, write eight escalation cards and shuffle them into a face-down pile; write your six standing probe questions on a separate card and leave it face up.
Set the phone timer for the four checkpoint intervals and start it with the dispatch line.
Deliver the initial size-up, priorities and assignments aloud into the recorder, moving counters onto the sketch as you commit companies.
At each timer alert, draw the top escalation card, flip it, read it once and turn it face down again before you speak.
Answer the escalation inside 60 seconds, then answer all six standing probe questions aloud on the record — including the ones that feel obvious.
At the final checkpoint, point at each counter in turn and state its current task out loud before stopping the recording.
Play the whole session back with the board untouched, marking every checkpoint where you changed the plan without naming a trigger and every counter you could not account for.
Write three specific transmissions to redo, and redo them on the record before you pack the board away.
solo_variant.self_score: Score out of ten: one point per checkpoint answered inside the timer (four), one per checkpoint with a named trigger for changing or holding (four), one for a full board accounted for at the end, one for a resource request re-sequenced rather than repeated. Eight or better, run a harder deck. Below six, rerun the same deck in three days and compare recordings.
solo_variant.not_covered: Solo running gives you no unpredictable probes. Your written questions are the ones you already thought to ask, so your blind spots stay blind. There is no pressure from someone watching you stall, no follow-up digging into the weak part of an answer, and no calibration against another candidate. Treat this as structure-building and get in front of real people before the process.

drills.title: Coaching an Underperforming Crew Member
drills.objective: Within 45 minutes, work a promotional-style personnel scenario: diagnose why a crew member is underperforming, plan and deliver a coaching conversation, handle two follow-up probes, then self-score against strong-supervisory-response indicators.
equipment: Scenario card (written by hand or printed)
Voice recorder or phone recording app
drills.setup: Oral-board style. Scenario: a three-year firefighter on your crew has become slow on hose deployment, quiet on the rig, and twice arrived late for shift change. No safety incident yet. You are the company officer and this is your crew.
steps: Read the scenario cold and take two minutes of notes: what you know, what you are assuming, and what you would want to find out before saying anything.
State aloud how you would open the conversation — where, when, and your first three sentences. Name why you chose that setting.
Work the diagnosis: list at least four plausible causes (skill gap, home life, morale, medical, conflict with a crew member) and how you would find out which it is without interrogating.
Deliver the coaching conversation aloud end to end — observation, impact on the crew, question, listening, agreed action, follow-up date.
Answer the probes: (a) he says 'nobody else gets picked on', (b) two weeks later nothing has changed, (c) another firefighter asks you privately what you are doing about him.
Debrief: score your own answer against the strong-response indicators, then note the one probe that exposed you and rewrite that answer.
learning_points: A strong supervisory response separates the behavior from the person: you describe what you observed and its effect on the crew, not what you think the firefighter is.
Coaching starts with a question, not a verdict — boards listen for whether you gathered information before deciding what kind of problem you had.
Every credible coaching answer ends with an agreed action and a named follow-up point; without it you have had a chat, not supervised.

Knowing when a performance conversation stops being coaching and becomes a matter for your department's formal process is itself a supervisory judgement — and saying so out loud is a strength, not a dodge.
common_mistakes: Weak answer: opening with discipline language when nothing has yet been coached or documented in your own notes.
Weak answer: doing it in front of the crew, or in the bay where anyone can walk through.
Weak answer: assuming attitude when the likelier cause is a skill gap nobody has corrected or something going on at home.
Weak answer: promising the crew you will 'sort him out' — discussing one member's performance with peers.
Reasoning trap: describing the perfect conversation with no plan for what happens if it does not work.
safety_notes: Study exercise only — do not rehearse using a real named colleague as the scenario subject.

Where your own department has policies, SOGs, or contractual processes — including any performance or HR process — those govern over anything in this drill; localize terminology and procedures before using this for group training.
success_criteria: Names at least four plausible causes before choosing a response
Delivers a conversation containing observation, impact, question, agreed action, and follow-up date
Handles the 'nobody else gets picked on' probe without arguing or backing down
States clearly where coaching ends and the department's formal process begins, without claiming to know that process's content

variations.name: Senior Firefighter
variations.description: The underperformer has eighteen years in and trained you when you were probationary.
variations.adds: Tests whether the candidate can supervise upward in experience without either deferring or overcompensating.

variations.name: Acting Officer
variations.description: You are acting up for four shifts and will hand the crew back to the substantive officer.
variations.adds: Forces a handover element: what you record, what you pass on, and what is not yours to start.

drills.solo_note: Needs someone to play the firefighter and push back. Alone, use scenario cards and rehearse the whole conversation aloud into a recorder, then score the playback.

solo_variant.substitutions: Replace the facilitator with three index cards you write and leave face down: the scenario, the probe set, and the strong-response indicators. Film yourself rather than only recording audio — a crew member reads your face and posture, and playback of audio alone cannot show what you looked like saying it. Voice the firefighter yourself, giving the most awkward honest answer you can think of.
steps: Write the scenario and the three probes on cards before you start, so you cannot soften them mid-drill.
Set a timer for two minutes of note-taking, then start filming at eye level.
Speak the whole coaching conversation aloud in real time — both voices, no stopping to restart when a sentence comes out badly.
Answer each probe card in turn, drawing them face down so the order surprises you.
Stop recording and wait ten minutes before playback so you hear it as a listener, not as the author.
Play it back with the indicator card in front of you and mark each indicator hit or missed — then watch once with the sound off, for what your face and posture were doing.
solo_variant.self_score: Score the playback on four things: did you state an observation before an opinion; did you ask a real question and leave silence for the answer; did it end with a specific agreed action and a date; did you name where coaching stops and the department's process starts. Count your filler too.
solo_variant.not_covered: Solo rehearsal cannot replicate a real person reacting badly, which is the actual difficulty. Voicing both parts, you hand yourself a firefighter who takes it well. You will not get the flat denial, the counter-accusation about your own leadership, or the silence you fill by talking yourself out of your position.

drills.title: Unsafe Act, Then Rebuilding Crew Trust
drills.objective: Within 50 minutes, work a two-part scenario: correct an unsafe act in the moment on the fireground, then handle the fallout with a crew that has decided you overreacted — and self-score both halves against strong-supervisory-response indicators.
equipment: Voice recorder or phone recording app
drills.setup: Oral-board style, two-part. Part one: at a working residential fire, your senior firefighter removes his facepiece in a smoke-filled hallway to talk to a crew member. Part two: back at quarters, the crew has gone quiet, and you hear that they think you humiliated him on the fireground.
steps: Part one, live correction: state aloud exactly what you say and do in the first ten seconds. Justify why that and not more.
Explain the difference between what you say on the fireground and what you say afterwards — and why the two are different conversations.
Part two, the follow-up conversation with the individual: deliver it aloud, covering the act, the risk, why you corrected it there and then, and what you expect next time.

Part two, the crew: the atmosphere has changed and one firefighter says you made an example of him. Answer aloud, in front of the crew, without either apologising for the correction or lecturing them.

Probe set: (a) he is your most experienced firefighter and you are two years in the seat, (b) you later learn his facepiece seal had failed, (c) the crew's version of events is more dramatic than what happened.
Debrief: score both halves separately. A candidate can pass the correction and fail the trust rebuild, and boards score that as a fail.
Rewrite your weakest answer and run only that segment again.
learning_points: Immediate risk gets an immediate, short, unambiguous correction — the conversation about it belongs afterwards, in private, at length.
Correcting an unsafe act is not what damages crew trust; failing to explain it afterwards is, and boards test the second half far more often than candidates expect.
Being wrong about a fact — the failed seal — does not make the correction wrong, and how a candidate handles that probe reveals whether they can hold a position and update it at the same time.
Officer presence is built in the ordinary shift, not in the incident: the crew's willingness to accept a hard correction was decided weeks before it happened.

You cannot rebuild trust by seeking the crew's agreement that you were right — only by being consistent, explaining your reasoning, and not doing it differently next time because it was uncomfortable.
common_mistakes: Weak answer: delivering a full explanation on the fireground while the hazard is still live.
Weak answer: saying nothing at the time and saving it all for the debrief, which tells the crew the act was tolerable.
Weak answer: apologising for the correction itself to buy the crew's mood back.
Weak answer: reversing the correction when the failed-seal probe lands, rather than separating the act from the reason for it.
Reasoning trap: treating the crew's reaction as insubordination to be handled rather than a trust problem to be repaired.
safety_notes: Table-top study exercise only — no live fire, smoke, or SCBA evolution is part of this drill.

Where your own department has policies, SOGs, or contractual processes — including safety-reporting and personnel processes — those govern over anything in this drill; localize terminology and procedures before using this for group training.
Use fictional scenarios only; do not rehearse against a real incident involving named colleagues.
success_criteria: Correction in part one is under ten seconds, unambiguous, and stops the hazard
Candidate explicitly separates the fireground correction from the later conversation and says why
The crew conversation neither retracts the correction nor lectures the crew
Candidate names at least one thing they will do over the following weeks to rebuild presence, not just one conversation

variations.name: Professionalism, Not Safety
variations.description: Swap the unsafe act for the same firefighter making a demeaning remark to a member of the public at a medical call.
variations.adds: Removes the immediate-danger justification, so the candidate must justify the timing of the correction on conduct grounds alone.

variations.name: You Were Watching
variations.description: It emerges that you saw the same behavior twice before and said nothing either time.
variations.adds: Tests whether the candidate can own a supervisory failure of their own without collapsing their authority.

variations.name: New To The Crew
variations.description: You transferred in nine days ago and have no relationship credit at all.
variations.adds: Strips out accumulated trust and forces the candidate to build presence from a cold start.

drills.solo_note: Needs role-players for the firefighter and the crew. Alone, run it from written cards, speak every part aloud into a recorder, and score the playback in two halves.

solo_variant.substitutions: Write five cards before you start and leave them face down: the fireground scene, the private conversation, the crews challenge, the three probes, and the indicator list. Film yourself rather than only recording audio — a crew reads your face and bearing, and audio playback cannot show those. Stand for the fireground segment, sit for the station segments.
steps: Draw the fireground card and respond within five seconds of reading it — part one gives you no thinking time.
Film the private conversation in full, uncut, both voices, without restarting when a line comes out clumsy.
Record the crew conversation with the challenge stated as bluntly as you can bear to say it about yourself.
Draw the three probe cards in random order and answer each on the recording before reading the next.
Leave the recording for at least ten minutes, then watch it back with the indicator card in hand — once with sound, once without, for bearing and eye contact.
Score the two halves separately on paper and write down which half was weaker.
Re-record only the weakest ninety seconds, then compare the two takes.
solo_variant.self_score: Score part one on three things: was the correction short, was it unambiguous, did it stop the hazard. Score part two on four: did you explain the public timing, avoid apologising for the correction itself, separate the act from the failed-seal assumption, and name sustained behavior over weeks. Over ninety seconds on the crew conversation is over-talking.
solo_variant.not_covered: Solo rehearsal cannot replicate a real person reacting badly, which is the whole difficulty here. Voicing the senior firefighter yourself, you hand yourself a man who listens — not one who goes silent, gets loud, or turns it onto your own performance. You cannot simulate a crew's flat room either. Sit down with one trusted colleague and let them be genuinely difficult before your board.

drills.title: Mayday Declaration & LUNAR Radio Drill
drills.solo_note: An instructor reads scenario cards and runs distracting radio traffic; reps are scored

solo_variant.substitutions: Instructor's scenario cards become a shuffled deck you write yourself and draw blind. Phone voice recorder replaces the scoring officer and the training channel. A second phone playing a fireground radio traffic clip on speaker replaces the instructor's distracting traffic.
steps: Write 12 index cards, one trigger each: through the floor, entangled, lost, low air no exit, pinned by collapse, firefighter down beside you, disoriented in a basement, hoseline lost, ceiling down on you, zero visibility no wall, SCBA failure, stairs collapsed behind you.
Shuffle face down. Set your phone recording and say the time or rep number out loud so you can find each rep on playback.

Draw a card, read it, and start the recorder rep: declare 'Mayday, mayday, mayday' followed by Location, Unit, Name, Assignment and air, Resources needed. Say the emergency-button activation out loud as part of the sequence.
Add stress: 30 seconds of hard work — bear crawl, stair repeats, weighted carry — then draw and transmit immediately. No SCBA, no air restriction, breathe freely.
Add interference: start the fireground audio clip on the second phone, then draw and transmit over it. You must speak through the traffic, not wait for a gap.
Run the officer side too: after each mayday, switch hats and record the acknowledgement — repeat the LUNAR back, clear the channel, assign RIT.
Play the recording back with your LUNAR card in hand. Mark each rep for missing elements before you run another block.
solo_variant.self_score: On playback: stopwatch from the end of the card read to the word 'mayday' — under 10 seconds. Tick all five LUNAR elements per rep; Location must be present every time. Any word you cannot make out on the recording counts as a failed rep.
solo_variant.not_covered: You are cueing your own triggers, so it never tests recognising a mayday you did not expect. It does not cover the cultural barrier — the hardest part is keying up in front of a crew and a chief, and a phone does not judge you. No real RIT response, no actual channel discipline with other units, no officer receiving under real load.

drills.objective: Declare a mayday correctly and immediately when trigger conditions occur, delivering LUNAR (Location, Unit, Name, Assignment/Air, Resources needed) under stress.
equipment: Optional: physical stress inducer (bear crawl, air restriction per SOP)
drills.setup: Members isolated from each other. Instructor reads a scenario card (through the floor, entangled, lost, low air, trapped by collapse).
steps: Review mayday triggers: lost/disoriented, trapped, through a floor/roof, entangled and not immediately free, low air without a known exit, any firefighter down.
Cold reps: member hears the scenario, keys the radio, declares 'Mayday, mayday, mayday' plus LUNAR.
Add physical stress: 30 seconds of hard work immediately before the transmission.
Add radio traffic: instructor runs distracting traffic the member must break through.
Officer variant: receive a mayday, acknowledge, clear the channel, and initiate the response sequence.
Score every rep: trigger recognition delay, LUNAR completeness, transmission clarity.
learning_points: Firefighters die having never declared — the cultural barrier to calling the mayday is the first thing this drill attacks.
Declare early; you can always cancel a mayday. You cannot rewind a delayed one.
LUNAR under stress collapses without reps; Location is the element that saves you and the one most often omitted.
Activating the radio emergency button (if equipped) is part of the sequence.
common_mistakes: Firefighter delays the mayday hoping to self-rescue, calling only after air and options are gone.
The LUNAR report omits location, so command cannot start a targeted search.
The mayday is stepped on by routine radio traffic because emergency traffic was never cleared.
safety_notes: Use a training channel — never the operations channel.
success_criteria: Mayday declared within 10 seconds of trigger recognition
All LUNAR elements present
Understandable under stress

variations.name: While-Working Mayday
variations.description: Member is mid-task in a prop (entanglement, collapse sim) and must declare while managing the emergency.
variations.adds: Integration with survival skills; talk and work simultaneously.

lodd_connection.incident: NIOSH firefighter fatality reports repeatedly cite delayed or absent mayday declarations as a contributing factor
lodd_connection.lesson: The mayday is a survival tool with an expiration timer. Train the declaration until hesitation is gone.

references: IAFF Fire Ground Survival program
Department mayday SOPs

drills.title: Downed Firefighter Assessment & Air Conversion
drills.solo_note: Written for a RIT of 3-4; rotate all members through the air-connection role
drills.objective: Locate a downed firefighter, assess, convert or supplement their air supply with the RIT pack, package, and prepare for removal.
drills.setup: Manikin positioned face down in a room off a hallway. RIT of 3-4 with pack and tools.
steps: Approach and assess: identify the firefighter, check responsiveness, call the find to command.
Air first: check their gauge; connect the RIT pack per the department connection (universal air connection or facepiece swap per SOP).
Confirm air flow before anything else — a moved firefighter without air is a recovered firefighter.

Convert the SCBA harness to a drag rescue device if your packs are so equipped, or apply the webbing package — confirm which before the drill. A crew reaching for a DRD their harness does not have loses the exact seconds this drill is about.
Orient the firefighter for removal (head toward the exit) and initiate the drag.
Rotate all members through the air-connection role; it is the perishable skill.
learning_points: Air trumps everything in the sequence — the downed firefighter's clock is their cylinder.
The RIT pack connection must be practiced gloved and blind; fumbling it burns the victim's remaining minutes.
The find is transmitted immediately — command's clock and resource decisions depend on it.
Packaging done right makes the drag possible; done wrong, the rescuers exhaust themselves in the first 20 ft.
common_mistakes: RIT packages and drags before establishing air, moving a firefighter who is still running out of air.
Crew fumbles the RIT-pack connection because it was only ever practiced bare-handed in daylight.
The find is not transmitted immediately, so command's clock and resource push never start.
safety_notes: Manikin weight appropriate to crew capability with progression.
Real SCBA on the manikin so connections are authentic.
success_criteria: Air connection under 90 seconds from contact
Find transmitted
Package complete and drag initiated

variations.name: Facepiece Emergency
variations.description: Scenario: downed firefighter's facepiece is compromised; execute the SOP alternative.
variations.adds: The harder air problem beyond a simple supply swap.

variations.name: Two-Firefighter Find
variations.description: Two downed firefighters; RIT must triage and call for a second team.
variations.adds: Resource reality — one RIT rarely removes even one firefighter alone.

references: NFPA 1407
Department RIT SOPs
drills.prerequisites: Confirm before the drill whether your SCBA harnesses have an integrated drag rescue device or whether your crews rely on a webbing package, and whether your RIT air method is a UAC transfill or a facepiece swap. A crew drilled to reach for a DRD their harness does not have has rehearsed a motion that fails on the fireground.

drills.title: Denver Drill
drills.solo_note: The Denver lift is two interior rescuers plus an exterior ladder rescuer
drills.objective: Lift an unresponsive firefighter out of a high window from a confined 28 in wide space where standard lifts are impossible, using the two-rescuer Denver technique.
equipment: Denver prop (canonically a 28 in wide corridor with a 20 in window at a ~42 in sill — measure yours and brief any difference)
Rescue manikin in full PPE/SCBA (165+ lb — confirm yours; a light dummy lets crews cheat the platform mechanic)
Ground ladder at the window exterior
drills.setup: Prop per published Denver drill dimensions. Two interior rescuers, one exterior ladder rescuer.
steps: Brief the origin: this replicates the exact space where Denver Engineer Mark Langvardt was trapped in 1992, and why conventional lifts failed.
Rescuer 1 positions at the victim's head against the wall below the window and creates a seat/prop position.
Rescuer 2 straddles the victim and lifts the torso onto Rescuer 1's knee platform.
Sequential lift: Rescuer 1 becomes a human ramp/platform; Rescuer 2 drives the victim upward toward the sill.
Exterior rescuer receives the victim onto the ladder.
Rotate positions; run until the lift completes in under target time (commonly 2 minutes from contact).
learning_points: Confined-space lifts are technique-dependent — strength alone fails in 28 inches of width.
Position 1's platform role is counterintuitive and must be drilled; it is the mechanical key to the lift.
This drill exists because rescuers on scene in 1992 had no rehearsed answer; the fire service built one afterward.
Real proficiency means completing it exhausted — run it after a work circuit for realism.
common_mistakes: Rescuers try to lift the downed firefighter straight up in a space too tight for a vertical lift.
The team works without assigned roles, piling into the confined space and stalling.
Rescuers exhaust themselves on brute force instead of using leverage and a step or platform.
safety_notes: Spotters during early reps.
Back mechanics brief; this is a high-injury-potential lift done wrong.
success_criteria: Victim through the window under target time
Correct position mechanics
No unsafe lifting observed

variations.name: Reduced Crew
variations.description: Attempt with a single interior rescuer to demonstrate why two are required, then reinforce the call-for-help lesson.
variations.adds: Resource-request discipline in RIT work.

lodd_connection.incident: Mark Langvardt, Denver Fire Department (1992) — trapped in a confined storage room; rescuers could not complete the lift in time
lodd_connection.lesson: The fire service turned this loss into a rehearsed national technique. Drilling it honors him with competence.

references: Denver Fire Department drill documentation
NFPA 1407
drills.prerequisites: Confirm this evolution is authorized for your members at their certification level and that a qualified instructor is present. This is a high-spinal-load lift with real injury potential done wrong — it is not a self-directed company drill. Confirm your prop's actual dimensions against the published Denver figures before the first rep; the technique is dimension-dependent.

drills.title: Nance Drill: Firefighter Through the Floor
drills.solo_note: Needs a victim below plus a team hauling on hose or a 2:1 advantage
drills.objective: Rescue a firefighter who has fallen through a floor into the level below, using handline, hose rescue loop, and ladder-assisted techniques.
equipment: Hole prop (floor opening to lower level) or drill tower configuration
Rescue manikin or live 'victim' (uninjured scenarios only)
drills.setup: Simulated floor hole with a 'below-grade' space. Victim firefighter at the bottom, responsive for early rounds.
steps: Approach the hole safely: sound, distribute weight, work from the sides.
Method 1 — hose loop: lower a bight of hose; victim mounts the loop; team hauls using the hose as a rescue strap.
Method 2 — ladder slide: lower a ground ladder into the hole; victim climbs or is assisted up it.
Method 3 — unresponsive victim: rescuer descends (ladder), packages with webbing, team hauls with a 2:1 improvised advantage.
Run each method, then scenario rounds where the team must choose based on victim status.
Debrief the decision logic: responsive victim = tools down to them; unresponsive = rescuer must go down.
learning_points: A firefighter through the floor is the mayday with the shortest survival window — fire below, victim in it.
The hoseline is the most available rescue tool on any fireground; every crew has one within reach.
The edge of the hole is failing floor — rescuer discipline at the lip prevents a second victim.
Method choice is driven by victim capability, not rescuer preference.
common_mistakes: Crew tries to haul the firefighter straight back up the hole instead of converting to a lower or alternate egress.
No air is established for the fallen firefighter before rescue work begins.
Rescuers approach the hole without protecting themselves from falling through the same weak floor.
safety_notes: Fall protection or limited depth for live-victim rounds.
Structural props inspected before every session.
success_criteria: Victim out via all three methods
Correct method chosen in scenario rounds
No edge-safety violations

variations.name: Zero Visibility
variations.description: Locate the hole and victim by sound and feel.
variations.adds: The realistic condition under which floors fail.

lodd_connection.incident: John Nance, Columbus Division of Fire (1987) — fell through a floor into a basement; rescue attempts with available techniques failed
lodd_connection.lesson: Through-the-floor rescue techniques exist because improvisation failed that night. The methods must be pre-loaded.

references: Columbus Fire training documentation
NFPA 1407
drills.prerequisites: Confirm your members are authorized to rig an improvised mechanical advantage at their certification level before running Method 3 — many departments restrict any mechanical advantage to rope-operations or technical-rescue-certified members. Live-victim rounds require fall protection and rated anchor points at the prop; if you do not have both, run limited depth or manikin only.

drills.title: Full RIT Activation Evolution
drills.solo_note: Multi-company: RIT, attack crew, command, safety officer, and a mayday trigger
drills.objective: Execute a complete RIT activation: staged readiness, mayday received, deployment, search for the downed firefighter, air, package, and removal — while command maintains the original incident.
equipment: Full RIT cache per your department SOP (typically pack, irons, search rope, TIC, saw) — inventory yours before the drill
Multiple radios and a command element
drills.setup: One company as RIT (staged with tools, performing proactive recon). Interior 'fire attack' underway as background. Instructor triggers the mayday.
steps: RIT stages correctly: tools assembled, 360 recon done, ladders thrown proactively, listening to fireground traffic.
Mayday transmitted by the 'down' firefighter (LUNAR); command acknowledges and deploys RIT.
RIT enters on the best intelligence, searches, and locates the firefighter.
Air connection, find report, packaging, removal — additional companies requested and integrated as needed.
Command simultaneously maintains fire attack and initiates the mayday command sequence (channel management, PAR, additional alarm).
Full debrief with timeline reconstruction from radio logs.
learning_points: RIT is a proactive assignment — the recon and ladder work done while staged is what makes the deployment fast.
One RIT team locating a firefighter typically exhausts itself before removal; the second and third teams are the plan, not the backup.
Command's hardest task is running two incidents at once: the fire and the rescue.
Timeline reconstruction shows the crew how long a 'fast' rescue actually takes — usually far longer than anyone estimates.
common_mistakes: RIT stages without tools staged and ready, then scrambles for equipment when activated.
Command assigns RIT on arrival but never briefs them on layout, crews, and hazards.
RIT is deployed piecemeal one member at a time instead of as an organized team with a plan.
safety_notes: Dedicated safety officer for the evolution.
Clear separation between drill traffic and any real emergency traffic.
success_criteria: Deployment within 60 seconds of activation order
Air established at the victim
Removal completed
Command maintained both operations

variations.name: Unknown Location
variations.description: Down firefighter cannot give location; RIT searches from last known assignment.
variations.adds: The realistic hard version — search discipline plus radio direction-finding (feedback-assisted if equipped).

references: NFPA 1407
Department RIT SOPs

drills.title: Mayday Trigger Recognition: 5-Second Decision Deck
drills.objective: Sort a 30-card deck of fireground conditions into MAYDAY NOW / URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY / NORMAL with a spoken decision inside 5 seconds per card, scoring 27 of 30 correct against the answer key on two consecutive runs.
equipment: 30 index cards and a marker (a notes app with one condition per screen works if you have no cards)
Phone timer with an audible 5-second countdown or interval beep
Full PPE and SCBA, air off — donned for the second half of the drill
Three floor markings, buckets, or taped sheets to serve as sort piles
drills.setup: Write one fireground condition per card — the conditions you can find yourself in, not the ones you would see from outside. Lay three sort piles on the apparatus bay floor labeled MAYDAY NOW, URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY, NORMAL, and put a written answer key face-down beside the deck so you cannot score yourself generously after the fact. No radio traffic is transmitted in this drill; the voice recorder captures your spoken calls instead.
steps: Build the deck before you start: at minimum include entangled and not free within one attempt, fallen through a floor, trapped under collapse, separated from your crew with no contact, lost and cannot find the hoseline, low-air alarm sounding and exit path not known, SCBA failure, zero visibility with an unknown egress, caught in a flow path with rising heat, an unexpected floor sag, a partner who stops responding, plus routine conditions such as a normal gauge check, a planned tool hand-off, and a routine crew move-up.
Shuffle the deck face-down and start the interval timer at 5 seconds.
Turn one card, say your call out loud — 'MAYDAY NOW', 'URGENT', or 'NORMAL' — and place it in that pile before the beep. A card you did not call before the beep counts as a miss.
Work the full deck without stopping to think about scoring, then turn the answer key and count your hits, misses, and the direction of every miss.
Run the deck a second time in full PPE with SCBA donned, hood up, facepiece on and air off, gloved hands turning cards — the same 5-second interval.

Play back the recording and mark every card where you hesitated, hedged ('probably a mayday'), or downgraded a MAYDAY NOW card to URGENT. Rebuild those cards into a short 10-card deck and run it twice more.
Write on the back of each card you missed the one sentence that names why the condition is a mayday, and re-shuffle it into the full deck for the next session.
learning_points: Firefighters rarely die because they could not describe a mayday — they die because they spent two or three minutes trying to solve the problem privately first. Those minutes are the RIT's entire head start, and they are spent before anyone outside knows a firefighter is in trouble.

The decision has to be pre-made. Under stress you do not reason your way to a novel conclusion; you retrieve the nearest rehearsed answer. Sorting 30 conditions on the bay floor is how the answer gets stored where you can retrieve it at 800 degrees with a low-air alarm going.
Hedging is the failure mode this drill hunts. 'I think I might need help' is not a mayday and does not start a RIT deployment — it invites a clarifying question you may not have the air to answer.
The URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY pile matters as much as the mayday pile. If everything is a mayday, nothing is, and the firefighter who cannot tell the difference eventually stops calling either one.
Downgrading your own emergency is the predictable direction of error. Almost nobody over-calls in training; nearly everyone under-calls. Knowing your own bias by name is what lets you override it.
common_mistakes: Building a deck of only obvious conditions — collapse, fall, entrapment — so every card is an easy MAYDAY NOW and the drill never trains the ambiguous middle where real hesitation lives.
Reading the card, deciding, and then narrating the reasoning, which blows the 5-second window and rehearses exactly the deliberation the drill exists to eliminate.
Calling 'URGENT' as a comfortable hedge on cards that belong in MAYDAY NOW, then scoring it as close enough.
Scoring from memory instead of a written key, which quietly converts a 22 of 30 into a 27 of 30.
Running the deck only in station uniform, so the drill is never rehearsed with gloved hands, a facepiece, and restricted vision — the exact conditions that slow the real decision.
safety_notes: SCBA air stays off for the entire drill and the facepiece comes off the moment you feel any breathing restriction — this is a decision-making evolution, not an air-consumption evolution.
Working in full PPE in a warm bay is a heat-stress load: keep water at the sort piles, run the PPE half in short blocks, and stop if you stop sweating or get a headache.

Do not transmit any part of this drill on a working radio channel. Use the voice recorder, or a radio that is powered off, so no simulated mayday language can reach a dispatcher or a working incident.
success_criteria: 27 of 30 cards sorted correctly against the written answer key on two consecutive full runs.
Every card called out loud before the 5-second beep, with no cards left uncalled.
Zero MAYDAY NOW cards placed in the URGENT or NORMAL piles on the final run.
Recording playback contains no hedging language — every call is one of the three terms, spoken once, with no qualifiers.

variations.name: Physical Stress Load
variations.description: Do 60 seconds of stair climbs, sledge strikes on a tire, or bay laps in full PPE immediately before each 10-card block, and keep the 5-second interval.
variations.adds: Trains the decision while breathing hard and thinking slowly, which is when the real one gets made — and exposes whether your sort accuracy is stress-durable or only rested-accurate.

variations.name: Second-Person Cards
variations.description: Add 10 cards written about a crew member rather than yourself: partner unresponsive, partner missing at a doorway, partner's alarm sounding and no answer.
variations.adds: Trains calling the mayday for someone else, which firefighters delay even longer than their own because it feels like escalating another person's problem.

variations.name: Blind Draw
variations.description: Have the deck read to you aloud from a recording you made earlier, so you never see the card and must sort by ear with your eyes closed.
variations.adds: Removes the visual scan and forces the decision off auditory information only — closer to how you actually receive a partner's cue or your own alarm in zero visibility.

variations.name: Cold Open
variations.description: Leave the deck staged and run it once, unannounced, at some point in a normal shift day rather than as a scheduled block.
variations.adds: Tests retrieval without warm-up, which is the only condition that matters — no real mayday follows a briefing.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH firefighter fatality investigation reports document delayed mayday transmission, where a firefighter recognized trouble but attempted to self-rescue before calling for help
lodd_connection.lesson: The interval between recognizing trouble and transmitting is the interval in which the outcome is decided. Training the recognition-to-declaration reflex separately from the radio format is what shortens it.

references: IFSTA Essentials of Fire Fighting — firefighter survival and mayday procedures chapter
NIOSH Fire Fighter Fatality Investigation and Prevention Program reports (pattern-level, publicly available)
Department mayday declaration SOP/SOG (operator supplies the local answer key)
drills.solo_note: Fully solo as written: you build the deck, run your own timer, call out loud, and score against a written key you made in advance. Nobody else is needed in any role.

drills.title: Emergency Button & PASS: Gloved, Blind, Under 4 Seconds
drills.objective: From four different body positions with eyes closed and structural gloves on, locate and activate the radio emergency button and manually activate the SCBA PASS device in under 4 seconds each, 8 of 10 repetitions per position.
equipment: Your own assigned portable radio with its emergency button, and your own assigned SCBA — the drill is worthless on a spare you will never wear
Full PPE including structural gloves and hood
Phone timer or stopwatch with a start/stop you can hit with a gloved thumb
Phone voice recorder to capture the audible PASS activation and your own timing calls
Index cards to log reps per position
A cleared apparatus bay floor or driveway with room to lie prone, supine, and on both sides
drills.setup: Cleared bay floor, all four positions marked with tape: standing, prone, supine, and lying on your radio-side hip. Confirm before you begin whether your radio's emergency button transmits to dispatch on the channel it is set to — if it does, change to a training or unused channel, or remove the battery and rehearse the motor pattern against the powered-off unit, and coordinate with your communications center before any transmission is possible. Radio model, button location, and PASS activation method are department- and manufacturer-specific examples here: substitute your own issued equipment and your department's emergency-button policy before running this drill.
steps: Don full PPE and SCBA, air off, hood up, structural gloves on. Confirm the radio channel or battery status is safe per the setup before a single rep.
Standing, eyes closed: start the timer, locate the emergency button by feel alone, activate it, and stop the timer. Log the time on a card. Ten reps.
Repeat the ten reps prone, then supine, then lying on the hip your radio rides on — the position that buries the button under your own body weight.
Switch to the SCBA PASS device: from each of the same four positions, eyes closed and gloved, find the manual activation and trigger it, logging the time. Ten reps per position.

Run five combined reps per position: activate the emergency button, then manually activate PASS, then hold still and count ten seconds out loud so you rehearse staying put and making noise instead of moving on.
Review your logged cards and identify the slowest position and the reps where you fumbled the glove-on grip. Run that one position ten more times.
Finish with five reps from the hip-down position after 45 seconds of hard physical work, and compare those times against your fresh times on the same card.
learning_points: The emergency button is the one alert that reaches command without needing your voice, your air, or a clear channel. A firefighter pinned, entangled, or too winded to transmit still has a thumb — but only if the location is stored in muscle memory rather than in a mental picture of the radio.

The environment takes your vision first and your dexterity with it. Any reach you can only make with clear sight and bare hands is a reach you do not have — structural gloves turn a button you find instantly into one that disappears.

PASS is what turns your radio transmission into a location. Command now knows there is a mayday; the manual activation is what lets the RIT walk to you in zero visibility instead of searching for you.

Lying on the radio side is the hardest and the most likely — firefighters go down where they fall, not into a convenient position. If you only rehearse standing, you rehearsed the one position you will probably not be in.
The ten-second hold at the end is the discipline half of the drill: after alerting, staying put and audible beats crawling somewhere new and leaving the RIT searching an area you already left.
common_mistakes: Rehearsing with the radio in your hand instead of in its normal carry position, so the drill never trains reaching to where the radio actually rides on your gear.

Cheating the constraint — eyes-closed drifting to eyes-squinting after a few reps, or peeling the glove off just for one when the grip gets fussy. Both improve your times by training a hand and an eye you will not have.
Drilling on a spare or bay radio with a different button geometry than your assigned unit.
Activating the button and then immediately crawling — moving after alerting undoes the location the PASS just established.
Skipping the confirmation of whether the button transmits live, and dropping a real emergency alert into a working dispatch channel.
safety_notes: Confirm before the first rep whether the emergency button will transmit to dispatch on the current channel. Move to a training or unused channel, or pull the battery and rehearse the motor pattern only, and notify your communications center before any live activation is possible.
SCBA air stays off for this drill; the facepiece is worn for grip and vision realism only and comes off immediately if breathing feels restricted.
