Full PPE in a closed bay is a heat-stress load, and repeated drops to prone and supine on concrete bruise knees, elbows and hips. Break between position blocks, hydrate, and stop on any dizziness rather than pushing for one more rep.
success_criteria: 8 of 10 emergency-button activations under 4 seconds in each of the four positions, timed and logged.
8 of 10 manual PASS activations under 4 seconds in each of the four positions, with the audible alarm captured on the recording.
Zero repetitions completed with a glove removed or with eyes open, verified against the recording narration.
Combined reps show the ten-second hold after activation with no movement from the activation position.

variations.name: Entangled Arm
variations.description: Loosely tuck your dominant hand into your coat or hold it against your chest, and run ten reps per position using the off hand only. No entanglement prop, no wraps, no restraints — the hand simply stays out of the drill.
variations.adds: Trains the alert with one arm pinned or occupied, which is the realistic condition when a firefighter is caught, and exposes whether the whole skill lives in one hand.

variations.name: Post-Exertion Reps
variations.description: Precede each block with 60 seconds of stair climbs or sledge strikes in full PPE so every rep is performed winded.
variations.adds: Shows how much fine motor control the button demands and how much of it exertion removes — a 3-second skill rested is often a 7-second skill breathing hard.

variations.name: Position Roulette
variations.description: Record yourself calling the four positions in random order with random gaps, play it back, and assume and execute from whichever position is called.
variations.adds: Removes the block-practice advantage of knowing what's next and forces the retrieval to be position-independent.

variations.name: Sound-Off Verification
variations.description: Run the PASS reps at the far end of the bay with the door open, and check the recording for whether the alarm is actually audible over the ambient noise from 50 ft.
variations.adds: Trains the follow-through — that PASS is only useful if it can be heard, which drives the decision to also make noise by striking a tool on the floor.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH firefighter fatality investigation reports document downed firefighters whose PASS device was not activated, or was activated late, delaying location by rescuers
lodd_connection.lesson: Alerting hardware only works if activation is automatic under stress and in the position the firefighter actually ends up in. Manual activation rehearsed by feel is what closes the gap between the alarm existing and the alarm sounding.

SCBA and portable radio manufacturer operating instructions for the operator's own issued equipment
NIOSH Fire Fighter Fatality Investigation and Prevention Program reports (pattern-level, publicly available)
Department portable radio emergency-button and mayday SOP/SOG
drills.solo_note: Fully solo: your own gear, your own timer, your own rep log. Air stays off and nothing is entangled, so no safety person is required — but clear the channel question with dispatch first.

drills.title: Air Decision Points: Turnaround Math on Your Own Gauge
drills.objective: Given 12 timed scenario cards stating a gauge reading, an estimated exit distance, and a complication, call CONTINUE / TURN AROUND NOW / MAYDAY within 10 seconds each and state the reason in one sentence, scoring 11 of 12 against a key built from your own department's air-management policy.
equipment: 12 index cards with a marker (notes app works)
Your assigned SCBA, air off, worn for the gauge-check reps
Full PPE including gloves and hood
Phone timer and phone voice recorder
A written copy of your department's air-management policy — the drill cannot be scored without it
A cleared apparatus bay or driveway with a measurable out-and-back path
drills.setup: Write your department's air-management decision points at the top of the answer key before you write a single card — the point at which your policy says to exit, what your low-air alarm activation means locally, and when an air problem becomes a mayday rather than a withdrawal. Any pressures, percentages, or cylinder ratings used in the cards are examples only: substitute your department's air-management policy and your own cylinder rating before running this drill. Mark an out-and-back path in the bay in known lengths so the distance figures on the cards mean something you have actually walked.
steps: Write the answer key first, straight from your department's air-management policy, and write one plain sentence next to each decision point explaining what it is protecting against.

Build 12 cards, each with three elements: a gauge reading, an estimated distance and difficulty to the exit, and a complication such as a partner slowing down, a stairwell you came up but have not descended, a hose you have lost contact with, or a low-air alarm that just activated.
Don full PPE and SCBA, air off. Draw a card, start the 10-second timer, and call CONTINUE, TURN AROUND NOW, or MAYDAY out loud into the recorder, followed by one sentence of reason.

Work all 12 cards without stopping, then score against the key and mark the direction of every miss — pushing deeper when you should have turned, or calling mayday for something that was a withdrawal.
Walk the marked out-and-back path in full PPE at a working pace and time it, so you have a real number for how long your own exit actually takes rather than an optimistic guess.
Re-run the six cards you found hardest, this time stating the decision plus the exit time your walk just produced, and check whether any CONTINUE calls survive contact with your real number.
Log your final scores and the walked exit time on a card kept with your gear, and re-run the deck at the start of each set of shifts.
learning_points: Air is a countdown that starts when you mask up, not when the low-air alarm sounds. The alarm is not a warning that you should think about leaving — by most department policies it means you are already late, and the drill is about the decisions made well before it.

The exit takes longer than the entry, always. You came in on fresh legs with visibility and no fatigue, and you leave tired, disoriented, and possibly dragging equipment or a person. A firefighter who budgets the return at entry speed budgets it wrong.

The most common air failure is not an unread gauge — it is a gauge read correctly and then argued with. Declaring feels like admitting a mistake, which is exactly why it gets delayed past the point where it was still cheap.

There is a hard line between an air problem that is a withdrawal and one that is a mayday. Low air with a known short exit is a withdrawal; low air with an unknown exit, a failed SCBA, or an entanglement is a mayday, and calling it early is the only thing that buys the RIT time.
Knowing how long your own exit path takes in gear, as a measured number rather than a feeling, is what makes the turnaround call arithmetic instead of optimism.
common_mistakes: Building the answer key from memory or something read online rather than the department's actual air-management policy, and guessing the exit walk time instead of walking and timing it — both leave the arithmetic resting on a number you invented.
Calling CONTINUE on cards where the exit distance is genuinely unknown — an unknown exit is not a distance you can budget against.
Treating low-air alarm activation as the moment the decision starts rather than the moment it should already be finished.
Reserving MAYDAY for total air failure and calling everything short of that a withdrawal, including situations with no known way out.
Explaining the reasoning for 30 seconds and counting it as a pass because the answer was right — the 10-second window is part of the skill.
safety_notes: SCBA air stays off for the entire drill. This is a decision-making and gauge-reading evolution, not a consumption test — do not breathe down a cylinder to make it feel real, and take the facepiece off at any sense of breathing restriction.
The timed exit walk is done at a working pace in full PPE and is a real cardiovascular load: walk it, do not race it, and stop if you feel chest pressure, dizziness, or heat illness.
Full PPE in a closed apparatus bay builds heat fast — keep water at the card table, break between blocks, and end the drill rather than push through heat symptoms.
success_criteria: 11 of 12 cards scored correct against the answer key built from department air-management policy.
Every call made inside the 10-second window, verified on the recording.
Every call followed by a one-sentence reason naming the specific factor that drove it — gauge, distance, or complication.
A measured exit-path time in full PPE written on the log card, not estimated.

variations.name: Partner in the Card
variations.description: Rewrite six cards so the air problem belongs to a partner rather than to you — their gauge, their alarm, their slowing pace.
variations.adds: Trains the call on someone else's behalf, which firefighters delay longer than their own, and forces the crew-exit decision rather than the individual one.

variations.name: Post-Exertion Deck
variations.description: Run the deck immediately after 90 seconds of stair climbs or sledge work in full PPE, keeping the 10-second window.
variations.adds: Exposes how much worse the arithmetic gets when winded, which is the only state in which the real decision is ever made.

variations.name: Loaded Exit Walk
variations.description: Repeat the timed exit walk carrying a tool in each hand and dragging a weighted hose bundle or dummy the length of the path.
variations.adds: Produces a second, slower exit number for the rescue case, and shows how far off the unloaded figure was as a turnaround basis.

variations.name: Gauge by Feel
variations.description: For six reps, read your gauge with the facepiece on and hood down over the edges, in the dimmest light your bay allows, before calling the card.
variations.adds: Trains actually retrieving and reading the gauge under degraded vision, which is the step most often skipped between knowing the policy and using it.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH firefighter fatality investigation reports document firefighters who ran out of air while attempting to exit, having continued operations past the point where the remaining supply covered the return trip
lodd_connection.lesson: Air management fails at the decision point, not at the gauge. Rehearsing the turnaround call against a measured exit time is what makes the decision arithmetic rather than optimism.

Department air-management SOP/SOG and SCBA cylinder specifications (operator supplies both)
drills.solo_note: Fully solo: you build the deck from your own policy, run your own timer, walk and time your own exit path, and score against a written key. Air stays off, so no safety person is needed.

drills.title: SCBA Donning & Emergency Procedures
drills.solo_note: An instructor calls random failures; timed dons need someone on the clock

solo_variant.substitutions: Phone on a tripod facing the seat or the don spot with a visible stopwatch in frame — that is your timer and your evaluator both. Index-card deck for the emergency round: one failure per card, free-flow, no air at the regulator, facepiece damage, PASS activation, low-air alarm. Shuffle, draw face-down, flip and react.
steps: Full inspection of the SCBA before the first rep — cylinder pressure, seals, straps, regulator, PASS. Log any deficiency and stop if you find one.
Set the tripod so the phone sees your hands and the stopwatch together.
Timed seat don: coat, pack, mask, gloves, on air. Start the clock yourself, breathe, stop it. Record the time.
Timed ground don per SOP — over-the-head or coat method. Record.
Emergency round: draw a card face-down, flip it, and execute the correct response immediately. Talk through what you are doing so the recording captures it.
Work the bypass and purge deliberately, gloved. If your SCBA has a mask-mounted regulator, practice the swap.
Low-air round: run the cylinder to alarm at rest, then verbalize the immediate actions — notify, exit, stay with crew. Sitting still, no work, no exertion.
Do the whole session gloved. If you want the blackout variant, close your eyes for the don only, seated on the floor, off air, nothing to snag on.
solo_variant.self_score: Both dons under 60 seconds on the stopwatch, gloves on, no bare-hand cheats — the video will show them. On the emergency cards, count first-attempt correct responses against total cards drawn; anything under 100 percent means more reps. Review the footage for a strap you skipped or a seal check you did not do.
solo_variant.not_covered: No instructor calling a failure you did not write on a card, which is the whole point of the crew round — you cannot surprise yourself. No blacked-out entanglement or confidence-course work on air: that drill exists with an instructor because the instructor is the safety line, and alone you do not have one. No crew emergency procedures, no buddy-breathing, no RIC interface.

drills.objective: Don SCBA from the seat and from the ground in under 60 seconds, and execute emergency procedures for regulator and low-air events per manufacturer and SOP.
drills.setup: Individual stations; can run as a daily 10-minute standard.
steps: Timed seat don: coat, pack, mask, gloves, on air — record time.
Ground don (over-the-head or coat method per SOP), timed.
Emergency procedures round: instructor calls a failure (free-flow, no air at regulator, facepiece damage) and member executes the correct response.
Practice bypass/purge use and mask-mounted regulator swap if applicable.
Low-air recognition: identify alarm activation and verbalize the immediate actions (notify, exit with crew).
learning_points: Donning speed is earned in reps, not on the fireground.
Emergency procedures must be reflexive — a firefighter troubleshooting from memory at zero visibility is already behind.
The low-air alarm is an emergency, not a reminder — it means the exit should already be underway.
Gloves-on dexterity with every strap and buckle is the actual standard.
common_mistakes: Firefighter removes gloves to work buckles and straps, a habit that fails in a real IDLH.
The low-air alarm is treated as a reminder to start heading out rather than a late signal to already be leaving.
Donning is done step-by-step from memory instead of as a reflexive sequence, costing time under stress.
safety_notes: Inspect SCBA before drills; log any deficiencies.
success_criteria: Don under 60 seconds
Correct emergency procedure on first attempt
All manipulations completed gloved

variations.name: Blackout Don
variations.description: Don and troubleshoot with eyes closed or obscured facepiece.
variations.adds: Simulates donning in smoke after an emergency doff.

references: Manufacturer procedures
NFPA 1852

drills.title: Reduced Profile & Wall Breach
drills.solo_note: Safety requires instructor physical contact during blacked-out on-air prop rounds
drills.objective: Pass through restricted openings using low-profile and reduced-profile (pack shift) techniques, and breach a standard stud wall to escape entrapment.
equipment: Stud wall prop (16 in on center is the residential standard — build to the spacing that matches your district)
drills.setup: Prop sequence: stud bay, low crawl under obstruction, restricted window opening — measure and record your props' actual clear dimensions before the first rep. Obscured facepieces for scored rounds.
steps: Demonstrate the low-profile swim through a stud bay with the pack on.
Demonstrate reduced profile: loosen straps per SOP, shift the pack, pass through, re-don on the far side.
Wall breach: sound the wall, break gypsum with a tool, clear the bay, check for wires/pipes, pass through.
Run the full sequence blacked out, on air, timed.
Debrief air consumption for the sequence — this is also an air management data point.
learning_points: Full removal of the SCBA is a last resort; profile-reduction techniques keep air supply connected.
Wall breach turns a trapped firefighter into one room closer to egress — every interior wall is a potential door.
Check the bay before committing; electrical and plumbing runs are entanglement and injury hazards.
Air burned in these maneuvers is significant — the drill quantifies it for each member.
common_mistakes: Firefighter fully removes the SCBA when a profile shift would have kept the mask on air.
Crew enters the stud bay without sounding for wires and pipes, snagging or getting shocked.
Firefighter breaches at a stud instead of the bay center, wasting energy and air on the hard spot.
safety_notes: Instructor maintains physical contact capability in blacked-out rounds.
Establish a clear stop signal.
success_criteria: All openings passed without full SCBA removal (unless drill specifies)
Breach completed with bay check
Re-donned pack secure on far side

variations.name: Charged Line Follow
variations.description: Complete the sequence while maintaining hose contact.
variations.adds: Escaping along the line you came in on.

references: Firefighter survival curricula
IAFF Fire Ground Survival program

drills.title: Entanglement Prop / Wire Maze
drills.solo_note: Instructor must observe from outside with quick-release access along the prop
drills.objective: Recognize, prevent, and self-extricate from wire and cable entanglement while maintaining composure and air discipline.
drills.setup: Crawl-through prop with hanging wires and low obstructions. Instructor observes from outside the prop.
steps: Teach prevention first: stay low, keep profile tight, sweep ahead, back out the way you came in when snagged.
First pass with vision: feel how wires catch the cylinder valve and shoulder straps.
Blacked-out pass: on snag, stop, back up, identify the catch point by hand, clear or cut it.
Practice the swim technique and controlled reversal.
Scored pass: time, air used, and composure (breathing rate audible on regulator) all logged.
learning_points: The instinct to pull harder against a snag makes entanglement worse — stop and reverse is the skill.
Personal wire cutters are carried where a gloved hand can reach them, or they don't exist.
Composure is measurable: listen to your own regulator. Panic breathing halves your air.
Drop ceilings put the entanglement hazard at crawl height in every commercial building.
common_mistakes: Firefighter pulls harder against a snag instead of stopping, backing out, and working the wire off.
Wire cutters are buried in a pocket the firefighter cannot reach while entangled.
Breathing rate spikes with panic, burning air far faster than the entanglement itself costs time.
safety_notes: Prop must have quick-release/instructor access along its full length.
Claustrophobia events: stop, lights on, talk the member through.
success_criteria: Self-extrication without instructor assist
Controlled breathing throughout
Cutters accessed gloved

variations.name: Partner Assist
variations.description: Second firefighter clears a hopelessly snagged partner.
variations.adds: How to clear someone else's cylinder by feel — the RIT-adjacent version.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple LODDs, including residential and commercial incidents, document firefighters found entangled in wire from collapsed drop ceilings
lodd_connection.lesson: Entanglement plus low air is fatal math. Prevention posture and immediate, calm reversal are trained reflexes.

references: IAFF Fire Ground Survival program
drills.prerequisites: This drill assumes members are issued personal wire cutters and scores them on reaching them with a gloved hand. Confirm your members are issued or authorized to carry cutters before running it — if they are not, this drill surfaces a gear gap before it surfaces a skill gap, and that finding is worth more than the reps.

drills.title: Air Management Under Work
drills.solo_note: An officer calls air reports at intervals; medical monitoring for high-exertion work
drills.objective: Establish each member's personal air consumption baseline under work, and enforce point-of-no-return decision making using the rule of air management.
equipment: Work circuit (hose drag, stair climb, forcible entry sim, crawl)
drills.setup: Standardized work circuit. Each member starts with a full cylinder.
steps: Brief ROAM: know your air, manage it, exit BEFORE the low-air alarm — the alarm is your emergency reserve, not your work air.
Member works the circuit at fireground pace; officer calls for air reports at intervals.
Member must announce their own trigger points (e.g., half cylinder = evaluate, two-thirds used = exit).
Continue until the member's self-declared exit point; record total work time on the cylinder.
Compare members' consumption rates; discuss what changes them (fitness, composure, work type).
Repeat monthly and track trends per member.
learning_points: Air consumption varies 2-3x between members — crews must plan around their fastest breather.
The gauge check is a habit loop: task transition = air check.
Time-to-alarm under work is often shockingly shorter than members assume from station-wear experience.
Officers who know each member's baseline can make real air-based tactical decisions.
common_mistakes: Crew plans air around the average user instead of the fastest breather, who runs out first.
Firefighters check air only when the alarm sounds, never at the point-of-no-return.
Work rate is not managed, so the crew overexerts early and has no reserve for the way out.
safety_notes: Medical monitoring for high-exertion circuits per department rehab SOP.
success_criteria: Member exits before low-air alarm
Accurate self-reported air at each check
Baseline logged

variations.name: Large Area Overlay
variations.description: Run the consumption exercise inside a large-area search scenario where the exit takes real time.
variations.adds: Point-of-no-return becomes concrete: distance-in equals air-out.

lodd_connection.incident: Worcester Cold Storage (1999) and multiple other LODDs involved firefighters exhausting air deep inside large structures
lodd_connection.lesson: Your exit costs air. The deeper you are, the earlier the decision point. Manage air on the way in, not the way out.

references: NFPA 1404
Seattle-style air management rule

drills.title: Lost & Disoriented: Coupling Read to Egress
drills.solo_note: Instructor stays within arm's reach with a stop signal and scores the coupling read

solo_variant.substitutions: Phone stopwatch for the instructor's 15-second clock. A shuffled deck of 20 coupling photos (male/female, both orientations) for the instructor's random placements. A cardboard box or towel over your hands for the blind read, so you never need a facepiece cover. Voice memo app to record your LUNAR.
steps: Set the hard limits first: no SCBA, no facepiece obscuration, no hood over your head, no maze or confined prop, no charged line. Alone means you drill the read and the decision, not the crawl in the dark.
Lay 30-50 ft of uncharged hose across a cleared, flat bay floor with at least two full coupling sets in it. Walk the floor and remove every trip and pinch hazard before you start.
Dry review: state your department's convention out loud - smooth to the street, lugs to the fire, or whatever your local doctrine actually says. Confirm it against your own SOG, not memory.

Blind read reps: put a coupling set inside a box or under a towel, gloved hands only. Start the stopwatch, find the coupling, read it by feel, call the egress direction and the reason out loud. Stop the clock. Shuffle the orientation and run 20 reps.
Photo deck: 20 images, 5 seconds each, call the direction out loud before you flip. Score them.

Line-follow with eyes open, hands only: kneel at a random point on the line, look away, find the nearest coupling, read it, then follow the line hand-over-hand to the marked exit through two engineered snags without ever breaking hand contact.

Wall-follow: eyes closed, one hand committed, on cleared open floor only. Narrate 'right hand committed' aloud, walk the perimeter to a marked door. Open floor crossings are out - if the hand leaves the wall, that rep is a failure.
Radio rep: record a LUNAR transmission on your phone after 60-90 seconds of hard work (stair climb, sledge on a tire). Play it back and score it.
Log the day: reps, time per read, misses, and which convention you defaulted to under load.
solo_variant.self_score: 20 blind coupling reps: 18+ correct on first attempt, each called inside 15 seconds on the stopwatch. Photo deck 18/20. Zero lost-line events on the follow reps. Playback of the LUNAR contains location, unit, name, assignment/resources and air status - all present, in order.
solo_variant.not_covered: Everything the dark does to you. No obscured vision, no facepiece, no air consumption, no heat, no disorientation you did not create on purpose. You always know where the exit is, so the recognition step - the honest 'I am turned around' before you push on - cannot be trained here. It drills the read, not the panic.

drills.objective: Working blacked-out, each firefighter must locate the hoseline, correctly identify the direction of egress by coupling read within 15 seconds of finding the line, verbalize 'this way out' with the reason, and self-egress under air while transmitting an accurate LUNAR-style status.
equipment: SCBA with facepieces obscured or blacked-out (wax paper, obscuration covers, or taped shields)
One hoseline (charged preferred, uncharged acceptable) with a nozzle and at least two visible coupling sets
Training maze or partitioned bay with a minimum of two rooms and a connecting doorway
Cones to mark start points and the true exit
Furniture/obstacles to create snags (chairs, pallets, hose loops)
Portable radio or radio simulator per firefighter
drills.setup: Lay one hoseline through the maze from a marked 'exit' door, through the doorway, into a back room where the nozzle rests; add couplings so at least two full sets fall along the crawl path. IMPORTANT: this drill uses the coupling convention that the SMOOTH (female) coupling faces the exit and the LUGGED (male) end faces the fire/nozzle — confirm this matches YOUR department's convention before running, and correct the whole crew to local doctrine if it differs. Stage furniture and hose loops to create realistic snags, mark the true exit with a cone, and keep an instructor inside arm's reach of each working firefighter at all times.
steps: Brief the crew dry (facepieces clear) on the coupling read: hands find a coupling, thumb reads which half faces out, crew states aloud 'smooth to the street, lugs to the fire' or the local convention — then verify by feel, not memory.

Station 1 (recognition): with facepiece obscured, have each firefighter crawl a short leg, then instructor spins/relocates them; firefighter must recognize disorientation, stop forward motion, and announce 'I'm turned around' instead of pushing on.

Station 2 (coupling read): place the disoriented firefighter's hand on the line at a random point; they must locate the nearest coupling, read it, state the egress direction and the reason, and begin moving out — instructor scores the read for accuracy.
Station 3 (follow under load): firefighter follows the line to the exit managing at least two engineered snags and the doorway transition, maintaining hand contact with the line the entire way.

Station 4 (no line): remove hand from the hose; firefighter executes a wall-follow with one consistent hand, narrating that they are committed to that hand, and reaches an exit without crossing open floor blindly.

Scenario round: combine all elements — obscured firefighter is 'separated,' must recognize it, find the line or wall, establish direction, transmit a LUNAR status, and egress; partner observes and calls what they see.
Debrief each round on the decision timing: when did the firefighter stop searching and start leaving, and was the coupling read correct on the first attempt.
learning_points: A firefighter who cannot say which way is out is already in trouble — recognizing disorientation early, before air and options are gone, is the survival skill; pushing on 'just a little more' is what fills NIOSH reports.
The coupling read turns a panic problem into a task: smooth-to-the-street (or the local convention) gives a direction in seconds when a compass, a wall, and vision have all failed.
Following the line out under load with snags mirrors reality — a firefighter who lets go of the line to fight a snag can lose the line entirely and be back to zero orientation.
A consistent single-hand wall-follow prevents the loop-back trap where switching hands at corners walks a firefighter in a circle and burns the air they needed to get out.
Transmitting an accurate LUNAR status early gets help moving toward you while you still have air; a late or vague transmission means rescuers search blind for a member who could have self-rescued.
common_mistakes: Firefighter keeps advancing after losing orientation instead of stopping and admitting it — the single most dangerous failure this drill targets.
Reading the coupling from memory of 'which way I was going' instead of reading the actual coupling by feel, producing a confident wrong answer.
Letting go of the hoseline to clear a snag and never re-establishing contact with the same section.
Switching hands during the wall-follow at a doorway or corner, reversing direction without realizing it.
Transmitting a mayday/status that omits air state or location reference, so the message sounds calm but tells rescuers nothing actionable.
safety_notes: Obscured-vision evolution: an instructor must remain within arm's reach of each working firefighter and hold a stop-signal that halts all movement instantly.
No live fire, no elevated surfaces, no confined-space entry — keep all crawl paths at floor level and inspect the maze for pinch points and trip hazards before each round.
If a charged line is used, control the nozzle to prevent accidental discharge into the obscured firefighter; verify bale is closed and secured at the start of every round.
success_criteria: Firefighter verbally recognizes disorientation and stops forward motion before the instructor prompts them.
Coupling read produces the correct egress direction on the first attempt in at least 8 of 10 scenario reps across the crew.
Firefighter maintains continuous hand contact with the line from read to exit with no lost-line events.
Radio transmission includes location reference and air status and is completed before the firefighter reaches the exit.

variations.adds: Trains recognition and decision-making under real air consumption and elevated heart rate, when fine judgment degrades first.

variations.name: Broken Line
variations.description: Introduce a section where the line ends unexpectedly (uncoupled or nozzle with no continuation) forcing the firefighter to transition from line-follow to wall-follow mid-egress.

variations.name: Two-In Buddy Egress

variations.adds: Trains team reorientation and shared decision-making so one member's correct coupling read is communicated and trusted by the other.

variations.name: Photo/Tabletop Recognition

variations.adds: Builds the recognition and decision framework for crews without maze access, reinforcing the mental model before the physical skill.

lodd_connection.lesson: A recurring pattern in interior line-of-duty deaths is a member who becomes disoriented, continues to work instead of recognizing and reporting it, and loses the hoseline as their reference — this drill attacks the recognition and decision-timing failure directly.

drills.title: Blind Pack Check: Find Every Control by Touch
drills.objective: Seated and gloved with eyes closed, locate and correctly operate 8 named SCBA controls by touch — cylinder valve, bypass, purge/donning valve, regulator release, PASS manual activation, waist buckle, shoulder strap adjusters, and the emergency/buddy-breathing fitting if equipped — calling each aloud, with 8 of 8 found in under 60 seconds total and zero misidentifications.
equipment: Personal SCBA, air off, cylinder pressurized or empty per department practice
Index cards, one control named per card (improvised: a written list read aloud into a voice memo and played back)
Portable radio or phone voice recorder for self-scoring the call-outs
Cleared apparatus bay floor or a chair/mounted seat bracket
drills.setup: Stage the SCBA the way you actually carry it — seat-mounted bracket if your rig has one, otherwise flat on the bay floor next to a chair. Shuffle the index cards face down so the order of controls is random each round. Vision is restricted by eyes closed only, seated or kneeling and stationary — no blackout hood and no walking, so the drill stays safe for one member alone in the bay.
steps: Don full PPE and SCBA off air, gloved, and seat yourself as if riding in.
Start the recorder, draw the top index card, read it aloud, then close your eyes and start the timer.
Locate the named control by touch alone, say its name and what it does out loud, and demonstrate the operating motion — open/close, depress, release, or unbuckle — without opening your eyes.
Open your eyes only to draw the next card; repeat until all 8 cards are done, then stop the timer and log the total.
Play the recording back and mark any control you named wrong, hunted for more than 10 seconds, or operated in the wrong direction.
Run the deck twice more; the third round is the scored run.
Finish by writing the two slowest controls on a card and taping it inside your locker as next shift's target.
learning_points: In smoke you will never see your own pack — every control you find only by looking is a control you cannot use when it matters, and the search burns air you were already short of.

Bypass is the one control most firefighters have never touched under stress; a free-flowing or failed regulator is survivable only if your hand goes to bypass without thinking, because you are metering your own air by feel while you exit.
Gloved hands lose most of your fine touch. Practicing bare-handed builds a false map — the strap tab you can pinch with skin may be invisible through a structural glove.
Saying the control's function out loud forces recall of the procedure, not just the location; knowing where purge is does not help if you cannot say what it does to your air supply.
Repeatable timed reps alone in quarters are how this becomes reflex — component familiarity decays fast between annual checkouts.
common_mistakes: Cheating the eyes closed — peeking to orient before reaching. Recording your call-outs will not catch it, so keep your head down and hands moving only after your eyes shut.
Finding the control but never operating it, so the motion is never learned; touching the cylinder valve is not the same as knowing how many turns it takes and which way.
Practicing bare-handed 'because gloves make it hard' — that difficulty is the entire point of the drill.
Learning one hand only. On the fireground the other hand may be on a line, a tool, or a downed member.
Naming controls with department slang that does not match the manufacturer's manual, which makes the skill useless when you are on a different pack at a mutual-aid incident.
safety_notes: Vision is restricted by eyes closed while seated or kneeling and stationary. Do not walk, climb, or use a blackout hood alone — if you want an obscured-vision version, a second member must be present within arm's reach with an agreed stop signal ('STOP DRILL' called aloud).
Keep the bay floor cleared of hose, tools, and cords before starting; a stationary drill still ends with a gloved member standing up with restricted orientation.

Follow your department's practice on cylinder pressure for in-quarters handling, and if you open the cylinder valve at any point, close and bleed it before returning the pack to service-ready condition.
success_criteria: All 8 named controls located and operated by touch with eyes closed, gloved, in under 60 seconds total on the scored round.
Zero misidentifications on playback — every control named is the control touched.
No single control takes longer than 10 seconds to find on the scored round.
Pack is returned to ride-ready condition — straps extended, valve position and pressure per department practice — before the drill is logged complete.

variations.name: Weak-hand only
variations.description: Run the full deck using only the non-dominant hand; the dominant hand stays tucked in the SCBA waist strap the whole round.
variations.adds: Trains the pack map on the hand that is free when your good hand is committed to a hoseline, a tool, or dragging a member.

variations.name: Post-exertion reps
variations.description: Immediately before the scored round, do 60 seconds of stair climbs or a hose bundle carry to raise heart and respiratory rate, then sit and run the deck.
variations.adds: Shows how much fine motor location degrades under load, which is the only state you will ever actually need this skill in.

variations.name: Different pack
variations.description: Run the deck on a reserve or mutual-aid SCBA of a different make or generation than your assigned pack.
variations.adds: Builds the habit of orienting to an unfamiliar pack by function rather than by memorized position — the situation at a mutual-aid or spare-rig assignment.

variations.name: Doffed-pack version
variations.description: Start with the SCBA on the floor rather than worn, and find each control on the loose pack before donning it.
variations.adds: Covers the case where you are working on someone else's pack — a downed member's cylinder valve or a partner's bypass — where the geometry is reversed.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH firefighter fatality investigation reports document members who ran out of air or died with SCBA malfunctions or misused controls, with recommendations centering on SCBA familiarity, emergency procedure training, and regular hands-on proficiency
lodd_connection.lesson: The recurring finding is not exotic equipment failure — it is members who could not operate their own air supply under stress. Component familiarity by touch is the countermeasure, and it is trainable alone in quarters.

IFSTA Essentials of Fire Fighting — self-contained breathing apparatus chapter (donning, inspection, emergency operations)
Department SCBA inspection and daily-check SOP
drills.solo_note: Built for one member alone in quarters: index cards randomize the order, a phone timer scores it, and a recorder replaces the observer checking call-outs.

drills.title: Air Emergency Call-Out: Recorded Recall Under 10 Seconds
drills.objective: Drawing an air-emergency card at random, begin the correct first action aloud within 10 seconds and state a complete response — problem, immediate action, air plan, and radio traffic — for 6 of 6 cards, self-scored from the recording against a written key.
equipment: Full structural PPE and SCBA worn off air
Portable radio (turned to a training channel or off) or a phone voice recorder
Index cards — one air emergency per card
Phone timer with a visible second hand or stopwatch
A written answer key the member builds first from the SCBA manual and department SOP
drills.setup: Before any reps, build the answer key: open your SCBA manufacturer's emergency procedures and your department's SCBA and mayday SOPs, and write the correct response for each of six events on the back of its card — regulator free-flow, regulator failure/no air on demand, low-air alarm activation, facepiece lens damage, cylinder valve found partly closed, and hose/coupling or air-line separation between regulator and facepiece. The radio phrasing and channel used here are examples only: substitute your department's mayday and emergency-traffic procedure before running this drill.
steps: Don full PPE and SCBA, air off, and stand in a cleared area of the bay with the recorder running.
Shuffle the cards face down, draw one, and start the timer as you flip it.

Speak and physically begin the first action within 10 seconds — hand to the control you would use, body oriented the way you would move — then talk through the full response: what is wrong, what you do to the pack, what your remaining air means for your exit, and the exact radio traffic you would transmit.
Transmit that radio traffic into the recorder or the training-channel radio in the voice and pace you would actually use, not a summary of it.
Stop the timer, set the card aside without checking the key, and draw the next until all six are done.
Play the recording back with the answer key in hand and score each card pass/fail on four points: first action within 10 seconds, correct control, air/exit decision stated, radio traffic complete.
Rebuild the deck with your failed cards doubled and run it once more.
learning_points: An air emergency gives you seconds, not minutes, and the first move is the one that decides the outcome — rehearsing the decision out loud is what makes it available when your heart rate is 170 and you cannot see your own hand.

Naming the problem before acting is what stops the wrong fix: a free-flow and a no-air regulator feel like opposite emergencies but both send your hand toward the same area of the pack, and doing the wrong one wastes the air you were trying to save.
Every air emergency is also an exit problem. If your response ends at the pack and never states how much air is left and which way you are going, you have practiced half of it.

Radio traffic degrades badly under stress — members swallow words, forget their unit, or transmit a problem without a location. Recording yourself is the only way to hear what a caller actually sends.
Scoring against a written key you built from the manual keeps the drill honest; recall drills without a key reward confidence rather than accuracy.
common_mistakes: Talking through a smooth answer that never starts a physical action — the hand stays down while the mouth solves it, which is not how it happens in a building.
Summarizing the radio traffic ('then I'd call a mayday') instead of transmitting the actual words, which is the part that fails in practice.
Building the answer key from memory or from what someone said at a class, rather than from the pack manual and the department SOP.
Scoring generously on playback — counting a partially correct control or a mayday missing location as a pass.
Skipping the air and egress half of the answer, so the member trains a repair reflex without an exit decision.
safety_notes: SCBA is worn off air throughout — never restrict air, defeat a regulator, or remove the facepiece to simulate a malfunction; the failure is described on the card, not created on the equipment.
If a portable radio is used, confirm it is on a designated training channel or powered off so no simulated emergency traffic reaches a dispatch or operational channel.
Full PPE in a warm bay for 35 minutes carries real heat stress even without air — take the hood and gloves off between rounds and keep water at hand.
success_criteria: First physical action begins within 10 seconds on 6 of 6 cards, timed with a stopwatch.
Recording shows the correct control named and reached for each card when checked against the written key.
Every card's response includes both an air/exit decision and complete radio traffic containing unit identifier, location, and problem.
The answer key is written from the pack manual and department SOP before the first rep, not after.

variations.name: Post-exertion draw
variations.description: Do 90 seconds of stair climbs, hose drags, or a bundle carry immediately before drawing each card, so every response is given breathing hard.
variations.adds: Trains recall and radio clarity at the respiratory rate the emergency will actually happen at, where speech and sequencing degrade first.

variations.name: Compound card
variations.description: Draw two cards at once — for example low-air alarm plus lens damage — and require a stated priority order before acting.
variations.adds: Forces triage between simultaneous problems, which is the realistic version and the one members have never rehearsed.

variations.name: Sound-off playback review
variations.description: Replay the recording listening only for the radio transmissions, with the answer key covered, and write down what you can understand from the audio alone.
variations.adds: Reveals how much of the transmission a receiving officer would actually get — the traffic that is clear in your head but unintelligible on the air.

variations.name: Partner-pack card
variations.description: Rewrite three cards so the emergency belongs to another member you have found, not to you.
variations.adds: Shifts the response from self-rescue to assisting another member's air supply, where the controls are reversed and the decision is about moving them, not fixing them.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH firefighter fatality investigation reports document members who experienced air emergencies and either delayed calling for help or transmitted incomplete emergency traffic, with recommendations addressing SCBA emergency procedures and prompt, complete mayday transmission
lodd_connection.lesson: The pattern is delay and incomplete information, not lack of courage. Rehearsing the first action and the exact words — out loud, on a clock — is what shortens both.
