IFSTA Essentials of Fire Fighting — SCBA emergency operations and firefighter survival chapters
Department SCBA emergency and mayday/emergency-traffic SOPs (operator-provided)
NIOSH Fire Fighter Fatality Investigation and Prevention Program reports (pattern-level use only)
drills.solo_note: Fully solo: cards supply the randomness an instructor would, the recorder plus a written answer key replaces the evaluator, and a phone timer scores the 10-second window.

drills.title: Profile Reps: Pack Shift to a Taped Standard, Solo
drills.objective: Working alone at ground level, complete 10 consecutive passes through a taped and cone-marked opening — 5 low-profile with the pack on and 5 reduced-profile with one shoulder strap off and the pack shifted — averaging under 30 seconds per pass with the facepiece seal and regulator connection undisturbed on every rep.
equipment: Full structural PPE and SCBA worn off air, facepiece donned with regulator attached
Floor tape or chalk to mark the opening footprint
Two cones, two folding chairs, or a ground ladder laid flat and a pike pole to form an adjustable-height bar (improvised: two hose rollers or a spanner rack)
Index cards to log each rep's time
Cleared apparatus bay or driveway with a smooth, dry surface
drills.setup: Tape a rectangular opening on the bay floor and build a height bar over it from cones and a pike pole so the clear height can be lowered in 3-inch steps. No wall prop, no breaching, no entanglement material and no confined space — this is repetition practice for the movement itself, at ground level, where a single member can run it safely. Starting dimensions are an example: set the first height at roughly the depth of your pack on your back plus a hand's width, then lower it as reps get clean.
steps: Don full PPE and SCBA off air with the facepiece sealed and the regulator connected, exactly as you would work.
Set the bar at the starting height and run 5 low-profile passes with both straps on — head and one arm through first, body flat, pack rotated to clear — logging each time on a card.

Lower the bar 3 inches and run 5 reduced-profile passes: release one shoulder strap, slide the pack off that shoulder while keeping the regulator connected and the facepiece sealed, drive through, then recover the strap and reseat the pack on the far side before stopping the timer.
After every pass, check the facepiece seal with a hand and confirm the regulator is still locked in — log any rep where either was disturbed as a failed rep regardless of time.
Lower the bar another 3 inches and repeat only if all 10 reps were clean; a failed rep means the height stays where it is.
Finish by writing your average time, your lowest clean height, and the one thing that snagged most often on the card for next shift.
learning_points: The reduced-profile move is only useful if the facepiece stays sealed and the regulator stays connected — a member who clears the opening but breaks their air connection has traded a tight space for an air emergency in the same second.

Reps are what make this work under stress. This movement is not hard to understand and is very hard to do smoothly the first time in the dark, which is why the drill scores repetition and consistency rather than a single heroic pass.

Recovering the pack on the far side is part of the skill and the part usually skipped. A member who arrives through the opening with a strap trailing loose has created the snag that catches on the next obstacle.

Working at ground level with the bar lowered in small steps builds an honest picture of your own profile — most members overestimate what they can fit through and discover the truth in a place where discovering it is expensive.
Doing this dry and off air first is what makes it safe to do later on air with a crew; the technique should be boring before the environment gets hard.
common_mistakes: Breaking the regulator connection or the facepiece seal to make the pass easier — that is not a faster rep, it is a failed rep, and it trains a habit that kills.
Releasing both shoulder straps and pushing the pack ahead like a bag, which surrenders control of the air supply and is a much harder move to reverse in a tight space.
Stopping the timer on the far side of the opening before the strap is recovered and the pack reseated, so the recovery half is never actually trained.
Chasing a lower bar height before the reps are clean; the drill's progression is clean-then-lower, not lower-then-struggle.
Running the drill in station uniform rather than full PPE, which changes both the profile and the friction and makes the logged times meaningless.
safety_notes: Ground level only, with full vision — no blackout hood, no elevated prop, no entanglement material, and no confined space when running this alone.
The improvised height bar must rest loose so it falls free if struck; never fix, clamp, or wedge it in place where it could trap a member driving through the opening.

Check the floor before you start and stop when conditions turn: wet, oily, seams or drains underfoot, and the heat and CO2 load of a sealed facepiece with no air moving. Break the seal and rest rather than pushing through either.
success_criteria: 10 of 10 passes completed with facepiece seal and regulator connection intact, confirmed by hand check after each rep.
Average pass time under 30 seconds across the 10 logged reps, timed with a stopwatch.
On every reduced-profile rep, the strap is recovered and the pack reseated on the far side before the timer stops.
Bar height is lowered only after a fully clean set — the log shows no height change following a failed rep.

variations.name: Weak-side pass
variations.description: Run the reduced-profile set releasing the opposite shoulder strap from your usual side.
variations.adds: Removes the choice of side, which the building will also remove — the opening's geometry decides which shoulder comes off, not your preference.

variations.name: Tool in hand
variations.description: Carry a hand tool through every pass; the tool must arrive on the far side with you and never be left behind or thrown ahead out of reach.
variations.adds: Trains the real problem of moving through a restriction without abandoning the tool you will need to get out the other end.

variations.name: Fatigued set
variations.description: Precede each set with 60 seconds of stair climbs or a hose bundle carry so all reps are run breathing hard.
variations.adds: Exposes how technique collapses under load — the point where members start yanking straps and breaking the regulator connection.

variations.name: Supervised low-light version
variations.description: With a second member present within arm's reach and an agreed 'STOP DRILL' signal, repeat the clean set with the facepiece lens obscured.
variations.adds: Moves the technique from visual to tactile, which is the condition it is actually needed in — and it requires a second person, so it is not a solo option.

references: IFSTA Essentials of Fire Fighting — firefighter survival and SCBA emergency operations chapters
Department firefighter survival / self-rescue training program outline (operator-provided)
SCBA manufacturer's user manual for correct strap and regulator handling on the issued pack
drills.solo_note: Runs alone at ground level with full vision: a phone timer scores it and the seal/regulator hand check replaces an observer. The obscured-vision variation is not solo.

drills.title: Mechanical Advantage Systems: 3:1 and 5:1
drills.solo_note: Pair-scale haul with instructor-verified systems, a whistle drill, and rotating members

solo_variant.substitutions: A tyre, a stack of sandbags or a weighted sled replaces the crew-hauled load — light enough that you can hold it on the rope one-handed. Phone on a tripod recording the build replaces the instructor's verification: review it against a printed rigging reference. Phone timer replaces the timed rotation. A trigger release or simply dropping the tail replaces the whistle.
steps: Set a ground-level haul lane in the yard: rated anchor (apparatus point or engineered anchor) at one end, light load 50 ft away. No elevation, no drop, nothing overhead.
Dump the hardware in an unsorted pile. Start the timer and the camera.
Build a single-point anchor with a load-sharing backup. Say the anchor evaluation out loud to the camera — bombproof or built, and why.
Build the 3:1 Z-rig. Trace it by hand, physically following the rope, stating the force on each leg aloud.
Add progress capture. Stand outside the fall line of the rope, never step over it, and haul the light load until the pulleys stack. Reset and haul again.
Drop the tail with no warning to yourself — the solo whistle drill. Verify the capture holds the load with your hands off the rope.
Convert to 5:1 and haul the same distance. Note rope consumed and effort.

Break it down, reshuffle the hardware, repeat from cold. Then review the video frame by frame against your rigging reference and mark any misdressed pulley, cross-loaded carabiner or backwards prusik.
solo_variant.self_score: Correct 3:1 built from unsorted gear in under 5 minutes, 5:1 under 7 — clock it. Progress capture holds every single time you drop the tail; one slip is a fail, rebuild it. Video review shows no cross-loaded carabiners, no misdressed prusiks. MA traced aloud correctly on playback.
solo_variant.not_covered: Nobody verifies your system before you load it, so keep the load light and stay out of the fall line — this is a competence drill, not a rescue rep. You get no live-load work, no litter tending, no feel for a haul team finding its rhythm, and no second set of eyes, which is the thing that actually catches the fatal rigging error.

drills.objective: Build, explain, and operate 3:1 and 5:1 mechanical advantage systems with proper anchors, progress capture, and edge management — entirely at ground level (no elevation required).
equipment: Load (weighted sled or vehicle in neutral for pulling)
drills.setup: Ground-level haul lane: anchor at one end, load 50 ft away. No height, no location limitations.
steps: Anchor construction: single-point with load-sharing backup; discuss anchor evaluation (bombproof or built).
Build the 3:1 (Z-rig): trace the mechanical advantage by hand — every member physically follows the rope and states the force at each leg.
Add progress capture; haul the load; reset the system when the pulleys collide ('stack').
Convert 3:1 to 5:1; feel the difference in effort and rope consumed per foot of movement.
Whistle drill: at a random whistle, everyone off the rope — verify the progress capture holds.
Rotate every member through building the system from a pile of unsorted hardware, timed.
learning_points: Mechanical advantage is a trade: force reduced, rope and time multiplied — system choice matches the problem.
The progress capture is the safety of the whole system; the whistle drill proves it, not assumes it.
System building from unsorted hardware is the real test — organized kits hide skill gaps.
Ground-level haul lanes remove the excuse: rope competence doesn't require a cliff.
common_mistakes: The system is built without a progress-capture, so the load slips every time the haul is reset.
Members can build from an organized, pre-sorted kit but not from a pile of unsorted hardware.
The actual mechanical advantage is misstated because the rope legs were never traced.
safety_notes: No live loads (people) until systems are instructor-verified.
Gloves for hauling.
Inspect all software/hardware before sessions.
success_criteria: Correct systems built under 5 minutes from unsorted gear
MA correctly traced verbally
Progress capture holds on the whistle

variations.name: Low-Angle Evacuation
variations.description: Attach a stokes with a packaged manikin; haul team plus litter tenders move it up an embankment or stairwell.
variations.adds: The most probable real-world rope call for most departments.

variations.name: Piggyback System
variations.description: Add a 3:1 piggyback onto a loaded main line.
variations.adds: Converting a lower to a raise mid-operation.

references: NFPA 2500 (1006/1670 content)
Department rope rescue SOPs
drills.prerequisites: Ground-level, no-live-load rigging practice is appropriate at the Operations level in most jurisdictions. Anchor rating, live-load authorization, and who may verify a system before weight goes on it are set by your AHJ and rope SOP — confirm both before the session. Note that the Low-Angle Evacuation variation leaves this drill's ground-level scope and is technician-level in many jurisdictions.

drills.title: Patient Packaging & Litter Management
drills.solo_note: Litter carry needs 4-6 bearers, a caterpillar pass line, and a patient reporting jolts
drills.objective: Package a patient in a stokes basket with correct harness/lashing, manage the litter over ground obstacles, and execute a caterpillar pass line.
equipment: Obstacle course (stairs, narrow gate, rough ground)
drills.setup: Packaging station plus a 100 ft movement course with obstacles. No special location required.
steps: Package: padding, patient harness or lashing per SOP, feet-toward-downhill orientation, airway visible and accessible.
Verify: lift one end 45 degrees — patient must not shift.
Litter carry with 4-6 bearers, rotating positions, communication cadence ('step up,' 'gate ahead').
Caterpillar pass: bearers form a corridor and pass the litter hand to hand over an obstacle without walking it.
Stair descent: controlled, feet first, with a belay conversation (when is a rope required?).
Live-patient round (packaged loosely for comfort): the 'patient' reports every jolt — teams learn what rough handling feels like.
learning_points: Packaging quality is tested by tilt, not by looks — the 45-degree check is the standard.
Litter work is a communication drill; silent teams drop corners and wrench backs.
The caterpillar pass solves obstacles that carrying cannot, with less injury exposure.
A conscious patient's experience matters — the live round builds handling empathy no manikin teaches.
common_mistakes: Packaging is judged by looks instead of the tilt test, and the patient shifts on the first lift.
Litter bearers go silent, drop corners out of sync, and wrench the patient and their own backs.
Stair or slope descent starts without deciding whether a belay line is needed.
safety_notes: Lift mechanics brief.
Live patients only on flat, low sections.
success_criteria: Packaging passes the tilt test
Course completed without patient shift
Clean caterpillar pass

variations.name: Wide-Area/Trail Scenario
variations.description: Quarter-mile carry with terrain.
variations.adds: Endurance and rotation planning for wilderness-adjacent districts.

references: NFPA 2500
Department EMS packaging protocols

drills.title: Vehicle Extrication: Stabilization Through Dash Displacement
drills.solo_note: An officer states the plan while a crew stabilizes and runs hydraulic tools with a sharps watch
drills.objective: Complete a full extrication sequence on an acquired vehicle: scene control, stabilization, glass management, door removal, roof considerations, and dash displacement.
drills.setup: Vehicle on wheels for round one. Junkyard partnerships or tow companies are the standard source. Manikin as the trapped patient.
steps: Inner/outer circle survey: hazards, patient count, entrapment assessment, and the officer's extrication plan stated aloud.
Stabilize: step chocks/cribbing at four points, deflate or crib to steel per SOP; verify no vehicle movement.
Battery/hybrid check: locate 12V and high-voltage components; announce isolation steps.
Glass management with patient protection in place.
Door pop: create purchase, spread hinges or latch per damage pattern; take the door fully away.
Dash displacement: relief cuts and dash roll/lift, with cribbing following every inch of lift. Package and remove the manikin.
learning_points: The plan comes before the first tool — 'peel the car away from the patient' is a sequence, not a swarm.
Cribbing follows lift, always: space created and not captured is space that can collapse on rescuers.
Modern vehicles change everything: high-strength steel relocates cut points, EVs relocate hazards — car-by-car size-up is mandatory.
Patient contact and protection is a dedicated assignment from the first minute.
common_mistakes: Tool work starts before the vehicle is stabilized, so the car moves on the patient and rescuers.
Cribbing does not follow the lift, leaving a gap the vehicle can drop back into.
Crew runs a memorized routine without a car-by-car size-up, missing high-strength steel and EV hazards.
safety_notes: Full PPE with eye protection.
EMS/airbag standoff distances respected on undeployed systems.
Sharps management on every cut edge.
success_criteria: Vehicle stabilized (zero movement) before tool work
Door and dash evolutions completed
Cribbing followed all lifts
Patient 'removed' without contact with cut edges

variations.name: Vehicle on Its Side
variations.description: Same objectives with the vehicle on its side; buttress stabilization first.
variations.adds: The geometry change that defeats crews who only train on wheels.

variations.name: Under-Ride/Pinned Scenario
variations.description: Vehicle positioned under a larger prop or against an object.
variations.adds: Lift decisions: struts, airbags, and when extrication becomes heavy rescue.

variations.name: EV Scenario Overlay
variations.description: Run the sequence narrating an EV: isolation procedure, thermal runaway signs, and fire attack implications.
variations.adds: The growing hazard class most crews haven't touched.

references: NFPA 2500 vehicle rescue chapters
Manufacturer emergency response guides
drills.prerequisites: Vehicle rescue at the Operations level per NFPA 1006. The under-ride variation crosses into heavy rescue: strut and lift-bag operations are technician-level in most AHJs — run that variation as a decision exercise unless your crew holds that authorization. Settle the deflate-versus-crib-to-steel question from your SOP before the drill starts, not during it.

drills.title: Confined Space Permit & Attendant Discipline
drills.solo_note: The permit is completed as a team; a facilitator throws distractions during the attendant round

solo_variant.substitutions: Tape a space outline on the apparatus bay floor — no entry, none needed, and none permitted here. A duffel of gear or a rescue manikin replaces the member on the retrieval line. Phone alarms at random intervals replace the facilitator's distractions during the attendant round. Blank permit forms and a meter with sampling pump and tubing; you sign every line yourself.
steps: Tape the outline of a vault or tank on the bay floor and write the scenario on a card: worker down, unknown atmosphere, your first-due assignment.
Classify the space out loud and state why the majority of confined-space fatalities are would-be rescuers.
Run stratified sampling with the pump and tubing — top, middle, bottom of the proxy space, allowing full purge time between each. Record the readings and interpret against entry criteria.
Complete the entry permit line by line, out loud, treating every line as a hazard-control decision. No blanks, no N/A you cannot defend.
Rig the retrieval system on the tripod or simulated anchor, attach the duffel or manikin, and demonstrate a full non-entry retrieval. Nobody goes on the line but the dummy.

Solo attendant round: set six random phone alarms over ten minutes. Each time one fires, you must be able to state the entrant's location, elapsed time and last communication without looking anything up.

Decision round: rewrite the card to non-permissible atmosphere, victim status unknown. Talk the go/no-go into a recorder — ventilation options, PPE limits, non-entry retrieval, and your mutual-aid answer with the actual unit name and phone number.
Never enter the taped space. The tape is the whole point.
solo_variant.self_score: Permit complete with no undefendable line. Stratified samples taken with correct purge time at all three levels. Non-entry retrieval functional on the first attempt. Attendant round: six alarms, six correct entrant states — one miss is a fail. Mutual-aid technician resource named with a real number.
solo_variant.not_covered: The attendant round is easy when the distraction is a phone alarm and hard when it is a battalion chief asking you a question — the social pressure that actually pulls attendants off the entrant cannot be simulated alone. You also lose the permit argument, where somebody challenges a line you would have signed without thinking.

drills.objective: Work the confined-space decision sequence without requiring a real space: hazard assessment, atmospheric monitoring, entry permit logic, attendant duties, and retrieval system setup.
equipment: Tripod and retrieval system (or anchor-simulated equivalent)
A 'space' proxy: large culvert section, container, or simply a taped floor plan
drills.setup: This drill is deliberately designed for departments WITHOUT confined-space props — the decision skills transfer from a taped outline; the equipment skills use whatever proxy exists.
steps: Scenario brief: worker down in an underground vault/tank. Group identifies the space classification and why 60% of confined-space fatalities are would-be rescuers.
Atmospheric monitoring: sample at top, middle, bottom of the 'space' with the pump and tubing; interpret against entry criteria.
Complete the entry permit as a team — every line item is a hazard-control conversation.
Set up the retrieval system on the tripod or simulated anchor; attach a member and demonstrate a non-entry retrieval.
Attendant round: one member holds the attendant role while the facilitator throws distractions — the attendant's only job is the entrant.
Decision round: monitoring shows a non-permissible atmosphere and the 'victim's' status is unknown. Walk the go/no-go with brutal honesty about ventilation, PPE, and non-entry options first.
learning_points: Non-entry retrieval is the first-choice rescue, which is why the retrieval line goes on before entry, every time.
The atmosphere at the top of a space says nothing about the bottom — stratified sampling is the discipline.
The attendant who leaves or multitasks is the failure mode in the fatality reports.
Most departments respond TO confined spaces without owning entry capability — knowing your operational level and your mutual aid answer is itself the drill.
common_mistakes: The entrant goes in without a retrieval line rigged for a non-entry rescue.
Atmosphere is sampled only at the top, missing hazards stratified deeper in the space.
The attendant leaves the position or multitasks, losing continuous contact with the entrant.
safety_notes: This drill's design avoids live entry entirely; if using a real training space, full permit process applies for real.
success_criteria: Correct stratified monitoring
Complete, defensible permit
Retrieval system functional
Attendant never abandoned the role

variations.name: Trench Awareness Companion
variations.description: Same tabletop format for trench: soil types, spoil pile distance, protective system recognition, and the make-safe actions before the technical team arrives.
variations.adds: Second location-limited discipline made trainable anywhere.

lodd_connection.incident: NIOSH data has long shown that more than 60% of confined-space fatalities are would-be rescuers who entered after the original victim (NIOSH Alert 86-110)
lodd_connection.lesson: The instinct to go in is the killer. The discipline to monitor, ventilate, and retrieve without entry is what training must overwrite.

references: NFPA 2500 confined space chapters
NIOSH Alert 86-110 (confined-space fatalities)
drills.prerequisites: The decision and permit rounds are Awareness/Operations-level and are the point of this drill. The retrieval-system round is not: rigging a retrieval system and attaching a live person to it is technician-level work per NFPA 1006. If you are a make-safe department, build the system, have it inspected, and attach a weighted load — not a person. Knowing which of those two you are is what this drill is for. Entry criteria come from your AHJ and confined-space program, not from this drill.

drills.title: Trench Collapse: The Disciplined Non-Entry Rescue
drills.solo_note: An officer plus firefighters for the zone, vibration shutdown, and victim contact

solo_variant.substitutions: Spray chalk or cones mark the trench lip and spoil pile - a painted footprint only, never a real excavation. A weighted bag is the buried worker. Phone stopwatch for the 15-minute arrival window. Voice recorder for the size-up and resource order. A clipboard for the atmospheric log. Your own idling small generator or a bucket stands in as the vibration source.
steps: Mark a footprint on a flat training lot: lip line, spoil pile marker on one side, victim marker inside at simulated waist depth. Place the vibration prop nearby. Never use a real excavation, benched or otherwise.
Walk away, start the recorder and the stopwatch, and arrive fresh as if dispatched to a worker trapped.

Do the full 360 on foot, out loud, and record it: lip, spoil side, secondary collapse indicators, access, exposures. Never approach the edge - your standoff distance is your department's, and you hold it.
Establish and physically tape the no-entry zone yourself. Cones and banner tape all the way round. If you cross the lip line at any point, the rep is over.
Shut down the vibration source and say out loud what else you would shut down - apparatus positioning, foot traffic on the spoil side, road traffic - and where you would move the rig to.
Work ground pads from the standoff line toward the lip and stage a ladder for future protected egress, without stepping on bare ground near the edge.

Take a real atmospheric reading with the monitor on its sampling probe or tube from behind the standoff line, and log the value with a time. If your monitor can only sample where it sits, log that as a resource finding and order the capability - do not walk it to the edge.
Establish voice contact with the victim marker from a stable position: talk to them, state your top-side airway and shielding actions out loud.
Run the resource order aloud on the recording: what this company does now, what waits for technicians and protective systems, what you have ordered and the ETA.
Stop the clock. Play the recording back against the success criteria and log the times.
solo_variant.self_score: Zero crossings of the lip line - one foot over and the rep is a failure regardless of everything else. Atmospheric reading logged with a value and a time inside 15 minutes on the stopwatch, taken from behind the standoff line. Recording contains the vibration shutdown, the technician resource order with a stated ETA, and the this-crew-vs-technician split, all spoken.
solo_variant.not_covered: The discipline test is gone. This drill exists because a crew wants to run to the hole, and you cannot rehearse holding people back when there is nobody to hold. No intruder to turn away, no coworker already in the footprint, no firefighter arguing that the victim is right there. It trains your sequence, not your ability to enforce it on other people.

drills.prerequisites: Awareness/Operations-level per your AHJ trench program. Recognition, no-entry zone control, ladder access, atmospheric monitoring, and top-side airway protection are within Operations scope for many programs. Actual entry into an unprotected trench and installation of protective systems are TECHNICIAN-level and are NOT trained or authorized by this drill. Entry criteria — depth thresholds, protective-system requirements, and who may enter — come from your department's own trench program and the AHJ, not from this drill.
drills.objective: Company completes trench size-up and make-safe posture with ZERO personnel entering the trench footprint until protective systems and technician resources are confirmed en route, establishing a marked no-entry zone, ladder egress staged, atmospheric reading logged, and vibration sources shut down within 15 minutes of arrival.
equipment: Marked-out excavation footprint in a training lot or bay (spray-paint or cones simulating the trench lip and spoil pile)
Ladders (for staging near the lip, not for entry)
Cones, banner tape, and scene-control markers
A weighted dummy or marked spot representing a partially buried victim
A prop or bucket representing an idling vibration source (compactor, generator, nearby traffic simulation)
Clipboard/tablet for atmospheric log and resource tracking (taped floor plan acceptable where no lot is available)
drills.setup: Mark a trench footprint on the lot: define the lip line, place a spoil pile marker on one side, and place the victim marker inside the footprint at simulated waist depth. Position an 'idling equipment' prop nearby to be discovered and shut down. Distances, no-entry zone size, and depth thresholds used here are examples — substitute your department's trench program values before running this drill.
steps: Dispatch the company to a 'worker trapped, trench collapse' and time from arrival. Officer conducts a windshield and 360 size-up on foot, identifying the lip, spoil pile side, and any secondary collapse indicators without approaching the edge.

Officer declares the hazard zone and assigns a firefighter to establish and physically enforce a no-entry zone using tape/cones, keeping all personnel back from the lip (use your department's standoff distance as the example).
Assign a firefighter to shut down or direct shutdown of all vibration sources — the idling prop, nearby apparatus positioning, and foot traffic on the spoil side — and report completion.

Place ground pads from the standoff line and work them toward the lip to distribute load, and stage a ladder for future protected egress — nobody advances on bare ground near the edge, and no one steps into the footprint. Take and log an atmospheric reading using the monitor's sampling probe or tube, lowered into the trench from behind the standoff line: obtaining the reading must never require a member to stand at the lip. If your monitor can only sample where it sits, that is a real resource finding — record it and order the capability with the technician resources rather than walking the monitor to the edge.

Establish verbal contact with the victim from a stable position, begin top-side airway/exposure protection (voice reassurance, shielding from further spoil, oxygen if reachable from outside), and confirm the victim's condition and position.

Officer runs a resource-order round out loud: identify what THIS company can do now versus what waits for the technician team and protective systems, and confirm the trench-rescue resources ordered with ETA.
Run a mid-drill decision injection (see decision rounds) and hold a safety pause, then conduct the after-action debrief on hazard recognition and discipline.
learning_points: The second collapse kills rescuers — most trench fatalities include would-be rescuers who entered an unprotected trench. Naming that failure out loud is the point of this drill; speed toward the victim without protective systems is not heroism, it is the mechanism of a double fatality.

The spoil pile and the lip are the two most dangerous edges — surcharge load and edge failure drive secondary collapse, so load distribution with ground pads and standoff distance directly buy the buried worker time.
Vibration and traffic transmit energy into the trench walls — shutting down compactors, backing off apparatus, and stopping foot traffic on the spoil side reduces the force loading a failing wall.

Atmosphere in a trench can be a silent killer — heavier-than-air gases and displaced oxygen collect low; a reading logged from the edge tells you whether the victim is fighting the soil, the air, or both.

A company that cannot enter still saves lives — establishing the no-entry zone, protecting the airway from the top, and getting technician resources rolling is the highest-value work available and must be treated as a success, not a holding pattern.
common_mistakes: A firefighter drifts to the lip to 'get a better look' or to reach the victim, loading the exact edge most likely to fail.
The no-entry zone is taped but not enforced — nobody is assigned to physically turn people back, so bystanders or crew cross it.
The crew fixates on the victim and forgets to shut down the vibration source that is actively threatening a secondary collapse.
Officer treats non-entry as failure and pushes for premature action instead of confidently running the make-safe and resource-order sequence.
Ground pads and ladders get staged for entry instead of for load distribution and future protected egress, signaling an intent the crew is not equipped or trained to fulfill.
safety_notes: No personnel enter the marked footprint at any point in this drill — the footprint is a no-go zone for training as it would be on scene; instructor stops any evolution the moment a foot crosses the lip line.

If a real excavation or acquired site is used instead of a painted footprint, it must be inspected, benched or shored, and cleared by a qualified person before ANY approach — do not improvise an actual trench for training.
Air monitor must be bump-tested and calibrated before use so trainees practice reacting to a real, trusted reading.
success_criteria: Zero personnel cross the marked lip line into the footprint for the entire evolution.
No-entry zone is taped AND has an assigned enforcer who turns back at least one instructor-played intruder.
Atmospheric reading is obtained remotely from behind the standoff line — no member stands at the lip to get it — and is logged with a value and time within 15 minutes of arrival.
Vibration source is identified and shut down, and technician-level trench resources are ordered with a stated ETA, both verbalized by the officer.

variations.name: Multiple Victims, One Visible
variations.description: Add a second buried victim marker not initially visible; a coworker on scene reports 'two guys were down there.'
variations.adds: Trains the officer to resist committing to the visible victim and to size the incident and resource order to the true problem, not the obvious one.

variations.name: Deteriorating Atmosphere
variations.description: Instructor feeds a dropping oxygen / rising gas reading during the drill after the blower is staged.
variations.adds: Forces the ventilation and top-side protection decision and reinforces that the atmospheric picture changes over time, not just at arrival.

variations.name: Well-Meaning Coworkers Already Entered
variations.description: Start the scenario with a role-player 'coworker' standing in the footprint trying to dig the victim out.
variations.adds: Trains the hardest real decision — extracting untrained rescuers from the danger zone without adding another entry and without escalating the collapse risk.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH Fatality Assessment and Control Evaluation (FACE) reports document trench-collapse deaths, including secondary collapses that kill would-be rescuers
lodd_connection.lesson: The recurring pattern is untrained entry into an unprotected trench during a rescue attempt; the discipline of a non-entry posture until protective systems are in place is what breaks the double-fatality chain.

references: IFSTA Trench Rescue / Technical Rescue for Structural Collapse principles (Awareness/Operations level)
NIOSH FACE program trench-collapse fatality reports (public research)
Department trench-rescue program SOG (operator-provided, AHJ-specific entry criteria)

drills.title: Machinery & Elevator Entrapment: Prove Zero Energy First
drills.solo_note: An officer assigns patient contact and isolation; instructor stops the drill on early contact

solo_variant.substitutions: A de-energized shop prop with a real disconnect - unplugged, breaker off, cord in your hand - or a taped floor plan with labeled energy points if you have no prop. Your own LOTO kit. A weighted bag or a taped mark is the trapped person. Voice recorder for the size-up, the zero-energy announcement and the scope decision. Cribbing and wedges from the rig.
steps: Hard limits: machinery version only. No elevator, no hoistway, no pit, no shaft, no confined space of any kind - that half of this drill is not soloable and you skip it. The prop is de-energized and unplugged before you ever start, and stays that way.

Set the prop with one obvious energy source and one non-obvious one - a second disconnect, a raised load on gravity, a spring, a labeled capacitor, a charged accumulator. Set it, then leave it a day so you are not working from fresh memory.

Start the recorder and arrive. Walk the machine and name every energy source out loud: electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, mechanical/stored, gravity. Say the no-contact order out loud even though you are the only one who could break it.
Talk to the trapped-person marker: state what you would be asking - condition, exactly what is caught, could the machine still cycle - and say you are keeping that contact unbroken.
Locate, isolate, lock and tag every source you named. One isolation point, one key, and the key goes in your pocket and stays there.
Perform zero-energy verification out loud: test-before-touch with your meter or prop, then attempt-to-operate on the dead controls. Announce the verified state to the recorder with the time.
Stabilize the load with cribbing and wedges so nothing can shift, drop, or free-cycle.
Run the scope decision aloud: what you can do now with proven zero energy, what waits for the technician team or the mechanic, and what you have ordered with an ETA.
Only then perform the authorized make-safe action within Operations scope, then call a safety pause.
Play the recording back. Check whether you found the non-obvious source before you touched anything, or after.
solo_variant.self_score: Every energy source you planted is identified, isolated and locked/tagged BEFORE any contact - including the non-obvious one. Zero-energy verification announced on the recording with a timestamp that precedes your first touch on the playback. Key accounted for throughout. Scope decision and resource ETA both spoken aloud.
solo_variant.not_covered: You planted the hidden energy source, so you can never be genuinely surprised by one - the real skill is finding what someone else left live. No patient deteriorating in your ear, no pressure from a crew who want to start cutting. And the entire elevator half of this drill - car movement, counterweights, hoistway and pit atmosphere - is absent, because none of it can be done alone.

drills.prerequisites: Awareness/Operations-level per your AHJ. Lockout/tagout, zero-energy verification, load stabilization, patient contact, and scope-of-work decision-making are within Operations scope for many programs. Complex machine disassembly, hydraulic/pneumatic system intervention, and moving a stalled elevator car are TECHNICIAN-level and/or belong to the elevator mechanic — this drill does NOT train or authorize them. What this crew may do versus what waits for technicians or the elevator mechanic is defined by your department's program and the AHJ, not by this drill.
drills.objective: Company achieves and verifies zero energy state before any contact with the machine/car, applies lockout/tagout with a documented isolation point, stabilizes the load, and establishes continuous patient contact — with the officer correctly declaring the this-crew-vs-technician/mechanic scope line, all before any extrication action is attempted.
equipment: Machinery prop with a visible disconnect/energy source (or elevator prop 'stalled between floors'; taped floor plan with labeled energy points acceptable where no prop exists)
A shoring or panel prop if locally carried
A role-player or marked spot representing the trapped/entrapped person
Meter/glove or test-before-touch prop to represent zero-energy verification
drills.setup: Stage either a machinery prop with a limb-entrapment scenario or an elevator prop stalled between floors with a person inside/partially in the door. Provide at least one obvious energy source and one non-obvious one (e.g., a secondary control circuit, stored hydraulic/spring energy, or a capacitor label). Energy-isolation points, LOTO procedures, and elevator control-room access here are examples — substitute your facility's actual systems and your department's LOTO SOG before running.
steps: Dispatch to 'person caught in machinery' or 'person trapped in elevator between floors.' Officer size-up: identify all energy sources (electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, mechanical/stored, gravity), and assign no contact with the machine/car until zero energy is proven.

Assign a firefighter to establish continuous verbal contact with the trapped person — get their condition, exactly what is caught, and whether the machine could still cycle; keep that contact unbroken through the drill.

Locate, isolate, and lock/tag every energy source; assign one person to control the isolation point and hold the key. Then perform zero-energy verification (test-before-touch / attempt-to-operate on dead controls) and announce the verified state out loud.

Stabilize the load with cribbing, wedges, and shoring prop as applicable so nothing can shift, drop, or free-cycle once work begins; for elevator, address car movement and shaft/pit hazards including atmosphere.

Officer runs the scope-of-work decision round aloud: what can THIS crew do now with proven zero energy versus what must wait for the technician team or the elevator mechanic, and confirm those resources are ordered with ETA.

Execute only the authorized make-safe/relief action within Operations scope (e.g., relieving pressure on an extremity by hand once energy is proven dead), then hold a safety pause before any further action.
Conduct the after-action debrief focused on the zero-energy verification, the isolation-point discipline, and the correctness of the scope decision — not on how fast the person was freed.
learning_points: A machine believed to be off is not proven off — the killer is stored and secondary energy: a capacitor, a spring, a hydraulic accumulator, gravity on a raised load, or a control circuit on a separate disconnect. Test-before-touch is what separates a rescue from a rescuer amputation.

One isolation point, one key, one person — diffuse control of a disconnect means someone can re-energize the machine while a firefighter's hands are inside it; the lock and tag with a single accountable holder is a life-safety control, not paperwork.

An elevator 'stalled' is not a stable elevator — counterweights, brakes, and gravity can move a car; assuming the car is parked when it is only stopped has cost lives, so car and hoistway must be stabilized and controlled before anyone works at the threshold.

Continuous patient contact does two jobs — it manages the trapped person's airway, panic, and shock, AND it gives you a live early warning if the machine shifts or cycles, which the person will feel before you see it.

Knowing what you will NOT do is a skill — the mechanic and technician team exist because moving a car or disassembling a machine wrong makes the entrapment worse; a company that correctly hands off scope prevents a manageable entrapment from becoming a crush injury or fatality.
common_mistakes: Crew hits the obvious disconnect, sees the machine stop, and starts working without proving zero energy — missing stored or secondary energy.
The lockout is applied but no single person owns the key, so control is ambiguous and re-energization is possible.
Someone begins pulling the extremity free before the load is stabilized, so the machine or part shifts and worsens the injury.
Crew treats the stalled elevator car as parked and works the threshold without controlling car movement or checking pit atmosphere.
Officer lets the crew attempt technician/mechanic-level actions (moving the car, deep disassembly) because the person is distressed, instead of holding scope and expediting the right resource.
safety_notes: No hands, tools, or body parts enter the machine's or car's danger zone until zero energy is verified out loud by the assigned person — instructor stops the drill on any early contact.
Cribbing, wedges, and any shoring prop must be inspected before use; do not load a prop beyond its rated or intended training capacity.
For elevator/pit scenarios, treat the shaft and pit as a potential confined space and atmosphere hazard — monitor before committing, and stage a ladder for controlled access/egress.
success_criteria: All energy sources — including at least one non-obvious/stored source — are identified, isolated, and locked/tagged before any contact.
Zero-energy verification (test-before-touch / attempt-to-operate on dead controls) is performed and announced before work begins.
Continuous, unbroken patient contact is maintained from first assignment through the safety pause.
Officer verbalizes a correct this-crew-vs-technician/mechanic scope decision and orders the appropriate resource with an ETA.

variations.name: Hidden Stored Energy
variations.description: The primary disconnect kills the motor, but a raised load / spring / accumulator remains energized; instructor scores whether the crew finds and neutralizes it.
variations.adds: Sharpens the search for stored and gravitational energy beyond the obvious electrical disconnect.

variations.name: Elevator Between Floors, Deteriorating Patient
variations.description: Run the elevator version with a patient reporting worsening chest pain and a pit atmosphere alarm.
variations.adds: Forces the tension between medical urgency and the discipline of not moving the car or committing to the pit before it is controlled and the mechanic is en route.

variations.name: Second Disconnect, Wrong Circuit
variations.description: Provide two disconnects; the labeled one does not control the entrapping component. The machine appears dead but a live circuit remains.
variations.adds: Trains verification over assumption — proving the specific hazard is dead, not just that a switch was thrown.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple OSHA and NIOSH investigations document machinery and elevator entrapment injuries and deaths tied to failure to verify de-energization and to inadvertent re-energization
lodd_connection.lesson: The recurring pattern is contact with a machine or car that was assumed de-energized but never verified, or that was re-energized because control of the isolation point was not maintained; proven zero energy and single-point lockout control break that pattern.

OSHA control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout) general practice (public)
NIOSH FACE machinery-entrapment fatality reports (public research)
Department LOTO and elevator-emergency SOG (operator-provided, AHJ-specific)

drills.title: Oriented Search
drills.solo_note: Oriented search is an officer plus two searchers by definition
drills.objective: Complete a systematic primary search of a multi-room area using the oriented method, with the officer anchored to a reference point and searchers working rooms.
drills.setup: Furnish 3-4 rooms off a hallway. Hide a manikin. Officer plus two searchers.
steps: Brief the method: officer holds orientation at the hallway/doorway, searchers sweep rooms and return to the officer's voice.
Enter, officer establishes the anchor point and directs searchers into the first room.
Searchers sweep the room perimeter and middle, communicate findings, and return to the officer.
Officer advances the anchor to the next doorway; repeat through all rooms.
On victim contact, searchers call it, package, and the team converts to removal.
Debrief: map the search pattern from memory and compare to the actual layout.
learning_points: The oriented officer is the crew's map — searchers can move fast because someone always knows the way out.
Search is a communication drill as much as a movement drill; short, disciplined voice contact.
Room sweeps must include beds (on top and under), closets, and behind doors — where victims are actually found.
Drawing the layout afterward exposes whether the crew searched or just moved.
common_mistakes: The oriented firefighter leaves the wall or reference point, so the team loses its way back out.
The searcher sweeps only the open floor and misses the void spaces where victims are actually found.
Crew loses voice or touch contact in heavy smoke and keeps working as if still together.
safety_notes: Maintain crew integrity — no freelancing beyond voice contact.
Establish an emergency signal to halt the drill.
success_criteria: All rooms searched with no gaps
Victim located and removal initiated
Post-drill layout sketch materially correct

variations.name: TIC-Integrated
variations.description: Officer uses the TIC to direct searchers; then repeat with a simulated TIC failure mid-search.
variations.adds: TIC as a force multiplier — and proof the crew can finish without it.

variations.name: Team Search / Large Area
variations.description: Open commercial floor plan with a search rope.
variations.adds: Rope management, tether work, air discipline in big boxes.

lodd_connection.incident: Worcester Cold Storage (1999) — six firefighters lost in a windowless maze-like commercial building during search
lodd_connection.lesson: Orientation is survival. Large, complex buildings demand rope-based search discipline and ruthless air management.

references: NIOSH F99-47

drills.title: VEIS: Vent-Enter-Isolate-Search
drills.solo_note: Second firefighter heels the ladder and supports the sill; spotter for manikin lifts
drills.objective: Execute a window-initiated search of a target bedroom: ladder placement, controlled entry, immediate door isolation, sweep, and exit or removal.
equipment: Window prop or drill tower window
drills.setup: Second-floor window into a furnished room with a door to a hallway. Manikin in the room. Two firefighters: one enters, one heels the ladder and supports the sill.
steps: Confirm the VEIS assignment and the vent with command before you touch the glass — this window changes fire behavior building-wide. Then size up from the ladder: sound the floor, clear the opening completely.
Enter with control, staying low, and move IMMEDIATELY to locate and close the room door.
Announce door closed, then sweep the room fast — bed first in a bedroom.
On victim contact, move them to the window; sill firefighter assists the lift to the ladder.
If no victim, exit the way you came — the window is your only guaranteed egress.
Rotate positions and repeat on a different room configuration.
learning_points: Isolate is the step that makes VEIS survivable — the closed door removes the room from the flow path.
This is a targeted rescue tactic driven by known or high-probability victim location, not a default search method.
The window firefighter is a rescuer, safety officer, and orientation point in one.
Venting the window changes fire behavior in the building — coordinate with command before initiating.
common_mistakes: Firefighter enters without closing the door to the rest of the structure, letting fire follow the fresh air in.
The window is not fully cleared of glass and sash, snagging the firefighter on entry and exit.
VEIS is run as a default tactic on every job instead of a targeted rescue of a known or likely victim area.
safety_notes: Ladder heeled at all times.
Manikin lifts to a ladder require a spotter until technique is solid.
success_criteria: Door isolated within 15 seconds of entry
Complete room sweep
Controlled victim lift to ladder
Vent coordinated with command before the opening is cleared

variations.name: First-Floor VEIS
variations.description: Same sequence through a ground-floor window.
variations.adds: Higher-frequency variant; still demands door isolation discipline.

variations.name: Manikin Overweight
variations.description: Use a 165+ lb manikin.
variations.adds: Realistic lift mechanics; when to call for a second rescuer.

lodd_connection.incident: Multiple NIOSH reports document firefighter deaths in bedrooms when interior conditions changed before the door was controlled
lodd_connection.lesson: An open interior door puts the searcher in the flow path. Close it first, every time.

references: UL FSRI coordinated fire attack studies

drills.title: Conventional Forcible Entry: Irons Work
drills.solo_note: One on the bar, one striking; verbal strike commands and a position swap

solo_variant.substitutions: Phone on a tripod at 45 degrees to the door, stopwatch running in frame so the time is on the video. Webbing loop tied to the prop handle stands in for the second firefighter controlling the door. Shuffled index cards — inward, outward, lock high, lock low — deal you the setup instead of an instructor calling it.
steps: Inspect the prop and set the resistance you want. Eye protection on, full PPE, gloves on for every rep.
Draw a card. Set the prop to that swing direction and lock position, then step away and reset your feet at the approach.
Start the phone recording with the stopwatch in frame. Size up out loud: swing, lock count, material — say it so the recording captures it.

Gap alone: set the adze or fork at lock level and drive purchase using the halligan against the jamb and your body weight, no striker. If your prop allows a marry, strike with the axe only with your bar hand clear and stated aloud before the swing.
Set past the doorstop for inward, behind the door for outward. Bury the tool.
Force with lean, not yank. Drive from the legs and hips with the bar loaded against your body, not your arms.
The second the lock fails, get the webbing on the knob or handle and control the door closed. Do not let it swing. Stop the clock only when the door is forced AND controlled.
Reset the prop, draw the next card, repeat. Ten reps minimum, alternating swing directions.
solo_variant.self_score: Clock stops on forced AND controlled, not on forced — under 60 seconds is the standard. Review the video: bar hand clear on every strike, tool set past the stop before you loaded it, door controlled inside two seconds. Count reps where the door swung free — that number should be zero.
solo_variant.not_covered: This does not train the striker/bar conversation, which is the actual crew skill: hitting on command only, reading your partner's set, swapping positions mid-door. You also never learn to control a door while a partner is still on the tool. Solo force is a fallback, not the primary method — do not let smooth solo reps convince you your two-person timing is good.

drills.objective: Force inward- and outward-swinging doors with the irons using proper gap-set-force technique and controlled door management after force.
drills.setup: Prop configured for resistance. Two firefighters: one on the bar, one striking.
steps: Size up the door: swing direction, lock count, material, and what the door tells you about conditions inside — and know where the line is, because the door opens when the attack is ready for it.
Gap: set the adze or fork at the lock level, striker drives it to create purchase.
Set: bury the tool past the doorstop (inward) or behind the door (outward).
Force: controlled pressure — 'lean, don't yank' — until the lock fails.
Control the door immediately with webbing or a firefighter; do not let it fly open.
Swap positions; repeat on the other swing direction.
learning_points: Gap-set-force is a conversation between two firefighters — the striker hits on command only.
The door you force is a ventilation opening the moment it fails; control it or you've vented uncoordinated.
Outward doors (commercial) fail differently than inward residential doors — train both.
Tool placement beats muscle: a properly set bar forces with body weight.
common_mistakes: The striker swings before the tool position is announced and confirmed, endangering the firefighter setting it.
Crew muscles the door instead of setting the tool and reading the lock and door swing first.
The door is forced and left uncontrolled, venting the fire and changing conditions on the interior crew.
safety_notes: Striking tool discipline: verbal command before every strike, hands clear.
Eye protection mandatory on the prop.
success_criteria: Door forced in under 60 seconds
Door controlled after force
Clean verbal coordination

variations.name: Single-Firefighter Force
variations.description: One firefighter forces alone using the halligan and body mechanics.
variations.adds: Reality of understaffed companies.

variations.name: Through-the-Lock
variations.description: Pull the cylinder with a key tool follow-up on a lock prop.
variations.adds: Low-damage entry for commercial and multifamily lockouts and fire alarms.

variations.name: Drop Bar / Fortified
variations.description: Prop rigged with a drop bar or secondary devices.
variations.adds: Recognizing and defeating fortified doors; reading resistance feedback.

Department FE prop guidelines

drills.title: Ground Ladder Throws
drills.solo_note: 35 ft two-firefighter flat raise and heeling; throws are timed by someone else

solo_variant.substitutions: Phone on a tripod 30 ft off the wall, wide enough to catch the full ladder and the ground — stopwatch in frame. Chalk or tape marks the 50 ft carry start and the correct butt spread for 75 degrees at your tip height. Voice memo running for the overhead-hazard callout.
steps: Walk the drill area first and identify every overhead hazard — wires, branches, eaves. Mark the raise spots you will actually use.
Set the tripod so both the ladder and the building marks are in frame, stopwatch visible.
Carry the 24 ft from the 50 ft mark: shoulder carry out, suitcase carry back, high-shoulder beam raise into position. Repeat both carries until the transition is clean.

Timed solo throw, 24 ft: from the carry, beam raise against the building, extend the fly per SOP, roll the ladder to the target window. Call the overhead check out loud before every raise — the voice memo is the record.
Set climbing angle: boots at the butt, arms straight out, palms should land on the rung. Check the tape mark for butt spread.
Placement reps: tip at the sill for rescue, tip three rungs above for entry. Say which you are doing before each raise.
Lower under control, return the ladder to the start line, reset. Ten timed throws.
Do not climb. Nobody is heeling and nobody is tying it off. The throw is the drill today.
solo_variant.self_score: Timed 24 ft solo throw from carry start to correct placement, under 60 seconds. Angle checked against the arms-out test and the butt-spread tape mark on every raise. Review the video: count any raise where you did not look up first, and count any tip landing more than one rung off the stated purpose. Both counts should be zero.
solo_variant.not_covered: No two-firefighter 35 ft flat raise, no heeling, no fly-out coordination — that is a timing skill between two people and you have not touched it. No climbing, no sill mount, no manikin down the ladder. This builds your solo 24 ft only. Do not read a good solo time as readiness for the big stick.

drills.objective: Deploy, raise, and place ground ladders (single-firefighter 24 ft; two-firefighter 28-35 ft) to correct climbing and rescue angles.
equipment: Building or drill tower with windows
drills.setup: Apparatus or ladder rack staged 50 ft from the building. Windows marked as targets.
steps: Review carry positions: shoulder carry, suitcase carry, and the high-shoulder beam raise for one firefighter.
Single-firefighter 24 ft throw: carry, beam raise against the building, extend, roll to the window.
Two-firefighter 35 ft: flat raise, extend with fly out per SOP, and lower into the sill.
Set climbing angle (75 degrees — boots at the base, arms out to the rungs) and heel.
Placement drills: tip at the sill for rescue, tip above the sill for access, tip at the roof line for vent work.
Time individual throws; repeat until smooth under 60 seconds for the 24 ft.
learning_points: Ladder placement encodes purpose: sill for rescue, above sill for entry, at roof for work — placement tells the fireground what the ladder is for.
One firefighter CAN throw the 24 ft alone; departments that never drill it default to waiting.
Throwing ladders to every side of the building is firefighter survival infrastructure — ladders are egress.
Overhead hazards (wires) kill during raises — the look-up is part of every throw.
common_mistakes: Firefighter skips the overhead look for wires before raising the ladder into them.
The tip is set at the wrong height for the task (window rescue vs roof access), slowing the operation.
The department only drills two-firefighter throws, so a single firefighter freezes when working alone.
safety_notes: Check overhead before every raise.
Heel or tie every climbed ladder.
success_criteria: 24 ft solo throw under 60 seconds
Correct angle and placement for the stated purpose
Zero overhead-hazard misses

variations.name: Rescue Ladder Climb
variations.description: Climb, mount the sill, and bring a manikin down the ladder with a second firefighter.
variations.adds: The full rescue sequence, not just the throw.

variations.name: Laddering the Building
variations.description: Crew throws ladders to every window/side of a structure against the clock.
variations.adds: Egress-focused truck work supporting interior crews.

lodd_connection.incident: NIOSH reports repeatedly cite absence of ground ladders for egress when interior crews were trapped above grade
lodd_connection.lesson: A thrown ladder nobody uses costs nothing. A missing ladder when a firefighter is at a window costs everything.

references: NFPA 1932

drills.title: Vertical Ventilation Cut Sequence
drills.solo_note: Two cutters, an officer coordinating the vent, and a ladder crew
drills.objective: Perform a coordinated roof operation: sound, cut a 4x4 (or larger) ventilation hole with proper sequence, punch through, and get off the roof.
equipment: Roof ladder and aerial/ground ladder access
drills.setup: Roof prop at ground level for skill acquisition, then elevated per department capability. Two cutters, one officer, ladder crew.
steps: Officer confirms the vent order with interior/command — vertical vent is coordinated or it's freelancing.
Sound the roof moving from the ladder; work from known support (ridge, ladder) toward the cut location over or near the fire.
Cut sequence: top cut, sides, bottom last; never step past the cut line; keep the escape route behind you.
Louver or pull the panel, punch the ceiling below with the hook.
Read the smoke/heat from the hole and report conditions to command.
Exit the roof the way you came. Total roof time is part of the score.
learning_points: The hole means nothing until the ceiling below is punched — the vent must reach the fire compartment.
Roof crews are reading conditions the whole time; spongy roof or fire at the hole means leave now.
Cut sequence is designed so the saw operator never stands on the piece being cut.
Uncoordinated vertical vent can pull fire onto interior crews — the radio call before the cut is non-negotiable.
common_mistakes: Crew cuts the hole but never punches the ceiling below, so heat and smoke never actually vent.
The cut is made without coordination with the attack, pulling fire toward crews instead of lifting it.
Firefighter stands on the panel being cut or on the weak side of the cut, risking a fall through.
safety_notes: Ground-level prop until cut sequence is flawless.
Two means of egress from any elevated roof work.
Saw handling brief before every session.
success_criteria: Correct cut sequence
Ceiling punched
Coordination call made before cutting
Roof time under target

variations.name: Trench Cut Concept
variations.description: Cut a defensive trench on a long narrow prop (strip mall scenario).
variations.adds: Defensive ventilation to stop lateral spread — slow, resource-heavy, decision-focused.

variations.name: Saw Failure
variations.description: Primary saw dies mid-cut; complete with the backup tool.
variations.adds: Contingency habit: two saws or a hand tool goes to the roof.

references: UL FSRI ventilation studies
NFPA 1403 for any live-fire integration

drills.title: Victim Drags & Carries Circuit
drills.solo_note: Paired extremity carry, spotter required on all stair work, per-member logging

solo_variant.substitutions: Phone on a tripod at the doorway pinch with the stopwatch in frame — it is your evaluator for body mechanics. Cones or tape mark the 50 ft drag, the doorway, and the 30 ft hallway. A notes app or paper log replaces the per-member sheet; date every entry so the trend is real.
steps: Back-injury brief with yourself: legs not back, load close, no twisting under load. Say it out loud before you touch the manikin.
Lay the circuit out on one level: 50 ft open drag, doorway pinch, 30 ft hallway, back to start. No stairs.
Set the tripod low so it catches your back angle and hand position through the pinch.
Round one, no SCBA: clothes drag the full circuit. Focus on driving with the legs and keeping the manikin's head off the floor.
Round two: webbing harness drag — loop behind the shoulders and under the arms, drag from the hips. Note how much easier the grip is.
Round three: repeat in full PPE with SCBA on your back, air off, mask off. Watch the technique degrade and correct it in real time.
Time the last two rounds. Log time, technique, and PPE state.
Review the video for back angle and any point you dropped or dragged the head.
solo_variant.self_score: Circuit time logged per round and compared against your own previous sessions — the number has to trend down. Review video: count every rep where your back rounded under load, and count drops or head strikes on the doorway. Both should be zero before you chase speed.
solo_variant.not_covered: No two-rescuer extremity carry — that is a coordination skill you cannot fake alone. No stair descent at all: the crew version puts a spotter on stairs for a reason, and a solo stair drag with a 170 lb manikin is how you end up at the bottom under it. No window lift, no ladder transfer. You have trained drags on the flat, nothing more.

drills.objective: Move a victim manikin using multiple techniques matched to space, distance, and rescuer count: clothes drag, webbing drag, extremity carry, and stair descent.
drills.setup: Circuit: 50 ft open drag, doorway pinch, 30 ft hallway, stair descent (one flight).
steps: Demonstrate each technique fresh: clothes drag, webbing harness drag, two-rescuer extremity carry.
Run the circuit solo with drags only, focusing on body mechanics (legs, not back).
Run it as a pair with the extremity carry and a controlled feet-first stair descent.
Add PPE and SCBA; note the technique degradation and correct it.
Time final rounds; log per-member results for progress tracking.
learning_points: Technique selection is situational: drags for low visibility and low ceilings, carries for speed in clear space.
Stairs are where victim moves fail — control the descent with the rescuer below braking.
Webbing converts an impossible grip into a manageable one; every firefighter should carry a loop.
Fatigue changes everything; the second victim move on a real fire is done exhausted.
common_mistakes: Rescuer lifts from the back and shoulders instead of the legs, gassing out after one drag.
Firefighter drags the victim without controlling the head and airway over thresholds and stairs.
Crew picks a carry that does not fit the exit path, then has to re-package mid-rescue.
safety_notes: Back-injury prevention brief first.
Spotter on all stair work.
success_criteria: Correct technique per station
Circuit completed without dropping the manikin
Improving times across sessions

variations.description: Finish the circuit with a two-rescuer lift of the manikin to a window sill and transfer to a ladder rescuer.
variations.adds: Connects interior search to exterior removal.

variations.name: Firefighter Victim
variations.description: Manikin in full PPE/SCBA (or rescue randy dressed out).
variations.adds: Bridges directly into RIT drag work with the added weight and grab points of PPE.

drills.title: Utility Control & Building Systems
drills.solo_note: The quiz round needs an officer naming utility emergencies

solo_variant.substitutions: Index-card deck replaces the officer's quiz: write one utility emergency per card — gas smell in the basement, arcing service drop, sprinkler flowing, solar array on a working fire, EV or battery storage in the garage. Shuffle and draw. Phone stopwatch for the location times, voice memo for the verbalized action so you can hear whether it was actually correct.
steps: Pick three buildings you have legitimate access to — your own station, your own home, a district building you can lawfully walk the exterior of.
At building one, start the stopwatch and locate the gas meter. Identify the shutoff. Simulate the quarter-turn — hand near the valve, do not operate it. Stop the clock.
Repeat timed for the electrical service (meter and main) and the water shutoff, street side and building side.
Walk the building for solar arrays, rapid shutdown devices, inverters, and battery storage. Photograph what you find on your phone.
Draw a card. Start the voice memo, walk to the correct control point, and state out loud what you would do, in what order, and what you would not touch.
Repeat the card round until the deck is done. Move to the next building and run the whole sequence again.
Play back the voice memos and check your stated actions against your department SOP and the manufacturer guidance for anything solar or battery.
Build a district notes file from the photos: which commercial buildings have disconnects where.
solo_variant.self_score: All three utilities located in under 2 minutes per building, timed. Every solar or battery install on the property photographed — walk it again after and count what you missed. Play the voice memos back against SOP: any card where you stated an action outside your authority or missed the energized-panels point is a fail, redo the card.
solo_variant.not_covered: No live operation of anything, which is correct but means you have never felt a stiff gas valve or a painted-over shutoff. The crew version also gets you an officer's follow-up questions and district knowledge from members who have been there — index cards ask only what you already thought to write down. Your blind spots stay blind.

drills.objective: Locate and control gas, electric, and water utilities on residential and commercial buildings, and identify solar/battery hazards.
equipment: Photos of solar and battery installs
drills.setup: Use the station and district buildings during walkarounds. Never operate live utilities without authorization — simulate the action, verbalize the steps.
steps: Locate the gas meter; identify the shutoff and demonstrate (simulated) quarter-turn to off.
Locate electrical service: meter, main breaker; discuss what suppression crews can and cannot safely disconnect.
Locate water shutoff (street and building side).
Identify solar arrays, rapid shutdown devices, and battery storage locations; discuss why panels stay energized.
Quiz round: officer names a utility emergency, member walks to the control point and states the action.
learning_points: Utility control is often assigned to the least experienced member — make it automatic.
Solar systems remain energized in daylight even after the main is pulled.
Gas gets shut off at the meter, not guessed at inside.
Knowing your district's commercial disconnects before the fire is truck-company intelligence work.
common_mistakes: Gas is guessed at instead of confirmed shut at the meter, leaving fuel feeding the fire.
Crew assumes the solar array is dead after pulling the main, ignoring energized DC on the roof.
Firefighters attempt to cut electrical service that belongs to the utility, creating an electrocution risk.
safety_notes: Simulate only on live systems.
Never cut or pull electrical services — that is the utility's job.
success_criteria: All utilities located under 2 minutes per building
Correct verbalized actions
Solar/battery hazards identified

drills.title: Hydraulic & Coordinated Horizontal Ventilation
drills.solo_note: Attack crew, vent crew, radios, and a pump operator for the charged fog line
drills.objective: Execute coordinated horizontal ventilation: timing window openings with attack, setting up hydraulic ventilation, and positive pressure basics.
drills.setup: Single room-and-hallway layout. Attack crew and vent crew with radios.
steps: Brief the principle: ventilation serves the attack — openings are made when water is ready, not before.
Run the sequence WRONG once (vent before water) with smoke machine to show flow path change; debrief immediately.
Run it right: attack crew calls water on the fire, vent crew opens opposite the attack path.
Hydraulic vent: nozzle fog pattern at a window from 2-4 ft inside, covering ~90% of the opening; measure smoke clearance.
PPV round: fan placement covering the door, confirmed exhaust opening, and water on the fire — the fan spins when the attack is ready, same rule as every other opening.
Debrief with the flow-path drawing: where air entered, where products exited.
learning_points: Every opening is a ventilation decision, made or unmade — doors, windows, and the hole in the roof all count.
Hydraulic ventilation is fast and always available to the nozzle team post-knockdown.
PPV without a confirmed exhaust opening pressurizes the fire.
The wrong-way demonstration teaches flow path better than an hour of lecture.
common_mistakes: A window is opened for ventilation before the attack line has water, feeding the fire instead of relieving it.
The PPV fan is started without confirming an adequate exhaust opening, pressurizing the fire into voids.
Hydraulic ventilation is set with a fog pattern too small for the opening, moving little air.
safety_notes: Smoke machine environments still require respiratory protection per SOP.
PPV never started with crews in an uncontrolled flow path.
success_criteria: Vent timed to attack in all correct-sequence rounds
Effective hydraulic vent setup
Exhaust confirmed before PPV

variations.name: Basement Scenario
variations.description: Discuss and simulate vent decisions for below-grade fires where the stairwell is the chimney.
variations.adds: Highest-risk flow path configuration in residential firefighting.

lodd_connection.incident: NIOSH reports on basement and single-family fires repeatedly identify uncoordinated horizontal ventilation as a contributing factor
lodd_connection.lesson: Air moves fire. Ventilation without water ready is accelerant.

references: UL FSRI horizontal ventilation studies
